205:
The followers of the Asura king Vepacitti are included within the heavenly destination (deva-gati); there is no separate destination called the Asura realm (asurakāya).

Now, to demonstrate this very meaning, the passage beginning with "Nanu Kālakañcikā" (Is it not that the Kālakañcikās...) is undertaken. In that passage, "samānavaṇṇā" (similar appearance) refers to those who have similar physical forms and shapes, which are loathsome, deformed, and ill-favored. "Samānabhogā" (similar enjoyments) refers to those who have similar practices of sexual intercourse. "Samānāhārā" (similar food) refers to those who have similar food such as saliva, snot, pus, and blood. "Samānāyukā" (similar lifespan) refers to those who have similar life spans. "Āvāhavivāha" refers to the taking of a bride and the giving of a bride.

In the bright side (the side of the devas), "samānavaṇṇā" refers to those who have similar physical forms and shapes, which are beautiful, inspiring, lovely to look at, and endowed with radiance. "Samānabhogā" refers to those who have similar enjoyments of the five strands of sensual pleasure. "Samānāhārā" refers to those who have similar food such as sudhā (ambrosia). The rest of the sequence of words is as previously explained. The statement "Is there not an Asura realm?" serves only as evidence for the existence of the Asura realm. However, because that Asura realm is not defined as a separate destination (gati), it does not serve as evidence for it being a destination.

## Commentary on the Discussion of the Six Destinations (Chagatikathāvaṇṇanā).
## 2. Commentary on the Discussion of the Intermediate State (Antarābhavakathāvaṇṇanā).

Now follows the discussion on the intermediate state (antarābhava). In this discussion, those such as the Pubbaseliyas and Sammitiyas, having improperly grasped the scriptural term "antarā parinibbāyī" (one who attains Nibbāna in the interval), hold the view: "There is an intermediate state; in that intermediate state, a being—as if possessing the divine eye or as if possessing psychic power—remains for seven days or more than seven days, awaiting the union of the parents and the mother's fertile period." With reference to them, the question "Is there?" is asked by the Sakavādī (the proponent of the orthodox view), and the Paravādī (the opponent), standing by his own view, affirms it with "There is."

Then, in order to challenge the Paravādī by way of the three states of existence (bhava) taught by the Blessed One, the Sakavādī spoke the words beginning with "Is it the sense-sphere existence (kāmabhava)?" In this passage, the meaning is this: If, according to your wish, there is such a thing as an intermediate state, it must be one of the states of existence such as the sense-sphere existence, just like the five-constituent existence (pañcavokārabhava) and so on. Therefore, I ask you: "Is this intermediate state of yours the sense-sphere existence, or the fine-material existence (rūpabhava), or the immaterial existence (arūpabhava)?" The other party, not desiring it to be so, rejects all of them. The words "kāmabhavassa ca" (and of the sense-sphere existence) etc., mean that if there were an intermediate state, it would be like a boundary interval between two boundaries of these states of existence...
206:
...it is undertaken to challenge that it would be like a boundary interval (sīmantarikā). The Paravādī, however, not desiring it to be so, rejects all questions based solely on his own view and not in accordance with the Dhamma. For that very reason, the Sakavādī rebukes him, saying, "No, indeed, friend!"

Regarding the questions beginning with "Is that the fifth mode of birth (yoni)?", since that intermediate state is not included in the four modes of birth as defined, it is spoken to challenge that if it were so, it would have to be something extra beyond those various defined modes of birth. Regarding the question "Kamma leading to the intermediate state," it is spoken for the purpose of challenging that if that too were a single state of existence, then just as the Teacher has analyzed and shown that there are kammas leading to the sense-sphere existence and so on, there should likewise be kamma leading to that intermediate state. However, since in the opponent's doctrine there is no separate kamma called "kamma leading to the intermediate state," and they hold the view that a being is born in the intermediate state by the very kamma that leads to whichever state of existence they are to be reborn in, it is rejected with "Not indeed."

Even when asked, "Are there beings who have entered the intermediate state?", he rejects it with the view that those beings are simply those who have entered the sense-sphere existence. Even when asked questions such as "Are they born?", he rejects them because he does not desire birth (jāti), aging (jarā), and death (maraṇa), nor the succession of falling away (cuti) and rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi) in that intermediate state. Even when asked by way of the aggregate of form (rūpakkhandha) and so on, he rejects it because his view is that the form of a being in the intermediate state is invisible (anidassana), and the feelings (vedanā) and so on are not gross (oḷārika) like those of other beings. For this very reason, the rejection of it being a five-constituent existence (pañcavokārabhava) should also be understood.

Now occurs the comparison of existences (bhavasaṃsandana) beginning with "Is the sense-sphere existence a state of existence (bhava) or a destination (gati)?" In this, the intention of the Sakavādī is: If, according to your view, there were such a thing as an intermediate state, then just as the distinctions of existence, destination, etc., are found in the sense-sphere existence and so on, they should likewise be found there. Or, just as they are not found there, they should likewise not be found in these [sense-sphere existences, etc.]. Since they are equal in being a state of existence, what is the special reason why this analyzed distinction exists only in these and not in the other? The other party, again, by the power of mere view, both affirms and rejects various points.

When asked, "Do all beings have an intermediate state?", he rejects it because he does not desire an intermediate state for those going to hell (niraya), those going to the realm of unconscious beings (asaññasatta), and those going to the immaterial realm (arūpabhūmi). For that very reason, he affirms it in the reverse (paṭiloma) question. The passage beginning with "For one who has committed a heinous crime (ānantariya)" is spoken to first analyze those persons, such as those who have committed a heinous crime, for whom he does not desire an intermediate state.
207:
It is stated to show by analysis (the persons such as those who have committed an immediate-effective kamma, etc.). All of that should be understood according to the sequence of the Pāḷi text and together with the fulfillment of the Suttas.

## Commentary on Antarābhava-kathā.

## 3. Commentary on Kāmaguṇa-kathā.

Now follows the discussion on the strands of sensual pleasure (Kāmaguṇa-kathā). Therein, first, in our own school (Sakavāda), objective sense-pleasures (vatthukāma), defilement sense-pleasures (kilesakāma), and sensuous existence (kāmabhava) are all called the sensuous element (kāmadhātu). Indeed, among these three types of sensuous elements, objective sense-pleasures are called 'kāma' in the sense of being desired and craved, and they are called 'dhātu' (element) in the sense of being an ultimate reality, not a being, and empty of self; thus they are called 'kāmadhātu'. Defilement sense-pleasures are called 'kāma' both in the sense of being desired and in the sense of desiring, and they are called 'dhātu' in the same sense as previously mentioned; thus they are called 'kāmadhātu'. Sensuous existence is called 'kāma' for three reasons: in the sense of being desired, in the sense of desiring, and in the sense of being the place where objective sense-pleasures occur; it is called 'dhātu' in the same sense as previously mentioned; thus it is called 'kāmadhātu'.

In the view of the opponent (Paravāda), however, relying merely on the statement, "Monks, these are the five strands of sensual pleasure," they hold that only the five strands of sensual pleasure are the sensuous element (kāmadhātu). Therefore, for those who hold this view, such as the Pubbaseliyas at present, the question "Only five?" is the Sakavādī's question to make known the various distinctions of the sensuous element, and the affirmation according to their own view is the opponent's affirmation. The passage beginning with "Nanu atthi" is stated to show defilement sense-pleasures. In that context, "tappaṭisaṃyutto" means connected with the strands of sensual pleasure, having the strands of sensual pleasure as an object. "No ca vata re vattabbe pañceva" means that while these factors such as desire (chanda) connected with the strands of sensual pleasure exist, it should not be said that "only the five strands of sensual pleasure are the sensuous element." Indeed, these factors such as desire are also called 'kāma' in the sense of being desired and are also 'dhātu'; thus they are 'kāmadhātu'. It means they are also called 'kāmadhātu' because they are elements known as 'kāma' in the sense of desiring.

The passage beginning with "manussānaṃ cakkhu" is stated to show objective sense-pleasures. In that context, the opponent, having rejected the non-sensuous element status of the six bases (āyatana) due to their being objective sense-pleasures, again when asked "manas" (mind), affirms that it is not the sensuous element, referring to the sublime (mahaggata) and supramundane (lokuttara) consciousness. Since all mundane consciousness belonging to the three planes is indeed the sensuous element, the Sakavādī refutes the opponent with a Sutta.
208:
The passage beginning with "Kāmaguṇā bhavo" is stated to show that existence is the sensuous element. However, because there is no usage of the term 'existence' (bhava) for the mere strands of sensual pleasure, the opponent (Paravādī) denies it saying, "Not indeed" (naheva). The entire passage beginning with "Kāmaguṇūpagaṃ kammaṃ" is stated to show that the mere strands of sensual pleasure are not the sensuous element. This is because there is only kamma that leads to sensuous existence, which is called the sensuous element, and there are only beings who have reached sensuous existence. It is only in that sensuous existence that beings are born, grow old, die, pass away, and are reborn, not in the strands of sensual pleasure. In this manner, the meaning should be understood in all respects.

## Commentary on Kāmaguṇa-kathā.

## 4. Commentary on Kāma-kathā.

513-514. Now follows the discussion on sensuality (Kāma-kathā). Therein, those such as the Pubbaseliyas, relying merely on the Pāḷi statement, "Monks, these are the five strands of sensual pleasure," hold the view that only the five bases (āyatana) such as the visible-data base (rūpāyatana) are 'sensuality' (kāma). For them, the question "Only five?" is the Sakavādī's question to show that only defilement sense-pleasure is sensuality in the primary sense, and the affirmation is the answer of the other (the opponent). The remaining words here have an obvious meaning.

## Commentary on Kāma-kathā.

## 5. Commentary on Rūpadhātu-kathā.

515-516. Now follows the discussion on the fine-material element (Rūpadhātu-kathā). Therein, referring to the Andhakas who hold the view that "Material things (rūpino dhammā) are called the fine-material element (rūpadhātu)," the question "Are they material things?" is the Sakavādī's question, and the affirmation is the answer of the other. Furthermore, because the fine-material element is indeed fine-material existence (rūpabhava) and not mere matter, the Sakavādī says "Rūpadhātu" and so forth to challenge them with that meaning of fine-material existence. All of that should be understood in the same manner as stated in the discussion on the strands of sensual pleasure. When asked if that fine-material element is the sensuous element, the opponent denies it, seeing the contradiction in terms of the delimitation of the planes of existence. When asked again firmly, he affirms it according to his own view. In that case, it would follow that one is possessed of two existences; therefore, the Sakavādī says "And by sensuous existence" and so forth. The other (the opponent) denies it because one person cannot be possessed of two existences.

## Commentary on Rūpadhātu-kathā.
209:
## 6. Commentary on the Discussion of the Formless Element

517-518. In the discussion of the formless element (arūpadhātu), the meaning should be understood in this very manner. However, among the formless states, taking only the aggregate of feeling (vedanākkhandha), the teaching is presented in this discussion of the formless element by way of "feeling is existence" (vedanā bhavo) and so forth. Therein, the meaning should be understood thus: "Is feeling, which is designated as a formless state according to your view, one among existence and so forth?" The rest should be understood in the manner already stated below.

## Commentary on the Discussion of the Formless Element.

## 7. Commentary on the Discussion of the Bases in the Fine-material Realm

Now follows the discussion of the bases in the fine-material realm (rūpadhātu). Therein, relying on the Sutta, "Possessing form, mind-made, with all limbs and parts, and with unimpaired faculties" (DN 1.87), the Andhakas and Sammitiyas hold the view that for the beings in the Brahma-groups, the physical masses that are the signs and marks of the nose-sensitivity (ghānapasāda) and so forth are also indeed bases (āyatana); thus, their individual existence (attabhāva) possesses the six bases (saḷāyatanika). With reference to those proponents, the question "Does it possess the six bases?" is the Sakavādī’s question, and the affirmation according to their own view is the other's (Paravādī’s) reply.

Thereafter, in order to challenge that opponent regarding the bases such as the nose-sensitivity which do not exist in that fine-material realm, the inquiry "Is there the nose-base (ghānāyatana) there?" and so forth is initiated. Then the opponent, according to their view, affirms that in that fine-material realm, there exists the sign of the shape (saṇṭhānanimitta) of the three internal bases such as the nose, and that very sign of the shape is called a base. When questioned regarding the external bases such as the base of odors (gandhāyatana), they do not wish for the nose-sensitivity and so forth in that Brahma realm; therefore, desiring to deny the objective field of those [sensitivities], they reject it. In the reverse questions and the comparative questions as well, the meaning should be understood in this very manner.

The statement "There is the nose-base there, there is the odor-base, and with that nose one smells that odor" is said with reference to certain teachers even within the view of those opponents. It is said that those teachers desire the six internal bases to be complete in that fine-material realm. Considering that what is called a base must be accompanied by its own function, they also desire that with those [bases] such as the nose, they smell odors, eat, and touch. With reference to that view, the opponent affirms, "Yes".
210:
When questioned with such words as "Is there root-odor (mūlagandha) there?", the opponent rejects it, being unable to establish its existence. The statement "Is there not the sign of the nose (ghānanimitta) there?" and so forth is evidence that establishes only the shape (saṇṭhāna), not the base (āyatana), [specifically the nose-base]. Therefore, even though it is adduced, it is just as if it were not adduced.

## Commentary on the Discussion of the Bases in the Fine-material Realm.

## 8. Commentary on the Discussion that Matter Exists in the Formless Realm

524-526. Now follows the discussion that matter exists in the formless realm (arūpa). Therein, because of the statement "With consciousness as condition, name-and-form [arises]" (viññāṇapaccayā nāmarūpaṃ), those who hold the view—like the Andhakas—that even in the formless existence there is subtle matter (sukhuma-rūpa) which is distinct from gross matter, are referred to. The Sakavādī asks, "Is there matter?" and the other affirms it. The rest of the words in this discussion have a clear meaning.

## Commentary on the Discussion that Matter Exists in the Formless Realm.

## 9. Commentary on the Discussion that Matter is Kamma

527-537. Now follows the discussion that matter is kamma. Therein, those who hold the view—like the Mahīśāsakas and Sammitiyas—that matter known as bodily and vocal intimation (kāyavici-viññatti) is itself called bodily kamma and vocal kamma, and that this kamma is wholesome if it originates from a wholesome mind, and unwholesome if it originates from an unwholesome mind, are referred to. The Sakavādī asks, "Does it originate from a wholesome mind?" and the other affirms it. Thereafter, in order to challenge that opponent, "If that matter is wholesome, does that distinction of having an object (sārammaṇa), which is obtained in the wholesome, exist for that matter according to your view?", the inquiry "Does it have an object?" (sārammaṇaṃ) and so forth is initiated.

In that context, "aspiration" (patthanā) and "resolution" (paṇidhi) are merely synonyms for volition (cetanā). For wholesome volition itself is called "aspiration" when it is specifically planned and striven for, and it is called "resolution" because it is established by the power of that specific striving. Later, however, among states such as feeling, perception, volition, and faith that originate from a wholesome mind, the meaning of aspiration and resolution is obtained only in feeling (vedanā) and so forth, but not in volition. Why? Because two volitions cannot exist simultaneously. Nevertheless, it should be understood that this text has come down in this way because it falls within the flow of the teaching. The statement "the visible-data base" (rūpāyatanaṃ) and so forth is said for the purpose of showing the details of the state that was briefly shown in the previous section as "all that is wholesome".
211:
It has been stated for the purpose of showing the different aspects of the Dhamma shown in brief. The remaining methods of comparison, the Vacīkammakathā (Discourse on Verbal Action), and the entire arrangement beginning with "arising from an unwholesome mind" should be understood according to the Pāḷi text itself. Here, "impure" (asuci) refers to semen (sukka). The substantiation by the Sutta is quite clear in its meaning.

## Commentary on the Discourse: Matter is Karma (Rūpaṃ Kammaṃ).

## 10. Commentary on the Discourse: The Life Faculty (Jīvitindriya).

Now follows the Jīvitindriyakathā. In this discourse, the Pubbaseliyas and Sammitiyas hold the view that what is called the life faculty is only a mental phenomenon (arūpadhamma) dissociated from the mind (cittavippayutta); therefore, there is no physical life faculty (rūpajīvitindriya). With reference to them, the Sakavādin asks the question, and the other (Paravādin) affirms. In the question, "Is there no life (āyu) for material phenomena?", he denies it because he intends that the continuous occurrence of both sentient matter (upādinnarūpa) grasped by craving and views, and insentient matter such as grass and wood, is itself life (āyu), presence (ṭhiti), sustenance (yapanā), maintenance (yāpanā), movement (iriyanā), keeping going (vattanā), and protection (pālanā). In the question, "Is there?", he affirms for this same reason. In the question, "Is there a mental life faculty?", he affirms because he intends that there is a continuity of the life faculty dissociated from the mind for mental phenomena.

In the question, "Is the life of material phenomena a mental life faculty?", he affirms because he intends only the mental life faculty dissociated from the mind for all matter and mind, whether they be material or immaterial, in the continuity of beings.

In the questions concerning the attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti), he also denies and affirms with reference only to the mental life faculty dissociated from the mind. The Sakavādin, not accepting that view, says "Hañci" (If...) and so on, to argue that "When there is no continuous occurrence of mental phenomena, that life faculty which exists must be a material phenomenon." In the question concerning the aggregate of formations (saṅkhārakkhandha), he denies with reference to the aggregate of formations such as contact (phassa), and affirms with reference to the aggregate of formations such as bodily action (kāyakamma). The view of that Paravādin is that phenomena such as bodily intimation (kāyaviññatti), vocal intimation (vacīviññatti), right speech (sammāvācā), right action (sammākammanta), and the life faculty are also included in the aggregate of formations. The Sakavādin, not accepting that view, says "Is there the aggregate of feeling?" and so on, to argue that "If the aggregate of formations exists even when mental phenomena have ceased, then let all four aggregates exist." The other (Paravādin) denies with reference to the state within the attainment, and affirms with reference to the preceding and succeeding parts of one entering and emerging from the attainment.
212:
In the section concerning non-percipient beings (asaññasatta), the method is the same. Indeed, according to the view of that Paravādin, at the moment of rebirth of non-percipient beings, the mind arises and ceases; together with that rebirth-mind, the mental life faculty dissociated from the mind arises and continues for the duration of the lifespan. Therefore, when asked if those non-percipient beings have no life faculty, he denies it; when asked if they have it, he affirms. He also denies the aggregate of feeling and so on with reference to the continuous occurrence (pavatti) of those beings, and affirms them with reference to the moments of death and rebirth. The Sakavādin, not wishing to accept that view, said "Five-constituent existence" (pañcavokārabhavo) to argue that "If at that single moment of death or rebirth, the aggregates such as feeling exist, does it not result in the state of five-constituent existence?" The other (Paravādin) denies it for fear of contradicting the Sutta texts.

544-545. In the question, "Is a portion destroyed?", the view of that Paravādin is that the associated life faculty is destroyed, while the dissociated life faculty remains; therefore, he affirms. The question, "Are there two life faculties?", is the Paravādin's question, and the affirmation is the Sakavādin's affirmation. Indeed, there are two life faculties by way of material and mental; a being lives only because of these two, and is said to die upon the destruction of those life faculties. At the moment of death, both life faculties are destroyed simultaneously.

## Commentary on the Discourse: The Life Faculty (Jīvitindriya).

## 11. Commentary on the Discourse: Karma as Cause (Kammahetu).

Now follows the discourse named Kammahetukathā. In this discourse, the view that an Arahant who had previously slandered an Arahant in a past life falls away from Arahantship due to the cause of that karma is the view of the Pubbaseliyas and Sammitiyas. With reference to them, the question "Kammahetu" is the Sakavādin's question, and the affirmation is the other Paravādin's affirmation. The remaining statements are exactly as the method stated in the Parihānikathā (Discourse on Falling Away).

"Indeed, he slanders Arahants"—this statement is made to make him accept that karma, due to the cause of which one falls away from Arahantship. Thereafter, the Sakavādin, having made the Paravādin affirm that point, said "Ye keci" (Whoever...) and so on, to argue that "If it be so, then all those who have never slandered an Arahant before should attain Arahantship." The other (Paravādin) denies it because he does not see a certainty in the attainment of Arahantship because of that karma.

## Commentary on the Discourse: Karma as Cause (Kammahetu).

## The Eighth Chapter (Aṭṭhamo Vaggo).
213:
## 1. Commentary on the Discussion of One Who Sees the Benefits
## 9. The Ninth Chapter (Vagga)

Now is the Discussion of One Who Sees the Benefits (Ānisaṃsadassāvīkathā). In that discussion, in the view of the Sakavādī, it is concluded that the abandonment of fetters (saṃyojana) occurs for one who sees formations (saṅkhāra) as a disadvantage (ādīnava) and Nibbāna as a benefit (ānisaṃsa). However, opponents such as the Andhakas hold a one-sided view: "The abandonment of fetters occurs only for one who sees the benefit in Nibbāna." The Sakavādī questions them with this in mind, and the opponent (Paravādī) admits it. Then, to show the distinction—that the disadvantage in formations must also be seen—the Sakavādī says "Saṅkhāre" and so on.

In the problem, "One also attends to formations as impermanent and is one who sees the benefit in Nibbāna," this is the intended meaning: the opponent's view is that the abandonment of fetters occurs for one who sees the benefit. When asked, "Does the abandonment of fetters not occur for one who attends to formations as impermanent?" the opponent admits, "Yes, it does." Because of that admission, the Sakavādī asks, "According to your view, both these things occur: one attends to formations as impermanent and is also one who sees the benefit in Nibbāna. Do you accept this?" Then the opponent denies it with reference to a single mind-moment (ekacittakkhaṇa), but when asked a second time, admits it by way of different mind-moments. The Sakavādī, pressing the opponent's view, asks, "Since you admit both the attention to impermanence and the seeing of benefit together, does a conjunction of two touches (phassa) and two minds (citta) occur?" The opponent denies the conjunction of the two because they do not see it. In the problems "Dukkhato" (as suffering) and so on, the method is the same.

What is the conclusion here? Does the abandonment of fetters occur for one who attends as impermanent and so on, or for one who sees the benefit in Nibbāna, or for one who does both together? If abandonment were to occur for one who attends as impermanent and so on, it would occur only by the insight-mind (vipassanācitta). If it were for one who sees the benefit, it would occur only by the insight-mind for one who sees the benefit in Nibbāna by way of hearsay. If it were for one who does both together, there would be a conjunction of two touches and so on. In reality, at the moment of the Noble Path (ariyamagga), the task of attending as impermanent and so on reaches completion, because the nature of taking things as permanent and so on no longer arises; and in Nibbāna, the seeing of benefit is accomplished through direct perception. Therefore, by the power of the completion of the task...
214:
The abandonment of fetters should be understood to occur for the person who attends as impermanent and so on, and for the person who sees the benefit in Nibbāna by way of its occurrence as an object.

The Sutta "One who repeatedly sees happiness in Nibbāna" (Nibbāne sukhānupassī) only establishes the state of repeatedly seeing happiness and so on in Nibbāna; it does not establish the abandonment of fetters merely by being one who sees the benefit. Therefore, the cited evidence is just like evidence that has not been cited.

## Commentary on the Discussion of One Who Sees the Benefits ends.

## 2. Commentary on the Discussion of the Deathless as an Object

Now is the Discussion of the Deathless as an Object (Amatārammaṇakathā). In that discussion, opponents such as the Pubbaseliyas, having wrongly grasped the meaning of Pali passages like "He perceives Nibbāna" (Nibbānaṃ maññati), hold the view: "There is a fetter that takes the Deathless (Amata) as an object." The Sakavādī questions them with this in mind, and the opponent admits it. Then, to challenge them, "If there is a fetter that takes the Deathless as an object, then the Deathless would become fetter-forming (saṃyojaniya) and so on," the Sakavādī says, "Is the Deathless fetter-forming?" and so on. The opponent denies everything for fear of contradicting the Suttas. By this method, the meaning should be understood in all sections (vāra). The cited Sutta "Nibbāna as Nibbāna (he knows)" is spoken with reference to Nibbāna in the present life (diṭṭhadhammanibbāna), therefore it does not serve as proof.

## Commentary on the Discussion of the Deathless as an Object ends.

## 3. Commentary on the Discussion: "Matter has an Object"

552-553. Now is the Discussion: "Matter has an Object" (Rūpaṃ sārammaṇanti). In that discussion, matter is called "sārammaṇa" in the sense of being with a cause (sappaccayaṭṭhena), but not in the sense of taking another object by way of the object-condition (ārammaṇapaccaya). Opponents such as the Uttarāpathakas hold the view that "Matter has an object" without distinction. The Sakavādī questions them to show the distinction in the meaning of the word "ārammaṇa," and the opponent admits it. The rest here should be understood according to the Pali text. In the question "It should not be said," the Sakavādī's admission is with reference to the support-object (olumbārammaṇa). In the second question, the admission of that same Sakavādī is with reference to the cause-object (paccayārammaṇa). Thus, the state of having an object (sārammaṇatā) is established here only in the sense of being with a cause.

## Commentary on the Discussion: "Matter has an Object" ends.
215:
## 4. Anusayā Anārammaṇakathāvaṇṇanā

554-556. Now, the discourse titled "Latent tendencies are objectless" (Anusayā Anārammaṇakathā) is presented. In this discourse, the Andhakas and some Uttarāpathakas hold the view that latent tendencies (anusaya) are dissociated from mind (cittavippayutta), rootless (ahetuka), and indeterminate (abyākata); and for that very reason, they are objectless (anārammaṇa). With reference to them, the question "Are latent tendencies (objectless)?" is the question of the Sakavādī, and the affirmation is that of the Paravādī. Then, to challenge the Paravādī that "a thing which is objectless must have such a nature," the passage beginning with "Is it matter (rūpa)?" is stated. In the problem beginning with "sensual lust" (kāmarāga), it is shown because of its non-difference from the latent tendency of sensual lust (kāmarāgānusaya). In the problem "Is the aggregate of formations (saṅkhārakkhandha) objectless?", he rejects it with reference to the aggregate of formations associated with mind. He affirms it with reference to latent tendencies, the life-faculty (jīvitindriya), and matter such as bodily action (kāyakamma), which are included within the aggregate of formations. In this manner, the meaning should be understood in all sections.

In the problem concerning "one possessed of latent tendencies" (sānusaya), the state of being possessed of latent tendencies is conceded because the latent tendencies have not yet been abandoned. It is not conceded because of the manifest occurrence of latent tendencies. For a latent tendency that has not been abandoned is not past, not future, and not present. This defilement (latent tendency) which is to be abandoned by the Path is said to "exist" only because it has not been abandoned. It should not be said of such a nature that "it has such and such an object." Therefore, its state of having an object is rejected. Such rejection applies not only to latent tendencies but also to lust (rāga) and so on; therefore, (this argument) does not prove the objectless nature of latent tendencies.

## Anusayā Anārammaṇakathāvaṇṇanā.

## 5. Ñāṇaṃ Anārammaṇantikathāvaṇṇanā

557-558. Now, the discourse titled "Knowledge is objectless" (Ñāṇaṃ Anārammaṇantikathā) is presented. In this discourse, because an Arahant who possesses eye-consciousness is called "one who has knowledge," and at that moment that knowledge has no object, the Andhakas hold the view that "knowledge is objectless." With reference to them, the Sakavādī questions and the Paravādī affirms. The rest of the meaning here should be understood in the same manner as stated in the Anusaya-kathā.

## Ñāṇaṃ Anārammaṇantikathāvaṇṇanā.

## 6. Atītānāgatārammaṇakathāvaṇṇanā

559-561. Now, the discourse titled "Past and future objects" (Atītānāgatārammaṇakathā) is presented. In this discourse, because there is no such thing as a past or future object, the mind that takes that object...
216:
...due to the non-existence of the object, it must be with an objectless mind; thus the Uttarāpathakas hold the view that the past is objectless. With reference to them, the question "Past object" is the Sakavādī's, and the affirmation is the other's. The rest of the matter here proceeds according to the Pāḷi text itself.

## Atītānāgatārammaṇakathāvaṇṇanā.

## 7. Vitakkānupatitakathāvaṇṇanā

Now is the discourse titled "Following thought" (Vitakkānupatitakathā). In that discourse, what is called "following thought" (vitakkānupatita) is of two kinds: by way of object and by way of association. Among these, because there is no fixed rule that "such and such a mind is not the object of thought," it might be that sometimes all consciousness is followed by thought. However, because consciousness dissociated from thought (vitakkavippayutta) clearly exists, not all consciousness is followed by thought. Without making this distinction, those like the Uttarāpathakas hold the view that all consciousness is followed by thought without exception. With reference to them, the Sakavādī questions and the other affirms. The rest of the matter here proceeds according to the Pāḷi text itself.

## Vitakkānupatitakathāvaṇṇanā.

## 8. Vitakkavipphārasaddakathāvaṇṇanā

Now is the discourse titled "Sound as the diffusion of thought" (Vitakkavipphārasaddakathā). In that discourse, because it is said "Initial and sustained thoughts are verbal formations," those like the Pubbaseliyas hold the view that for one who is thinking and pondering in every way, even at the time of the occurrence of the mind-element (manodhātu) at the very least, the diffusion of thought is itself sound. With reference to them, the Sakavādī asks "In every way?" and the other affirms. Then, to challenge the Paravādī that "if the mere diffusion of thought were sound, then the diffusion of contact (phassa) and so on would also be sound," he says "For one who is touching in every way," and so on. The other (Paravādī), not seeing such a scriptural basis, rejects it. Asking "Is the sound which is the diffusion of thought cognizable by ear-consciousness?", he asks by making the mere diffusion of thought to be sound, not (the sound) produced by the diffusion of thought.
217:
The other (Paravādī) rejects the sound of those who are asleep or heedless. The statement "The sound produced by the diffusion of thought is not cognizable by ear-consciousness" shows his own view. For he says that the mere diffusion of thought is sound, and that sound is not cognizable by ear-consciousness. The other (Sakavādī), however, says that it is indeed cognizable by ear-consciousness, according to the scriptural statement: "Having heard the sound of the diffusion of thought, he points it out" (Dī. Ni. 3.148).

## Commentary on the Vitakkavipphārasaddakathā.

## 9. Nayathācittassa Vācātikathāvaṇṇanā

Now is the discourse titled "Speech not in accordance with the mind" (Nayathācittassa Vācātikathā). In that discourse, because someone intending to say one thing says another, the Pubbaseliyas hold the view that speech not in accordance with the mind is not conformable to the mind, does not follow the mind, and can occur even without the mind. With reference to them, the Sakavādī questions and the Paravādī affirms. Furthermore, to challenge him that "if there were no mind producing that speech, then contact (phassa) and so on would also not exist at that moment," he says "For one without contact (aphassakassa)," and so on. In the passages beginning with "He does not desire to speak," even though he says one thing while intending to say another, he is still one who desires to speak, and therefore he rejects it saying "Not so."

In the passages beginning with "Is there not someone who, intending to say one thing," if one desires to say "cīvara" but says "cīra," the mind that desires to say one thing is of one kind, and the mind that actually speaks is of another kind. Thus, because it is not similar to the preceding mind, he is called "one whose speech is not in accordance with the mind." Because of such a slip of the tongue, there is only a non-offense (anāpatti) for him. However, it is not that there is no mind producing the word "cīra." Thus, although he establishes his view as "speech not in accordance with the mind" using this example, intending the meaning that such speech is mindless, it is not truly established.

## The Commentary on the Discourse on Speech not in Accordance with the Mind is finished.
218:
## 10. Commentary on the Discourse on Bodily Action of One with a Mind Not in Accordance (Nayathācittassa Kāyakammantikathāvaṇṇanā)

566-567. Now follows the Discourse on Bodily Action of One with a Mind Not in Accordance (Nayathācittassa Kāyakammantikathā). In that discourse, some person, thinking "I will go to another place," happens to go to that other place. Therefore, the bodily action of one with a mind not in accordance is neither in conformity with the mind nor following the mind, and it occurs even without the mind—such is the view of the Pubbaseliyas. With reference to them, there is the question of the Sakavādī and the affirmation of the other. The rest of the matter here should be understood in the same manner as stated below.

## Commentary on the Discourse on Bodily Action of One with a Mind Not in Accordance.

## 11. Commentary on the Discourse on Possession of the Past and Future (Atītānāgatasamannāgatakathāvaṇṇanā)

568-570. Now follows the Discourse on Possession of the Past and Future (Atītānāgatasamannāgatakathā). In that discourse, two types of designations should be understood: the designation of possession (samannāgatapaññatti) and the designation of attainment (paṭilābhapaññatti). Of these two, one who is endowed with present states is called "possessed" (samannāgata). Regarding one who has attained the eight attainments (samāpatti), although those attainments do not occur at the same single moment—some being past, some future, and some present—nevertheless, because they have been penetrated and not lost, such a person is called an "attainer" (lābhī). Among those two types, without grasping this distinction, the Andhakas hold the view that because those who have attained jhāna also have past and future jhānas, "they are possessed of the past and the future." With reference to them, there is the question of the Sakavādī and the affirmation of the other. The remaining meaning here is clear. The statement beginning with "one who meditates on the eight liberations (vimokkha)" establishes only the state of being an attainer (lābhī), not the state of being possessed (samannāgata).

## Commentary on the Discourse on Possession of the Past and Future.

## Ninth Chapter (Navamo Vaggo).

## 10. Tenth Chapter (Dasamavagga)

## 1. Commentary on the Discourse on Cessation (Nirodhakathāvaṇṇanā)

571-572. Now follows the Discourse on Cessation (Nirodhakathā). In that discourse, for those who hold that simultaneously with the moment of dissolution (bhaṅgakkhaṇa) of the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) which is designated as the state of rebirth (upappattibhava), the functional (kiriya)...
219:
...the five aggregates, namely the four mental aggregates—wholesome or unwholesome—called functional (kiriya) because they cause bodily and vocal actions, and mind-produced matter (cittasamuṭṭhānarūpa), arise simultaneously with the moment of dissolution (bhaṅgakkhaṇa) of the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) which is desired as the state of rebirth (upappattibhava). Indeed, if those five aggregates did not arise, there would be a break in the continuity upon the cessation of the life-continuum—such is the view of the Andhakas. With reference to them, the Sakavādī asks using the term "upappattesiye" (belonging to rebirth), and the other (Paravādī) affirms. In those four terms such as "upappattesiye," the singular locative case is used in the sense of the plural locative. The meaning here is: before the five aggregates belonging to rebirth have ceased (the four mental aggregates arise).

The word "dasannaṃ" (of the ten) is spoken in terms of the variety of the aggregates belonging to rebirth (upappattesiya-khandha) and the variety of the functional aggregates (kiriya-khandha). Between these two, in the first problem, the Sakavādī rejects the view by stating that those ten aggregates are only five in name, according to the characteristics of the aggregates such as being oppressed (ruppana) and according to their functional nature. In the second problem, the Paravādī affirms, referring to the distinction between the preceding aggregates belonging to rebirth and the succeeding functional aggregates, and between the nature of rebirth and the functional nature. When asked about the conjunction of two contacts (phassa) and two minds (citta), the Sakavādī rejects it because there is no indication in the Pāḷi texts.

By the phrase "kiriya cattāro" (four functional ones), the four mental aggregates, wholesome or unwholesome, are taken excluding matter (rūpa). "Kiriya-ñāṇa" (functional knowledge) refers to the path-knowledge without an object that is allowed for an Arahant at the moment of being endowed with eye-consciousness, according to the Paravādī. "Does the path arise after cessation?" the Paravādī asks. The Sakavādī affirms because it does not arise before cessation. "Does a dead person develop the path?" the Paravādī asks by way of a trick. Since a being is called "living" from the moment of rebirth-linking until the death-consciousness (cuticitta), the Sakavādī rejects it, saying "It is not so."

## Commentary on the Discourse on Cessation.

## 2. Commentary on the Discourse on "Matter is the Path" (Rūpaṃ Maggotikathāvaṇṇanā)

573-575. Now follows the Discourse on "Matter is the Path" (Rūpaṃ Maggotikathā). In that discourse, the Mahīsāsakas, Sammitiyas, and Mahāsaṅghikas hold the view that "Right Speech, Right Action, and Right Livelihood are matter (rūpa)." With reference to them, the Sakavādī asks "maggasamangiassa" (of one endowed with the path), and the other affirms. Then, in order to challenge that Paravādī, saying "If, according to your wish, Right Speech and so on are matter and not abstinences (virati), then just as the path of Right View and so on has the nature of having an object (sārammaṇa), so too should that matter have an object," the Buddha spoke the words beginning with "sārammaṇo." Therein, the rejection and the affirmation should be understood according to the view of the Paravādī. The remaining meaning is clear.

## Commentary on the Discourse on "Matter is the Path".
220:
## 3. Commentary on the Discussion of the Path for One Endowed with the Fivefold Consciousness

Now follows the discussion of the Path for one endowed with the fivefold consciousness (pañcavijñāṇasamangissa maggakathā). In this discussion, based on the sutta "Having seen a form with the eye, one does not grasp at signs," those like the Mahāsaṅghikas hold the view that "One endowed with the fivefold consciousness has the development of the Path." Referring to them, the Sakavādī (the proponent of our own school) asks the question, and the other (the Paravādī) acknowledges. Then, to challenge that Paravādī, [the Sakavādī] says, "If there is development of the Path for that person, the Path must be of the same nature as the fivefold consciousness, or the fivefold consciousnesses must be of the same nature as the Path. Those fivefold consciousnesses do not have the nature of the Path because they do not take Nibbāna as an object and because they are not supramundane. The Path also does not have the nature of the fivefold consciousness because it is not included within their characteristics," and so on, starting with "Do the fivefold consciousnesses have a physical base that has arisen?"

The meaning here is: If there were development of the Path for one endowed with the fivefold consciousness, the mind-consciousness associated with the Path would also exist in the continuity of one endowed with the fivefold consciousness. If this were so, instead of saying the characteristic "The fivefold consciousnesses have a physical base that has arisen," one should have said "The six consciousnesses." However, since it was not said so, but only "the fivefold consciousnesses" was said, it should not be said that "One endowed with the fivefold consciousness has the development of the Path." Since this is the only meaning here, the Sakavādī, having made the Paravādī accept that characteristic, says, "Indeed, it should not be said that one endowed with the fivefold consciousness has the development of the Path."

Another way: The fivefold consciousnesses have a physical base that has arisen; the Path may also be without a physical base. Those [fivefold consciousnesses] have an object that has arisen; the Path has an object (Nibbāna) that cannot be described [as past, future, or present]. Those fivefold consciousnesses only have a physical base that has arisen previously; the Path may also be without a physical base. Those [fivefold consciousnesses] have an object that has arisen previously; the Path does not have an object that has arisen previously. Those fivefold consciousnesses only have an internal physical base; the Path may also be without a physical base. Those fivefold consciousnesses have external objects by way of forms and so on; the Path has Nibbāna as its object. Those fivefold consciousnesses, because they occur depending on a physical base that has not yet ceased, have an unbroken physical base; the Path may also be without a physical base. Those [fivefold consciousnesses], because they occur by taking forms and so on that have not yet ceased as objects, have an unbroken object; the Path has Nibbāna as its object. Those [fivefold consciousnesses] have various physical bases; the Path is either without a physical base or has a single physical base. Those [fivefold consciousnesses] have various objects; the Path has a single object. Those [fivefold consciousnesses], because they occur only in their respective domains such as forms and so on, do not experience each other's domain of objects; the Path does not take even a single object among forms and so on. Those [fivefold consciousnesses], because they arise having the functional mind-element as a precursor, do not arise without attention or without mental advertence; the Path is indeed without advertence (nirāvajjanova). Those fivefold consciousnesses arise mixed with receiving (sampaṭicchana) and so on; for the Path, there is no such mixing at all. Those [fivefold consciousnesses]...
221:
...occur in a sequence of before and after; for the Path, there is no such sequence of before and after with them, because the Path arises at the time of keen insight (tikkha-vipassanā) when they do not occur, and in the formless realm (āruppa) where they do not occur. Those [fivefold consciousnesses], because they are separated by receiving and so on, do not arise in immediate succession to each other; for the Path, there is no such state of being separated by receiving and so on. For those [fivefold consciousnesses], there is no function other than the initial impact (abhinipāta), not even a mere advertence; for the Path, there is the function of uprooting the defilements (kilesasamugghātana). Since this is also the meaning here, the Sakavādī, having made the Paravādī accept by these means that the Path does not follow the nature of the fivefold consciousness, says, "Indeed, it should not be said that one endowed with the fivefold consciousness has the development of the Path."

"Taking emptiness (suññata) as an object" means: [The Sakavādī] asks, "Just as the supramundane Path arises taking the emptiness that is Nibbāna as an object, and the mundane insight Path arises taking the mere heap of formations as an object, does your eye-consciousness arise in the same way?" The other (Paravādī) rejects this because of the statement "Dependent on the eye and forms [eye-consciousness arises]." When asked a second time, referring to the fact that whatever is signless (animitta) in that moment of eye-consciousness is indeed emptiness, he acknowledges it because of the statement "one does not grasp at signs." In both problems regarding "Dependent on the eye," this is the same method.

578-579. "Eye-consciousness taking the past and future as an object": The meaning here is: One endowed with mind-consciousness has the development of the Path, and mind-consciousness can arise taking even the past and future as objects; can your eye-consciousness also do the same? This is the same method for "taking contact (phassa) as an object" and so on. In the phrase "Having seen a form with the eye, one does not grasp at signs," the non-grasping at signs is spoken of regarding the moment of impulsion (javana), not the moment of eye-consciousness. Therefore, this statement, which refers to the mundane Path of insight, does not serve as proof.

## Commentary on the Discussion of the Path for One Endowed with the Fivefold Consciousness ends.

## 4. Commentary on the Discussion that the Fivefold Consciousnesses are also Wholesome

580-583. Now follows the discussion called "The fivefold consciousnesses are also wholesome" (pañcavijñāṇā kusalāpi). This should be understood in terms of its meaning according to the method already stated below [previously].

## Commentary on the Discussion that the Fivefold Consciousnesses are also Wholesome ends.
222:
## 5. Commentary on the Discourse on Fivefold Consciousness being Accompanied by Mental Adverting (Pañcavijñāṇā Sābhogātikathāvaṇṇanā)

584-586. Now follows the discourse named 'Fivefold Consciousness is Accompanied by Mental Adverting'. In this context, 'mental adverting' (ābhoga) refers to the nature of inclining towards an object by the power of the wholesome or unwholesome. The Blessed One also said: "Having seen a form with the eye, one is a grasper of signs, one is not a grasper of signs," and so forth. Taking this statement in an improper way, the Mahāsaṃghikas and others hold the view that "the fivefold consciousness is accompanied by mental adverting." With reference to them, the Sakavādī asks and the Paravādī acknowledges. The remaining points in this discourse are just like the previous discourse.

## Commentary on the Discourse on Fivefold Consciousness being Accompanied by Mental Adverting.

## 6. Commentary on the Discourse on Two Virtues (Dvīhi Sīlehītikathāvaṇṇanā)

587-589. Now follows the discourse named 'With Two Virtues'. In this context, according to the words "The wise man, established in virtue," and so forth, because a person who is virtuous through mundane virtue develops the supramundane path, the Mahāsaṃghikas hold the view that "one is endowed with two virtues: the mundane virtue that occurred previously and the supramundane virtue at the moment of the path." With reference to them, the Sakavādī asks using the term "one possessed of the path" (maggasamaṅgī), and the Paravādī acknowledges. Then, in order to challenge him, "If that person is endowed with both mundane and supramundane virtues in a single moment, then that person should also be endowed with two kinds of contact (phassa) and so forth," the Sakavādī speaks the words "with two contacts" and so forth. The Paravādī, not seeing such a method, rejects it. Regarding the question of mundane and supramundane virtues, he acknowledges with reference to the virtue undertaken previously before attaining the path, and the right speech (sammāvācā) and so forth that arise at the moment of the path.

The question "When mundane virtue has ceased?" is the Paravādī's question. The Sakavādī acknowledges it with reference to the cessation by momentary dissolution. The Paravādī, perceiving that cessation as if it were a transgression of virtue, speaks the words "immoral" (dussīla) and so forth. The argument to establish his view only shows the state of having unbroken virtue previously; it does not show the state of being endowed with two virtues. Therefore, that view is not established.

## Commentary on the Discourse on Two Virtues.
223:
## 7. Commentary on the Discourse: Virtue is Not Mental (Sīlaṃ Acetisikantikathāvaṇṇanā)

590-594. Now follows the discourse named 'Virtue is Not Mental'. In this context, because there is what is called the accumulation of virtue (sīlopacaya) caused by undertaking, which exists even after the virtue has arisen and ceased, and because a person is called virtuous solely by that accumulation, the Mahāsaṃghikas hold the view that "virtue is not mental." With reference to them, there is the questioning by the Sakavādī and the acknowledgment by the other, the Paravādī. The rest of this discourse should be understood in the same manner as stated in the discourse 'Giving is Not Mental'. The argument to establish their view is also not established because it is taken in an improper way.

## Commentary on the Discourse: Virtue is Not Mental.

## 8. Commentary on the Discourse: Virtue does not Concomit with Consciousness (Sīlaṃ Na Cittānuparivattītikathāvaṇṇanā)

595-597. Now follows the discourse named 'Virtue does not Concomit with Consciousness'. In this context, only the phrasing "does not concomit with consciousness" is different; the rest of the discourse is just like the previous one.

## Commentary on the Discourse: Virtue does not Concomit with Consciousness.

## 9. Commentary on the Discourse on Virtue having Undertaking as Cause (Samādānahetukathāvaṇṇanā)

598-600. Now follows the discourse named 'Virtue having Undertaking as Cause'. In this context, taking the meaning of the verse beginning with "Those who plant groves" in an improper way, and because of the statement "merit always increases," the Mahāsaṃghikas hold the view that "virtue having undertaking as its cause increases." With reference to them, there is the questioning by the Sakavādī and the acknowledgment by the Paravādī with reference to the accumulation of virtue that is dissociated from consciousness. The rest of the discourse is just like a portion of the previously mentioned Paribhogamayakathā.

## Commentary on the Discourse on Virtue having Undertaking as Cause.

## 10. Commentary on the Discourse: Intimation is Virtue (Viññatti Sīlantikathāvaṇṇanā)

601-602. Now follows the discourse named 'Intimation is Virtue'. In this context, because bodily intimation is taken as bodily action and vocal intimation as vocal action, the Mahāsaṃghikas and Sammitiyas hold the view that "intimation is virtue." With reference to them...
224:
The question "Is it intimation?" (Viññattīti) is the Sakavādī's question, and the acknowledgment is the other's (Paravādī's). Then, because virtue is indeed abstinence (virati) and not a material phenomenon (rūpadhamma), the Blessed One spoke the words "abstinence from taking life" and so forth to challenge them on that meaning. The phrase "Salutation is virtue" and so forth was spoken to extract and show the kind of intimation that the Paravādī considers to be "virtue". However, because that (salutation, etc.) is not abstinence, he spoke again "abstinence from taking life" and so forth. The Paravādī's view is not established because it is established through trickery.

## Commentary on the Discourse: Intimation is Virtue.

## 11. Commentary on the Discourse: Non-intimation is Immorality (Aviññatti Dussīlyantikathāvaṇṇanā)

603-604. Now follows the discourse 'Non-intimation is Immorality'. In this context, with reference to the accumulation of demerit dissociated from consciousness and the completion of the factors in acts such as taking life due to a command, the Mahāsaṃghikas hold the view that "non-intimation (aviññatti) is immorality (dussīlya)." With reference to them, the Sakavādī asks and the Paravādī acknowledges. Then, in order to challenge him, "If that non-intimation is immorality, would it be one of the acts such as taking life?" the Sakavādī speaks the words "taking life" and so forth. "Having undertaken an evil deed" means having undertaken evil by thinking, "I will kill such a person, I will steal such a person's goods" (referring to the one who gives the command). When asked, "Do both increase?", he rejects it with reference to the moment of giving when evil does not occur. When asked a second time, he acknowledges it with reference to the accumulation of evil dissociated from consciousness. The rest of the terms should be understood in the same manner as stated in the Paribhogamayakathā. The argument to establish the Paravādī's view only proves the preliminary stage of the undertaken evil; it does not prove that non-intimation is the state of immorality.

## Commentary on the Discourse: Non-intimation is Immorality.

## 11. Ekādasamavagga
## 1-3. Tissopi Anusayakathāvaṇṇanā
605-613. Now, there are three discourses on latent tendencies (anusaya), namely that latent tendencies are indeterminate (abyākata), rootless (ahetuka), and dissociated from consciousness (cittavippayutta). Among these three discourses on latent tendencies, an ordinary person (puthujjana) should be said to be 'with latent tendencies' (sānusaya) while wholesome or indeterminate consciousness is occurring. Whatever root (hetu) exists for that ordinary person at that moment, the latent tendencies are not 'with roots' (sahetuka) because of that root, nor are they associated with that consciousness. Therefore, the Mahāsaṃghikas and the Sammitiyas hold the view that 'those latent tendencies are indeterminate, rootless, and dissociated from consciousness.' With reference to them, in all three discourses, the question is that of the Proponent (Sakavādī), and the affirmation is that of the Opponent (Paravādī). Since the rest of the sequence of words can be understood through the method already stated below according to the Pali text, it is not elaborated further.

## Tissopi Anusayakathāvaṇṇanā.

## 4. Ñāṇakathāvaṇṇanā
614-615. Now is the discourse on knowledge (ñāṇakathā). In that discourse, although ignorance (aññāṇa/moha) has disappeared due to path-knowledge, the Mahāsaṃghikas hold the view that 'one should not be called one possessing knowledge (ñāṇī)' because that path-consciousness does not occur while consciousness dissociated from knowledge is occurring again by way of eye-consciousness and so forth. With reference to them, the question is that of the Proponent, and the affirmation is that of the Opponent. Then, in order to challenge that Opponent, saying: 'If there were no designation as "one possessing knowledge" even when ignorance has disappeared, then when lust and so forth have disappeared, there would also be no designation as "one free from lust" (vītarāga) and so forth; therefore, you are unskilled in the designation of persons (puggalapaññatti),' the Proponent said 'rāge vigate' (when lust has disappeared) and so forth. The other (the Opponent) rejects it because he does not see the logical reason for being 'with lust' (sarāga) and so forth when those [lusts] have disappeared. In the end, because one deserves to be called 'one possessing knowledge' due to the attainment of knowledge, the rejection 'na hevaṃ' (it is not so) is the point of the Proponent.

## Ñāṇakathāvaṇṇanā.
226:
## 5. Commentary on the Discourse: "Knowledge is Dissociated from Mind"
616-617. Now is the discourse called "Knowledge is Dissociated from Mind" (Ñāṇaṃ cittavippayuttanti-kathā). In that discourse, an Arahant who is endowed with eye-consciousness and so on is called "one possessing knowledge" with reference to the path-knowledge already attained. Even though so called, that knowledge of the Arahant is not associated with that consciousness such as eye-consciousness. Therefore, the Pubbaseliyas hold the view that "knowledge is dissociated from mind." With reference to them, there is the question of the Proponent and the affirmation of the Opponent. Then, to challenge him, "If your knowledge is dissociated from mind, it should be one of the things dissociated from mind, such as matter (rūpa)," the phrase "Rūpaṃ" and so on is stated. The Opponent rejects it. The rest of the explanation is just as stated below. At the end, however, when asked "Is he one possessing wisdom (paññavā)?", he affirms it because he desires that designation by way of attainment.

## Commentary on the Discourse: "Knowledge is Dissociated from Mind."

## 6. Commentary on the Discourse: "This is Suffering"
618-820. Now is the discourse called "This is Suffering" (Idaṃ dukkhanti-kathā). In that discourse, the Andhakas hold the view: "At the moment of the supramundane path, the practitioner (yogāvacara) utters the words 'This is suffering'; and for him who thus utters the words 'This is suffering', the knowledge 'This is suffering' occurs." With reference to them, there is the question of the Proponent, and the affirmation of the Opponent with reference to such utterance of words and occurrence of knowledge at the moment of the path. However, that Opponent holds that only a worldling utters words connected with the remaining truths, and he does not desire that such knowledge occurs for that worldling; therefore, he rejects the questions regarding the origin (samudaya) and so on. "Matter is impermanent" and so on is stated by way of showing the synonyms (pariyāya) of suffering. The Opponent rejects it because he does not find such usage in his own tradition. The letters "I", "daṃ", and so on are stated to show that if knowledge occurs to him regarding suffering, it should occur through four knowledges in sequence for the syllables I-character, Daṃ-character, Du-character, and Kha-character. The Opponent rejects it because he does not desire such an occurrence.

## Commentary on the Discourse: "This is Suffering."

## 7. Commentary on the Discussion of the Power of Psychic Potency

621-624. Now follows the discussion named the Discussion of the Power of Psychic Potency (Iddhibalakathā). In this context, the question of the Sakavādī, "Can one endowed with the power of psychic potency remain for an aeon?" is directed at those, such as the Mahāsaṅghikas, who hold the view that "one endowed with the power of psychic potency can remain for an aeon," having wrongly grasped the meaning of the benefits of the development of the bases of psychic power (iddhipāda-bhāvanā). In that regard, an aeon (kappa) is of three kinds: a great aeon (mahākappa), a portion of an aeon (asaṅkheyyakappa), and a life-span aeon (āyukappa). In the passage, "Monks, there are these four incalculables of an aeon," only the great aeon is called an aeon. In the passage, "The life-span of the Brahmakāyika deities is one aeon," a portion of an aeon (asaṅkheyyakappa) is meant. In the passage, "He is boiled in hell for an aeon; he rejoices in heaven for an aeon," a life-span aeon is meant. A life-span aeon means the arrangement of life, the limitation of life either by the power of the result of kamma or by the number of years. Among these, the Sakavādī asks with reference to the great aeon, and the other (the Paravādī) affirms it.

Then the Sakavādī, in order to refute that Paravādī, says, "Is that life produced by psychic power?" and so on, meaning: "If, according to your wish, one endowed with psychic power were to live for a great aeon or for a portion of a great aeon, which is beyond the life-span aeon defined as 'he who lives long lives for a hundred years or a little more,' then that person's life must be a life produced by psychic power." The other (the Paravādī) rejects this because it is said, "There is no such thing as a life faculty (jīvitindriya) produced by psychic power; it is only originated by kamma."

What then is the distinction of the one with psychic power? Is it not that even one without psychic power can remain for a life-span aeon? This is the distinction: the one with psychic power is able to prevent untimely death (akālamaraṇa) in the interval by warding off with the power of psychic potency those states that cause danger to the continuity of the life faculty throughout his life-span. One without psychic power does not have this power. This is the distinction between them.

He (the Sakavādī) rebukes him because he affirmed that "one can remain for an aeon" in a general sense without specifying "past" or "future." The words "two aeons" and so on are spoken for the purpose of rebuking: "If one with psychic power is able to exceed the limitation of life, he should be able to remain not only for one aeon but for many aeons as well." The words "arisen contact" and so on are spoken to show that not everything can be obtained by psychic power, and that there are things beyond the scope of psychic power. The remaining words are clear in meaning.

## Commentary on the Discussion of the Power of Psychic Potency.

## 8. Commentary on the Discussion of Concentration

625-626. Now follows the Discussion of Concentration (Samādhikathā). In this discussion, there is the view of the Sabbatthivādins and the Uttarāpathakas that "the continuity of mind (cittasantati) is concentration," based on the words, "He can dwell experiencing absolute happiness for seven days and nights," and so on, instead of taking the one-pointedness (ekaggatā) arisen in a single mind-moment as concentration in the sense of being well-composed. With reference to them, the Sakavādī asks, "Is the continuity of mind concentration?" and the other affirms it. Then, to rebuke that Paravādī, he asks, "Is it past...?" and so on, meaning: "If the continuity of mind is concentration, the continuity of mind exists in the past and also in the future. Indeed, a single present mind alone cannot be called a continuity of mind; if so, is that entire continuity of mind concentration according to your wish?" The other rejects it, not desiring the past and future to be concentration.

The words "The past has ceased" and so on are spoken to show: "In the continuity of mind, only the present mind can perform a function; the past and future minds do not exist because they have ceased or have not yet arisen; how then can they be called concentration?" The question "Is it of a single mind-moment?" is the question of the Paravādī. Thereafter, the Sakavādī affirms it with reference to the meaning taught in his own school in such passages as, "Monks, develop concentration," where one-pointedness associated with a present wholesome mind is called concentration. The words "One endowed with eye-consciousness" and so on are spoken by way of a quibble (chala), taking only the literal words "of a single mind-moment," and therefore it is rejected by that same Sakavādī. The sutta, "It was said by the Blessed One," establishes only the unmixed nature of concentration occurring in a prior and posterior sequence, not the state of concentration being a continuity of mind; therefore, it does not serve as a proof.

## Commentary on the Discussion of Concentration.

## 9. Commentary on the Discussion of the Stability of Phenomena

Now follows the Discussion of the Stability of Phenomena (Dhammaṭṭhitatākathā). In this discussion, there is the view of the Andhakas that "there is a single thing called the stability of phenomena, known as dependent origination (paṭiccasamuppāda), and that is a produced (parinipphanna) phenomenon," based on the words, "That element (dhātu) remains stable." With reference to them, the Sakavādī asks, and the other affirms it. Then, to that Paravādī, "If of the produced ignorance (avijjā) and so on..."
229:
"Other causes called Dhammaṭṭhitatā (stability of phenomena) have the nature of being produced (parinipphanna); because of that Dhammaṭṭhitatā, another produced stability (ṭhitatā) arises"—to challenge this, the phrase beginning with "tāya ṭhitatā" was spoken. The opponent (paravādī) rejects this because such a view does not exist [in their doctrine]. When asked a second time, they admit it with reference to the proximity condition (anantara-paccaya) and mutuality condition (aññamañña-paccaya). The rest of the words are clear in meaning as stated below.

## Commentary on the Discourse on the Stability of Phenomena (Dhammaṭṭhitatā-kathā).

## 10. Commentary on the Discourse on Impermanence (Aniccatā-kathā)

Now comes the Discourse on Impermanence. In that discourse, the Andhakas hold the view: "The impermanence (aniccatā) of conditioned things such as form (rūpa), which are impermanent, is also a produced (parinipphanna) phenomenon just like form and so on." With reference to them, the proponent (sakavādī) asks, and the other (paravādī) admits. Then, to challenge them: "If, according to your wish, impermanence is produced like form and so on, then for that impermanence, there must be another produced impermanence," the phrase beginning with "tāya aniccatāya" was spoken. The other (paravādī) rejects it because two impermanences do not exist simultaneously; then (when asked again), they admit it because that impermanence is not permanent and disappears along with that impermanent thing. Then, the proponent, giving no opening for an excuse, wishing to attribute the fault of infinite regress (anupaccheda-dosa) through the second impermanence admitted by him and further impermanences beyond that, spoke the phrase beginning with "tāya tāyeva." The passage beginning with "jarā parinipphannā" (decay is produced) is spoken by way of investigating the distinctions of impermanence, because there is no other impermanence apart from the decay and death of a produced conditioned thing. There too, the admission and rejection of the opponent should be understood in the same manner as the previous method.

"Rūpaṃ parinipphannaṃ" (form is produced) and so on are spoken to compare with those phenomena like form that possess impermanence. In this regard, thinking, "Just as produced things like form have impermanence, decay, and death, so produced things like impermanence do not have those [impermanence, decay, and death]," they simply reject it absolutely.

## Commentary on the Discourse on Impermanence (Aniccatā-kathā).

## The Eleventh Chapter (Ekādasamo Vaggo).

## 12. Dvādasamavagga
## 1. Saṃvaro Kammantikathāvaṇṇanā
630-632. Now is the discourse: Is restraint action? (saṃvaro kammanti). In that discourse, based on the sutta, 'Having seen a form with the eye, one is a grasper of signs (nimittaggāhī) [with defiled mind], one is not a grasper of signs,' etc., those such as the Mahāsaṃghikas hold the view that 'both restraint (saṃvara) and non-restraint (asaṃvara) are action (kamma).' With reference to them, the question is that of the Proponent, and the affirmation is that of the Opponent.

Then, to challenge that Opponent: in his own doctrine, whatever volition (cetanā) is called 'action' by the Buddha, just as that volition receives the name 'bodily action' (kāyakamma) and so forth when it occurs in the doors of body, speech, and mind; likewise, 'if restraint were action according to your wish, that restraint should also receive the name "eye-action" (cakkhukamma) and so forth when it occurs in the doors of the eye-faculty (cakkhundriya) and so forth,' the Proponent said 'cakkhundriyasaṃvaro cakkhukammaṃ' and so forth. The Opponent, not seeing such a sutta passage, rejects it regarding the four doors, and regarding the fifth door, the body-door, he rejects it with reference to the sensitive body (kāyaprasāda) but affirms it with reference to bodily intimation (kāyaviññatti). This is because that Opponent desires both the sensitive body and bodily intimation to be merely the body-faculty (kāyindriya). In the mind-door as well, he rejects it with reference to the resultant door (vipākadvāra), which is the life-continuum (bhavaṅga), but affirms it with reference to the action-door (kammadvāra), which is wholesome or unwholesome consciousness. The same method applies to non-restraint. The sutta beginning with 'Having seen a form with the eye' shows only restraint and non-restraint in those doors, not the status of that restraint and non-restraint as action; therefore, it means it cannot be used as evidence.

## Saṃvaro Kammantikathāvaṇṇanā.

## 2. Kammakathāvaṇṇanā
633-635. Now is the discourse on action (kammakathā). In that discourse, based on the sutta passage, 'Monks, I [declare] of actions performed with volition...', it is to show the view of those such as the Mahāsaṃghikas that 'all action is with result (savipāka).' To them, the Teacher has taught volition as 'action' in a general sense without distinction, saying, 'Monks, I say that volition is action.' To show this specific analysis—that only wholesome and unwholesome volitions are with result, while indeterminate (abyākata) volition is without result—the Proponent asks, 'Is all action [with result]?' and the Opponent affirms. Again, in the questions such as 'Is all volition [with result]?', the rejection with reference to indeterminate volition and the affirmation with reference to wholesome and unwholesome volitions should be understood. To show specifically the volition with result and the volition without result, the words 'vipākābyākatā' and so forth are said. In this discourse on action, the rest of the collection of words has an obvious meaning.
231:
It should be understood thus. The statement beginning with "Vipākābyākatā" was spoken to show specifically the volition that has a result and the volition that does not have a result. The rest of the words in this Kamma-kathā have a clear meaning. The sutta beginning with "O monks, I..." was spoken with reference to the experiencing of the result (vipāka) in the present life and so forth when the conditions are present; therefore, it cannot be used as evidence.

## Commentary on the Discussion of Kamma

## 3. Commentary on the Discussion: Sound is a Result

636–637. Now comes the discussion titled "Sound is a Result" (Saddo Vipākoti-kathā). Therein, for those opponents (paravādī) such as the Mahāsaṅghikas, who wrongly grasp the Pāḷi passage beginning with, "Because of having performed, accumulated, increased, and expanded that kamma, he has a voice like that of Brahmā," and hold the view that "sound is a result (vipāka)," the proponent (sakavādī) asks and the opponent admits, in order to show that "only mental phenomena (nāma-dhamma) produced by kamma receive the name 'result' (vipāka); however, this designation 'result' does not exist for material phenomena (rūpa-dhamma)." The statement beginning with "Sukhavedanīya" was spoken to show that "what is called a result has such a nature." The sutta "So tassa kammassa" was spoken to show the attainment of the marks (lakkhaṇa). Indeed, the Great Man (Mahāpurisa) has a pure retinue because of kamma, but the retinue is not a result; therefore, this statement does not serve as evidence.

## The Commentary on the Discussion: Sound is a Result ends.

## 4. Commentary on the Discussion of the Six Bases

638–640. Now comes the discussion on the six bases (Saḷāyatana-kathā). Therein, with reference to the opponents such as the Mahāsaṅghikas, who hold the view that "the six bases are results" because they arise due to kamma, the proponent asks, "Is the eye-base (cakkhāyatana) a result?" and the opponent admits it. The rest of the discussion follows the same method as stated below. In this statement "the six bases are results," the mind-base (manāyatana) could be a result. The remaining bases are merely material phenomena produced by kamma and are not results. Therefore, this statement does not serve as evidence.

## The Commentary on the Discussion of the Six Bases ends.
232:
## 5. Commentary on the Discussion of One Who is Seven Times at Most

641–645. Now comes the discussion titled "One Who is Seven Times at Most" (Sattakkhattuparama-kathā). In that discussion, because it was preached as "Sattakkhattuparama" (a person who has seven times at most as his limit), the Uttarāpathaka sect holds the view that "the Sattakkhattuparama person is fixed (niyata) in the state of being one who is seven times at most." To them, the proponent (sakavādī) asks and the opponent (paravādī) admits, in order to show this distinction: "Setting aside the Noble Path (ariya-magga), there is no other fixed law (niyāma) that causes that Sattakkhattuparama Sotāpanna person to be fixed in the state of being one who is seven times at most."

In the problems beginning with "killing the mother," the meaning is as follows: There are two kinds of fixed laws (niyāma): the fixed law of rightness (sammatta-niyāma) and the fixed law of wrongness (micchatta-niyāma). The fixed law of rightness is the Noble Path. That Noble Path fixes the state of not falling into the four woeful planes (avinipāta-dhammatā) and the arising of the fruit (phaluppatti). The fixed law of wrongness is the kamma with immediate result (ānantariya-kamma). That kamma fixes the rebirth in hell immediately after death. Among those two fixed laws, the Sattakkhattuparama person is fixed in the state of not falling into woeful planes and in the arising of the fruit by the Path of Stream-entry (sotāpatti-magga). For that person, the remaining fixed laws of the higher paths do not yet exist because they have not been attained; he is also incapable (abhabba) of committing an ānantariya-kamma. However, you, the opponent, desire the fixedness of that person; therefore, we wish to ask you: "According to your wish, does this fixed law of wrongness fix that Sattakkhattuparama person?"

In the problems beginning with "incapable in the interval (abhabbo antarā)," he rejects it with reference to the absence of ānantariya-kamma, and admits it with reference to the state of being one who is seven times at most. In the problem "Does that fixed law exist?", he rejects it because he does not find a fixed law that causes fixedness in the state of being one who is seven times at most. The statement beginning with "Do you have the foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna)?" is said to show the path-factors (magga-dhamma) called the fixed law. For that person, since the first path does not arise again, those path-factors also do not exist; therefore, he rejects it. The rest of the words here have a clear meaning. In the context of "Is that person not one who is seven times at most?", the Blessed One merely prophesied by the power of his own knowledge, "This person, having wandered through this many lives, will attain Parinibbāna"; he did not preach it by seeing any such thing as a fixed law of existence (bhava-niyāma). Therefore, it is said "Sattakkhattuparama," "Kolaṅkola," or "Ekabījī"; thus, this statement does not serve as evidence.

## The Commentary on the Discussion of One Who is Seven Times at Most ends.

646–647. The Kolaṅkola-kathā and the Ekabījī-kathā should also be understood in this same way.

## Commentary on the Discussion of Kolaṅkola and Ekabījī ends.
