## 8. Jīvitāvoropanakathāvaṇṇanā

648-649. Now is the Jīvitāvoropanakathā (Discourse on Depriving of Life). In this discourse, because the act of killing (pāṇātipāta) occurs with a mind associated with ill-will (dosa), and ill-will is not yet abandoned by one endowed with right view (a Sotāpanna), the Pubbaseliyas and Aparaseliyas hold the view that "one endowed with right view might intentionally deprive a living being of life." With reference to them, the question "Diṭṭhisampanno" is the question of the Sakavādī (the Proponent), and the affirmation is that of the other (the Paravādī/Opponent). However, regarding problems such as "intentionally (killing) one's mother," the Paravādī rejects it for fear of contradicting the Sutta which states, "This is impossible, it cannot happen." The statement regarding "disrespect for the Teacher" is made to show that one who is respectful toward the Teacher and others does not violate the training rules. The other (the Paravādī), however, rejects the idea that such a person has disrespect through the power of unwholesome states, and having accepted the state of being respectful, when asked again about "disrespect," affirms it with reference to the failure to perform acts like bowing or circumambulating (padakkhiṇa) a shrine (cetiya) due to lack of mindfulness or lack of attention while being distracted by various duties. Again, when asked in the manner of "Would he pass excrement (on a shrine)?", he rejects it because such an act is not done intentionally. The remaining meaning here is clear.

## Jīvitāvoropanakathāvaṇṇanā.

## 9. Duggatikathāvaṇṇanā

650-652. Now is the Duggatikathā (Discourse on Woeful States). In this discourse, those who take both the woeful rebirth and the craving for sense objects like forms experienced by beings in woeful states as "duggati," and then, without making such a distinction, say generally that "one endowed with right view has abandoned the woeful state," are like the Uttarāpathakas. With reference to them, the questions and affirmations occur. The phrase "Would he be lustful for forms in the states of loss?" is stated to challenge the Paravādī's view that the "duggati" (the objects of beings in woeful states) has not been abandoned by one endowed with right view. The remaining meaning here is clear. The phrase "Would he be reborn in hell?" shows either the abandonment of the woeful rebirth itself or the abandonment of the craving that leads to woeful states; it does not show the abandonment of craving for sense objects like forms experienced by beings in woeful states. Therefore, it does not serve as a proof.

## Duggatikathāvaṇṇanā.
234:
The same method applies to the Sattamabhavikakathā (Discourse on the Seventh Rebirth).

## The Twelfth Chapter.

## 13. The Thirteenth Chapter

## 1. Kappaṭṭhakathāvaṇṇanā

654-657. Now is the Kappaṭṭhakathā (Discourse on Remaining for an Aeon). In this discourse, based on the Pali text "Having split the harmonious Sangha, he is boiled in hell for an aeon (kappa)," the Rājagirikas hold the view that "the schismatic remains in hell for an entire aeon." With reference to them, the Sakavādī asks "Kappaṭṭho?" and the other affirms. The phrase "A Buddha in the world" is stated to show that schism in the Sangha cannot occur without the arising of a Buddha. The phrase "The aeon is established and the Sangha is split" is stated to show that "If he were to remain for an entire aeon, he would have to perform that deed from the time the aeon is established and be reborn and remain in that hell." The phrase "Atītaṃ" (the past) has the same meaning as stated below. In the problem "Is the one who remains for an aeon possessed of psychic power (iddhimā)?", it is rejected with reference to psychic power born of development (bhāvanā). In the view of the Paravādīs, they desire psychic power born of birth for that person; he affirms it with reference to that psychic power born of birth. The phrase "Chandiddhipādo" is stated for the purpose of challenging: "This view that he has psychic power because of birth-born power is merely a view; what is the use of that power? If he truly had psychic power, he should have developed the bases of psychic power (iddhipāda) in this manner." The Sutta "Āpāyiko nerayiko" refers to the life-span aeon (āyukappa) where one might remain for one part of a great aeon divided into eighty parts (an intermediate aeon); therefore, it does not establish their view.

## Kappaṭṭhakathāvaṇṇanā.

## 2. Kusalapaṭilābhakathāvaṇṇanā

658-659. Now is the Kusalapaṭilābhakathā (Discourse on the Acquisition of Wholesome States). In this discourse, according to the Sakavādī's own view, the person who remains for an aeon can only acquire sense-sphere wholesome states (kāmāvacara kusala). However, he cannot acquire those wholesome states, whether lofty (mahaggata) or supramundane (lokuttara), by which he could prevent that rebirth in hell. Without making this distinction, those who hold the general view that "that person does not [acquire] a wholesome mind"...
235:
The view that "it can be acquired" is the view of the Uttarāpathaka sect. To refute their view by showing the distinction, the Sakavādī asks the question and the other (Paravādī) gives the affirmation. The rest of the words in this discussion are clear in meaning.

## Commentary on the Discussion of the Acquisition of Wholesome States (Kusalapaṭilābhakathāvaṇṇanā).

## 3. Commentary on the Discussion of One Who Has Instigated an Immediate Offense (Anantarāpayuttakathāvaṇṇanā)

660-662. Now follows the discussion on one who has instigated an immediate offense (Anantarāpayuttakathā). In this context, an "instigator of an immediate offense" (anantarāpayutta) is one who commands an immediate offense (ānantariya kamma), such as matricide, which yields results in the existence immediately following the breaking up of the aggregates (death). In such a command, if a person commands with a fixed (irrevocable) command and that deed is to be done, that commander, because he has generated the volition that accomplishes the purpose (of killing), is fixed in wrongness (micchattaniyata) and is incapable of entering the path of rightness (sammattaniyāma). If a person commands with a non-fixed (revocable) command and that deed is to be done, that commander, because he has not yet generated the volition that accomplishes the purpose, is not yet fixed in wrongness and is still capable of entering the path of rightness. This is the conclusion in our own school (Sakavāda).

However, those like the Uttarāpathaka sect hold the view that even with a non-fixed command, one is incapable of entering the path of rightness. To refute their view, the Sakavādī first gives the opening part of the problem and has the Paravādī ask the question starting with "Anantarāpayutto". Therefore, the first question in this discussion is the Paravādī's question. The Sakavādī gives the affirmation, referring to the absence of the volition that accomplishes the purpose. After that, the Paravādī thinks, "That person is fixed in wrongness," simply because he has commanded a deed such as matricide. Therefore, he asks the question starting with "Micchattaniyāmañca". The Sakavādī, however, referring only to the fact that two fixed paths (the fixed path of wrongness and the fixed path of rightness) do not occur for a single individual, rejects it saying, "It is not so."

"Is it not that deed?" refers to the deed such as matricide. In that regard, referring to the non-fixed command, the Sakavādī affirms, "Yes." For, even in one who has instigated a non-fixed command, remorse (kukkucca) certainly arises, thinking, "I have done what is improper," and regret (vippaṭisāra) certainly occurs. The Paravādī says the statement starting with "Hañci" (If), taking only the occurrence of remorse, in order to establish his own view.

Now, since the Paravādī has prohibited the entry into the path of rightness for the instigator of an immediate offense who has given a non-fixed command, taking that same person...
236:
"Is the person who instigated an immediate offense incapable (of attaining the path and fruit)?" This question is the Sakavādī's question, and the other (Paravādī) affirms according to his own view. Then the Sakavādī, to challenge him, says "Has the mother been deprived of life?" and so on, meaning "An incapable person is one who performs deeds such as matricide; did he perform those deeds?" The other (Paravādī), not seeing such an act of killing because the mother and others are safe and sound, rejects it saying, "It is not so."

"Having withdrawn that deed" is said with reference to the non-fixed command. For, when one prevents the command, saying "Do not do what I commanded," it is called "withdrawn." Because it is withdrawn, remorse (kukkucca) is dispelled and regret (vippaṭisāra) is removed. Even though this is the case, the Paravādī, thinking that the initial command itself is fixed (niyata), affirms, "Yes." Then the Sakavādī, having made him accept that the deed has been withdrawn, says "If" (hañci) and so on to establish his own view.

Again, in the final question "Anantarāpayutto", the question is the Paravādī's, as in the first question, and the Sakavādī affirms. The inquiry "Is it not that deed (that was commanded)?" is the Paravādī's question, and the Sakavādī affirms, referring to the time of instigation before the time of withdrawal. Taking only the fact of having previously instigated, the Paravādī's attempt to establish his view with "If" (hañci) by way of a non-fixed (or fixed) command is his work. However, because this view is established in an improper way, it cannot be sustained.

## Commentary on the Discussion of One Who Has Instigated an Immediate Offense (Anantarāpayuttakathāvaṇṇanā).

## 4. Commentary on the Discussion of the Assurance of One Who is Assured (Niyatassa Niyāmakathāvaṇṇanā)

663-664. Now the discussion on the assurance of one who is assured (Niyatassa Niyāmakathā) will be shown. In that discussion, there are two kinds of assurance (niyāma): the assurance of wrongness (micchattaniyāma), which is the immediate offense (ānantariya kamma), and the assurance of rightness (sammattaniyāma), which is the Noble Path (ariya magga). Apart from these two assurances, there is no other assurance. All other remaining states belonging to the three planes are non-assured (aniyata). A person possessed of those states is also a non-assured person. However, a Bodhisatta who has been prophesied by the Buddhas through the power of their knowledge, "This being will reach enlightenment in the future," is called "assured" (niyata) because of the abundance of his merit. Taking only such a conventional term, "The Bodhisatta in his final existence..."
237:
"The Bodhisatta is capable of penetrating the Four Noble Truths in that birth," with this intention, the Pubbaseliyas and Aparaseliyas hold the view that "one who is fixed (niyata) enters the fixed path (niyāma)." With reference to them, the Proponent asks and the other (the Opponent) affirms. The words "wrongly fixed" (micchattaniyata) and so forth are spoken to show that for one who is fixed by one kind of fixed path, there is no other kind of fixed path. The words "having previously developed the path" and so forth are spoken to show the different types of fixed paths. The words "foundation of mindfulness" (satipaṭṭhāna) and so forth are spoken to show the distinction of specific dhammas even within a single fixed path. The statement "The Bodhisatta is capable" only shows the capability of the Bodhisatta; it does not show the entry into the fixed path by one who is already fixed. Therefore, it cannot be used as evidence (asādhaka). Indeed, that Bodhisatta, not yet being fixed by even a single fixed dhamma previously, entered the fixed path only by seeing the Truths at the foot of the Bodhi tree.

## Niyatassa Niyāmakathāvaṇṇanā.

## 5. Nivutakathāvaṇṇanā
665-667. Now is the discourse on one who is hindered (nivutakathā). In that discourse, because there is no task for a pure person to become pure, the Uttarāpathakas hold the view that "only one who is hindered, obstructed, and enveloped by hindrances (nīvaraṇa) abandons the hindrances." With reference to them, the Proponent asks "nivuto" (one who is hindered) and the other affirms. The words "one who is lustful [abandons] lust" and so forth are spoken to show the fault in the abandoning of hindrances by one who is hindered. The words "completely pure, bright" and so forth are spoken to show the purity of eradication (samuccheda-visuddhi) of one who is already pure through the purity of suppression (vikkhambhana-visuddhi). The words "for one who knows thus" and so forth show the destruction of taints (āsavakkhaya) for one who knows and sees; they do not show the abandoning of hindrances by one who is hindered. Therefore, it cannot be used as evidence (asādhaka).

## Nivutakathāvaṇṇanā.

## 6. Sammukhībhūtakathāvaṇṇanā
668-670. Now is the discourse on one in the presence (sammukhībhūtakathā). In that discourse, "sammukhībhūta" means one who has reached the state of being in the presence of the fetters (saṃyojana), the state of being possessed of them. The rest of the words here are just like the discourse on one who is hindered.

## Sammukhībhūtakathāvaṇṇanā.
238:
## 7. Commentary on the Discussion that One in Attainment Enjoys It (Samāpanno Assādetītikathāvaṇṇanā)

671-673. Now follows the discussion that one in attainment enjoys it. Therein, based on the statement "He enters and dwells in the first jhāna, and he enjoys it" (A.N. 4.123), the Andhaka school holds the view that "one who has entered attainment enjoys it, and that attachment to jhāna (jhānanikanti) has the jhāna itself as its object." With reference to them, the Sakavādī asks, "Does one in attainment enjoy it?" and the other (Paravādī) concedes. In the questions such as "Is that jhāna the object of that same jhāna?", although the opponent does not see the fact of it having itself as an object, he denies it out of fear of contradicting the Suttas, yet he concedes based merely on the words "he enjoys it." The Sutta "he enjoys it" refers to a jhāna-attainer who, having emerged from the jhāna, experiences the enjoyment of the jhāna; it does not establish that the craving which is attached to the jhāna has the jhāna as its object while within the attainment itself. Therefore, it is not a proof.

## Commentary on the Discussion that One in Attainment Enjoys It

## 8. Commentary on the Discussion of Lust for the Unpleasant (Asātarāgakathāvaṇṇanā)

Now follows the discussion of lust for the unpleasant (asātarāga). Therein, in the Sutta it is said: "Whatever feeling he feels, whether pleasant, painful, or neither-pleasant-nor-painful, he delights in that feeling, welcomes it" (M.N. 1.409), which was spoken in terms of delighting through wrong view (diṭṭhi). Based on the word "delights," the Uttarāpathaka school holds the view that "there is delight even in painful feeling through the power of lust that finds enjoyment; therefore, there is lust for the unpleasant (asātarāga)." With reference to them, the Sakavādī asks, "Is there lust for the unpleasant?" In that question, "lust for the unpleasant" means attachment to the unpleasant experience of pain, thinking, "O, would that this were mine!" The other concedes based on his own view, saying "Yes." The rest of the meaning here is clear.

675. In the Sutta "He delights in that feeling," however, there is no such thing as the arising of lust by taking the painful feeling itself as an object in a reversed manner. But by grasping as a whole, one who repeatedly views the phenomenon characterized by experiencing—or the painful feeling itself—as self, delights in the feeling through the delight of wrong view known as the obsession of views (diṭṭhi-maññanā). He delights in the change (vipariṇāma) of painful feeling; being overwhelmed by painful feeling, he [longs for] sensual pleasure which is the opposite of that painful feeling...
239:
...even while longing for (sensual pleasure), it is called "delighting in painful feeling." This is the intended meaning of delighting in painful feeling. Therefore, this does not prove the existence of lust for the unpleasant (asātarāga).

## Commentary on the Discussion of Lust for the Unpleasant

## 9. Commentary on the Discussion that Craving for Mental Objects is Indeterminate (Dhammataṇhā-abyākatātikathāvaṇṇanā)

676-680. Now follows the discussion that craving for mental objects (dhammataṇhā) is indeterminate. Therein, among the six cravings—craving for forms, etc.—because the very last craving is called "craving for mental objects," the Pubbaseliya school holds the view that it is indeterminate (abyākata). With reference to them, the Sakavādī questions and the Paravādī concedes. The meaning of the remaining questions follows the Pāḷi text. All six cravings are shown in summary by the three groups: craving for sensual pleasures (kāma-taṇhā), etc. Indeed, craving that proceeds by way of enjoying sensuality in the six objects such as forms is called craving for sensual pleasures. Craving accompanied by the eternalist view (sassata-diṭṭhi) that "the self and the world will exist" is called craving for existence (bhava-taṇhā). Craving accompanied by the annihilationist view (uccheda-diṭṭhi) that "they will not exist" is called craving for non-existence (vibhava-taṇhā). The term "craving for mental objects" (dhammataṇhā) only indicates the occurrence of craving with a mental object (dhammārammaṇa) as its basis; it does not indicate an indeterminate state. Therefore, this does not prove (the indeterminate nature).

## Commentary on the Discussion that Craving for Mental Objects is Indeterminate

## 10. Commentary on the Discussion that Craving for Mental Objects is Not the Origin of Suffering (Dhammataṇhā-nadukkhasamudayotikathāvaṇṇanā)

681-685. Now follows the discussion that craving for mental objects is not the origin of suffering. There too, because it is called "craving for mental objects," the Pubbaseliya school holds the view that it is not the origin of suffering. With reference to them, the Sakavādī questions and the Paravādī concedes. The rest is exactly like the previous discussion.

## Commentary on the Discussion that Craving for Mental Objects is Not the Origin of Suffering

## The Thirteenth Chapter (Teramaso Vaggo).

## 14. Fourteenth Chapter (Cuddasamavagga)

## 1. Commentary on the Discussion of the Succession of Wholesome and Unwholesome

686-690. Now, there is the discussion named Kusalākusala-paṭisandahana-kathā. In this discussion, since there is no wholesome state arising immediately after an unwholesome state, nor an unwholesome state arising immediately after a wholesome state, their mutual succession is not appropriate. However, those such as the Mahāsaṅghikas hold the view that because lust and aversion arise regarding the very same object, these two—wholesome and unwholesome—succeed each other. Referring to them, the proponent (Sakavādin) asks the question and the opponent (Paravādin) acknowledges. Both *āvaṭṭanā* (turning towards) and *paṇidhi* (aspiration/placement) are names for *āvajjana* (adverting). That adverting is called *āvaṭṭanā* because it turns the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*) around. It is called *paṇidhi* because it places or establishes the mind on an object other than the object of the life-continuum. By the passage "For one who does not advert to the wholesome," it is asked whether that wholesome state, which arises in succession to the unwholesome, occurs in the continuum of one for whom adverting (mind-door adverting) does not occur. The opponent, not seeing the arising of wholesome states without adverting, denies it. This statement, "For one who attends unwisely to the wholesome," is said for the purpose of challenging: if wholesome arises immediately after unwholesome, would it arise for one who attends unwisely through the very adverting of the unwholesome? The remaining passages are clear according to the Pāḷi text. The phrase "In the same object" shows only the arising of lust and the fading of lust regarding a single object; it does not show the immediate succession of wholesome and unwholesome. Therefore, it is an inconclusive argument.

## Commentary on the Discussion of the Succession of Wholesome and Unwholesome.

## 2. Commentary on the Discussion of the Arising of the Six Bases

691-692. Now, there is the discussion named Saḷāyatanuppatti-kathā. In this discussion, for spontaneously born beings (*opapātika*), the six bases arise together with the rebirth-linking consciousness (*paṭisandhicitta*) that seeks rebirth. For womb-born beings (*gabbhaseyyaka*), among the six internal bases, only the mind-base (*manāyatana*) and body-base (*kāyāyatana*) arise at the moment of rebirth-linking. The remaining four bases arise only when seventy-seven nights have passed. That these four bases arise due to the same kamma that took rebirth-linking, or due to another kamma, is the doctrine of our own school (Sakavāda). However, those such as the Pubbaseliyas hold the view that because a single kamma can produce all six bases, the six bases arise at the very moment of rebirth-linking in the mother's womb, just as the sprout of a tree with complete branches and twigs exists even at the stage of the seed. Referring to them, the proponent asks "The six bases..." and the opponent acknowledges. The phrase "Complete with all major and minor limbs" etc., is said for the purpose of challenging: if there were six bases, would one enter the mother's womb complete with all major and minor limbs? The question "For one who has entered the mother's womb" is the opponent's question. "It should not be said later" and "In the mother's womb... the hairs..." are the proponent's questions. In this discussion, the remaining groups of words are clear in meaning.

## Commentary on the Discussion of the Arising of the Six Bases.
241:
The phrase beginning with "If there are six bases, does one descend [into the womb] being of such a nature as having all limbs and organs?" is spoken for the purpose of a challenge. The question "mātukucchigata-ssa" (to one who has entered the mother's womb) is the Paravādin's question. Thereafter, the question "mātukucchigatassa pacchā kesā" (after entering the mother's womb, the hairs...) is the Sakavādin's question. The remaining text in this Saḷāyatanuppatti-kathā has a clear meaning.

## Commentary on the Discussion of the Arising of the Six Bases.

## 3. Commentary on the Discussion of Proximity Condition

693-697. Now, there is the discussion named 'Anantara-paccaya-kathā'. In this discussion, seeing the rapid change of seeing forms and hearing sounds in dancing, singing, etc., those such as the Uttarāpathakas hold the view that "these consciousnesses arise in immediate succession to one another." Referring to them, the question beginning with "cakkhuviññāṇassa" (of eye-consciousness) is the Sakavādin's question, and the acknowledgement is the Paravādin's. The statement beginning with "sotaviññāṇaṃ rūpārammaṇaṃyeva" (ear-consciousness has only a visible form as its object) is spoken to challenge that if ear-consciousness were to arise immediately after eye-consciousness, it would have a visible form as its object, like the resultant mind-element (vipāka-manodhātu). In the problems beginning with "dependent on the eye and visible forms, ear-consciousness arises," the opponent first denies it because of the absence of a Sutta in the Pali text, but later acknowledges it by the power of their own view, while noting the immediate arising. With the statement beginning with "is that same eye-consciousness that ear-consciousness?", the Sakavādin asks: just as the second impulsion (javana) is that same impulsion by being mind-consciousness immediately after the first impulsion, according to your (the Paravādin's) wish, are these two—eye-consciousness and ear-consciousness—also one and the same? In this manner, the meaning should be understood in all sections. The statement beginning with "naccati gāyati" (dances, sings) only shows the state of being mixed due to the rapid change in the meeting of objects; it does not show the state of proximity condition (anantara-paccaya). Therefore, it means the evidence is not established.

## Commentary on the Discussion of Proximity Condition.

## 4. Commentary on the Discussion of Noble Form

698-699. Now, there is the discussion named 'Ariya-rūpa-kathā'. In this discussion, those such as the Uttarāpathakas hold the view that Right Speech (sammā-vācā) and Right Action (sammā-kammanta) are form (rūpa), and that form is derived form (upādā-rūpa) because of the teaching: "All form consists of the four great elements and form derived from the four great elements." Referring to them, the question beginning with "ariya-rūpaṃ mahābhūtānaṃ upādāya" (is noble form derived from the great elements?) is the Sakavādin's question.
242:
This is the question of the Sakavādin. In this Ariyarūpakathā, it is called 'Ariyarūpa' (Noble Form) either because it is the form of the Noble Ones (Ariyas) or because it is form that is Noble. The opponent (Paravādin), standing by his own view, affirms, "It is so." When asked if it is wholesome (kusala), he also affirms it solely by the power of his own view. The same method applies to the questions on 'Anāsava' (taintless) and so forth. Setting aside the Sutta beginning with "Whatever form...", [the Buddha] shows only the derived nature (upādā-bhāva) of the remaining form based on the great elements (mahābhūta), but not the derived nature of Sammā-vācā (Right Speech) and Sammā-kammanta (Right Action). If for those [Sammā-vācā and Sammā-kammanta] even the mere state of being form is not established, how could the state of being derived form (upādā-rūpa) be established? Therefore, that view is without proof.

## Ariyarūpakathāvaṇṇanā.

## 5. Añño Anusayotikathāvaṇṇanā

700-701. Now follows the Añño Anusayotikathā (The discourse that latent tendency is different). In that discourse, because a worldling (puthujjana), while a wholesome or indeterminate (avyākata) consciousness is occurring, is said to be 'one with latent tendency' (sānusaya) but not 'one who is obsessed' (pariyuṭṭhita), those such as the Andhakas hold the view that the latent tendency (anusaya) is one thing and the obsession (pariyuṭṭhāna) is another. With reference to them, the Sakavādin asks, "Is the latent tendency of sensual lust (kāmarāgānusaya) different?" and the other affirms it. The rest should be understood according to the method stated below in the Anusayakathā. The words beginning with "Sānusayo" only show that at that time, because the latent tendency has not been abandoned, one is said to be 'one with latent tendency', and because the defilements have not arisen [as an outburst], one is said to be 'not obsessed'; it does not show that the latent tendency and the obsession are different. Therefore, that view is without proof.

## Añño Anusayotikathāvaṇṇanā.

## 6. Pariyuṭṭhānaṃ Cittavippayuttantikathāvaṇṇanā

Now follows the Pariyuṭṭhānaṃ Cittavippayuttantikathā (The discourse that obsession is dissociated from mind). In that discourse, because defilements such as lust (rāga) can arise even in a person who is attending [to objects] as impermanent (anicca) and so forth. It has also been said: "O Bhāradvāja, sometimes although I think, 'I will attend to it as foul (asubha)', I only attend to it as beautiful (subha)." Therefore, with reference to those such as the Andhakas who hold the view that obsession is dissociated from mind, the Sakavādin asks the question, and the other affirms it. The rest of the meaning here is clear.

## Pariyuṭṭhānaṃ Cittavippayuttantikathāvaṇṇanā.
243:
## 7. Pariyāpannakathāvaṇṇanā

703-705. Now follows the Pariyāpannakathā (The discourse on inclusion). In that discourse, because sensual lust (kāmarāga) underlies (anuseti) the sense realm (kāmadhātu) and is also said to be 'included in the sense realm' (kāmadhātu-pariyāpanna), those such as the Andhakas and Sammitiyas hold the view that lust for form (rūparāga) and lust for the formless (arūparāga) also underlie the form realm and formless realm, and are indeed included in the form realm and formless realm. With reference to them, the Sakavādin asks the question "Rūparāga..." and the other affirms it. In that question, 'underlies' (anuseti) means: just as sensual lust underlies the sense realm, known as sensual thought (kāma-vitakka), by way of co-nascent (sahajāta) influence, does lust for form underlie the form realm in the same way according to your view? This is the question. 'Included' (pariyāpanna) also means: just as that sensual lust is included in the three-fold sense realm by way of defiled sensuality (kilesa-kāma) and is thus 'included in the sense realm', is lust for form also included in the form realm in the same way according to your view? This is the question. The other, not grasping the intention of the Sakavādin, affirms "Yes" solely by the power of his own view. Then, to make him realize that meaning, the Sakavādin asks by comparing it with the states known as wholesome, resultant, and functional, such as 'samāpattesiya' (belonging to attainment), saying "Samāpattesiyo..." and so forth. The rest of the discourse here proceeds according to the Pali text. Does not the statement "Kāmarāga..." and so forth show only the latent nature and inclusion of sensual lust in the sense realm, and not of the others in the other realms?

## Pariyāpannakathāvaṇṇanā.

## 8. Abyākatakathāvaṇṇanā

706-708. Now follows the Abyākatakathā (The discourse on the indeterminate). In that discourse, the four-fold indeterminate (abyākata) states known as resultant (vipāka), functional (kiriya), form (rūpa), and Nibbāna are called 'indeterminate' because they do not produce fruit. However, a wrong view (diṭṭhigata) is called 'indeterminate' (unanswered) because it was not declared [by the Buddha] in terms of being eternal and so forth, as in: "Vaccha, this view that 'the world is eternal' is indeterminate (unanswered)." Without grasping this distinction, those such as the Andhakas and Uttarāpathakas hold the view that wrong view is also 'indeterminate' (karmically neutral) like the first-mentioned indeterminate. To show them that distinction, the Sakavādin asks "Diṭṭhigataṃ abyākataṃ?" and the other affirms it. The rest of the discourse here proceeds according to the Pali text.

## Abyākatakathāvaṇṇanā.
244:
## 9. Apariyāpannakathāvaṇṇanā
709-710. Now is the Apariyāpannakathā. In this Apariyāpannakathā, although an ordinary person (puthujjana) who has attained jhāna can be said to be free from lust (rāga) regarding sensual pleasures, they cannot be said to be free from wrong view (diṭṭhi). Therefore, the Pubbaseliyas hold the view that wrong view is "unincluded" (apariyāpanna) [in the mundane]. The question is asked by the Sakavādī with reference to them, and the other (Paravādī) accepts. The rest of the discussion here proceeds according to the Pali text.

## Apariyāpannakathāvaṇṇanā.

## Cuddasamovaggo (Fourteenth Chapter).

## 15. Pannarasamavagga (Fifteenth Chapter)

## 1. Paccayatākathāvaṇṇanā
711-717. Now is the Paccayatākathā. In this Paccayatākathā, the Mahāsaṅghikas hold the view that causal efficacy (paccayatā) is specifically delimited. Their reasoning is that when a certain state among the six root-causes (hetu) acts as a condition by way of the root-cause condition (hetupaccaya), although it assists its resultants through that root-cause condition, it does not assist those same resultants through the object (ārammaṇa), proximity (anantara), or contiguity (samanantara) conditions. Alternatively, when a certain state among the six objects acts as a condition by way of the object condition, it does not assist those same resultants through the proximity or contiguity conditions. Thus, they believe the efficacy known as being a condition is separately delimited for each. The question is asked by the Sakavādī with reference to them, and the other accepts. The rest of the discussion here proceeds according to the Pali text.

## Paccayatākathāvaṇṇanā.

## 2. Aññamaññapaccayakathāvaṇṇanā
718-719. Now is the Aññamaññapaccayakathā. In this Aññamaññapaccayakathā, in the doctrine of the Mahāsaṅghikas, there is only the Pali text stating "with ignorance as condition, formations arise," but there is no Pali text stating "with formations as condition, ignorance arises." Therefore, they hold the view that only ignorance is a condition for formations, but formations are not a condition for ignorance. With reference to them, the Sakavādī asks the question to show that there is also a mutuality condition (aññamaññapaccaya) between ignorance, formations, and so on, and the other accepts...
245:
In the view of the other (Paravādī), in this context of "Is ignorance conascent with formations?", only unmeritorious formations (apuññābhisaṅkhāra) are taken. Because unmeritorious formations are thus taken, in this Pali passage "Ignorance also arises due to formations as a condition," the conditionality should be understood by way of conascence (sahajāta), mutuality (aññamañña), presence (atthi), non-disappearance (avigata), and association (sampayutta). In this context of "Craving also arises due to clinging as a condition," excluding clinging to sense-pleasures (kāmupādāna), the remaining three types of clinging should be understood as conditions for craving, just as ignorance is for unmeritorious formations. The rest follows the Pali text. The question "Is it due to aging and death as a condition?" is the Paravādī's question, and the question "Does name-and-form arise due to consciousness as a condition?" is the Sakavādī's question.

## Commentary on the Discourse on Mutual Condition (Aññamaññapaccayakathā).

## 3. Commentary on the Discourse on Time (Addhākathā)

720-721. Now follows the Discourse on Time. In that Discourse on Time, based on the Sutta "Monks, there are these three topics of discussion" (A. iii. 68), some Paravādīs hold the view that there exists a produced thing called "time" (addhā), which is designated as time (kāla). To show the distinction that "There is no produced thing called time apart from the mere designation of time; rather, only the aggregates such as form are produced," the question "Is time produced?" is asked by the Sakavādī, and the affirmation is by the other (Paravādī). When he affirms, the Buddha (or Sakavādī) says "Is it form?" etc., to challenge him: "If that time is produced, it should be one of these, such as form." The other (Paravādī) denies it. The rest follows the Pali text.

## Commentary on the Discourse on Time.

## 4. Commentary on the Discourse on Moments, Instants, and Muhuttas (Khaṇalayamuhuttakathā)

722-723. The same method applies to the discourses on moments (khaṇa), instants (laya), and muhuttas. All these, such as moments, are merely synonyms for time (addhā).

## Commentary on the Discourse on Moments, Instants, and Muhuttas.

## 5. Commentary on the Discourse on Taints (Āsavakathā)

724-725. Now follows the Discourse on Taints. Therein, because there is no other taint beyond the four taints, by which the four taints would be conascent with taints...
246:
...the four cankers would be accompanied by cankers; therefore, the Hetuvādīs hold the view that the four cankers are "without cankers" (anāsava). The question is asked by the Sakavādī with reference to them, and the other accepts. Then, to challenge them, "If, according to your wish, the cankers are without cankers, then these cankers should possess the characteristics of the Path (magga) and so on," the Sakavādī speaks the words beginning with "Maggo." The rest of the discussion here has an obvious meaning.

## Commentary on Āsavakathā.

## 6. Commentary on Jarāmaraṇakathā
726-727. Now is the Jarāmaraṇakathā. In this Jarāmaraṇakathā, because old age and death (jarāmaraṇa) are not produced (aparinipphanna), they should not be called either mundane (lokiya) or supramundane (lokuttara). The reason is that in the dyad (duka) of "mundane states and supramundane states," jarāmaraṇa is pointed out neither in the mundane category nor in the supramundane category. Here, without taking this characteristic into account, the Mahāsaṅghikas hold the view that the old age and death of supramundane states is supramundane. The question is asked by the Sakavādī with reference to them, and the other accepts. The rest of the discussion here proceeds according to the Pali text.

## Commentary on Jarāmaraṇakathā.

## 7. Commentary on Saññāvedayitakathā
728-729. Now is the Saññāvedayitakathā. In this Saññāvedayitakathā, the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling (saññāvedayitanirodhasamāpatti) is not any particular state, but merely the cessation of the four aggregates. Therefore, that attainment is neither mundane nor supramundane. However, the Hetuvādīs hold the view that because it is not mundane, it must be supramundane. The question is asked by the Sakavādī with reference to them, and the other accepts. The rest of the discussion is similar to the previous discourse.

## Commentary on Saññāvedayitakathā.
247:
## 8. Commentary on the Second Discourse on the Cessation of Perception and Feeling

730-731. Now, because that attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling is not supramundane, it is mundane—this is the view held by the Hetuvādins. With reference to them, there is the question of the Sakavādin and the affirmation of the other (the Paravādin). The rest is the same as what was said before.

## Commentary on the Second Discourse on the Cessation of Perception and Feeling.

## 9. Commentary on the Third Discourse on the Cessation of Perception and Feeling

Now, because there is no fixed law (niyāma) regarding the mortality of beings, such as 'this person is of a nature to die, that person is not of a nature to die,' those such as the Rājagirikas hold the view that even a person who has attained the cessation of perception and feeling (saññāvedayitanirodhasamāpatti) might pass away. To show the time of death and the time of non-death even for one who has attained that state, there is the question of the Sakavādin and the affirmation of the other. Furthermore, since one who passes away must possess contact (phassa) and so on occurring at the moment of death, the Sakavādin asks, 'Does one who has attained the cessation of perception and feeling have contact at the moment of death?' and so forth, in order to challenge them in that manner.

When asked questions such as 'Does one without contact pass away?', the Paravādin denies it with reference to other beings besides those who have attained the cessation of perception and feeling. When asked 'Would poison enter?', etc., he denies it with reference to the power of the attainment. In the second round, he affirms it with reference to the natural state of the body. If he affirms it thus, the Sakavādin interrogates him, saying that there is no such thing as the power of the attainment, and for that very reason, he is not one who has attained cessation.

733-734. The question 'Can one not die?' is the question of the Paravādin. Regarding the Paravādin's problem, 'Is there such a fixed law (niyāma)?', the Sakavādin denies it because there is no such thing as that kind of fixed law. The passage beginning with 'one endowed with eye-consciousness' is stated by the Sakavādin to show that 'even if there is no fixed law, one dies only at the time of death, not at a time that is not the time of death.' The meaning therein is this: if passing away were to occur due to the absence of a fixed law, it would also occur for one endowed with eye-consciousness. Then there would be a contradiction with the Sutta which says, 'One does not pass away or take rebirth with the five consciousnesses.' Just as there is no passing away for one endowed with eye-consciousness, so it should be understood that there is no passing away for one who has attained cessation.

## Commentary on the Third Discourse on the Cessation of Perception and Feeling.

## 10. Commentary on the Discourse on Leading to the Unconscious Realm

Now there is the discourse on leading to the unconscious realm (Asaññasattūpikā-kathā). In that discourse, both the unconscious attainment (asaññasamāpatti) and the attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti), which occur through the development of revulsion toward perception, are called 'attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling' (saññāvedayitanirodhasamāpatti). Thus, there are two kinds of attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling: mundane and supramundane. Among them, the mundane attainment of the worldling (puthujjana) leads to the unconscious realm; the supramundane attainment of the Noble Ones (ariya), however, does not lead to the unconscious realm. But without making this distinction, those such as the Hetuvādins hold the view that, without qualification, the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling leads to the unconscious realm. With reference to them, the Sakavādin asks and the Paravādin affirms. Furthermore, since one who has entered the unconscious attainment possesses non-greed (alobha) and so on, while one in the attainment of cessation does not, the Sakavādin says 'Atthi' (There is) and so on, to challenge them by way of those states.

Here too, in the question 'Asaññī' (Is he unconscious?), unconsciousness is conceded here in the sense of having attained it through revulsion toward perception, and there in the unconscious realm by virtue of being an unconscious being. Therefore, the Paravādin who establishes his view by taking this affirmation does so by means of a verbal trick (chala). Or else, unconsciousness is conceded here with reference to the attainment of cessation. There too, it is conceded with reference only to the attainment of cessation of a Non-returner (anāgāmī) who has passed away from here. Therefore, the view established by this affirmation is indeed not established.

## The Commentary on the Discourse on Leading to the Unconscious Realm is finished.

## 11. Commentary on the Discourse on the Accumulation of Kamma

Now there is the discourse on the accumulation of kamma (Kammūpacaya-kathā). Therein, those such as the Andhakas and Sammitiyas hold the view that what is called 'accumulation of kamma' is something other than kamma, dissociated from mind (cittavippayutta), indeterminate (abyākata), and without an object (anārammaṇa). With reference to them, the Sakavādin asks 'Is it other than kamma?' and the Paravādin affirms. Then, to challenge him by saying 'If the accumulation of kamma is other than kamma, then there should also be an accumulation of contact (phassūpacaya) other than contact (phassa), etc.', the Sakavādin says 'Is it other than contact?' and so forth. The other denies it because they do not hold such a view.
249:
738-739. In the questions 'Is it co-nascent (sahajāta) with kamma?', he denies it with reference to the accumulation dissociated from mind, and affirms it with reference to the accumulation associated with mind. In the questions 'Is it wholesome (kusala)?', he also denies it with reference to the accumulation dissociated from mind and affirms it with reference to the accumulation associated with mind. In the subsequent questions 'Is it unwholesome (akusala)?', the method is the same.

740. When asked 'Does it have an object (sārammaṇa)?', the Paravādin denies it because he definitely desires it to be without an object. The phrase 'when the mind is perishing' (cittaṃ bhijjamānaṃ) means that when the mind perishes, kamma also perishes. Or, it is the nominative case used in the sense of the locative (sattami), meaning 'while the mind is perishing' (citte bhijjamāne). Or, this very reading 'citte bhijjamāne' is the original text. Therein, because that which is associated with mind perishes while that which is dissociated does not, he both affirms and denies.

741. 'Is there accumulation in kamma?' means that if there is kamma, there is accumulation, or if kamma is established, accumulation is established; and only from the accumulation of kamma does the result (vipāka) arise. He affirms this because he holds the view that when that kamma has ceased, the accumulation of kamma remains until the result arises, just as a seed remains until the sprout is produced. The question 'Is that kamma itself the accumulation? Is that accumulation itself the result of kamma?' is asked to inquire about the identity of these three, because he holds the view that there is accumulation in kamma and that it remains until the result arises. The question 'Does the result have an object?' is asked as a challenge, implying 'Is not the accumulation, which is of the nature of a result, also connected with an object just like the result itself?'. The other (Paravādin), however, affirms one and denies the other by the power of his view. In the inverse (paṭiloma) questions as well, the method is the same. The rest here should be understood according to the Pali text itself.

## Commentary on the Discourse on the Accumulation of Kamma.

## 16. Soḷasamavagga
## 1. Niggahakathāvaṇṇanā
743-744. Now begins the Niggahakathā (Discourse on Restraint). In this Niggahakathā, if those persons in the world who have attained the power of knowledge and have achieved mastery were unable to restrain the minds of others, what would be the use of their attainment of power? What would be the nature of their mastery? Indeed, it is the view of the Mahāsaṅghikas and others that, because of their attainment of power and their mastery, such persons can certainly and definitely restrain the minds of others. With reference to those persons, the question "Does one restrain the mind of another?" is the question of the Sakavādī, and the affirmation is that of the opponent. In that question, "restrains" means being able to prevent one from falling into defilement (saṅkilesa). The remaining words in this Niggahakathā follow the Pali text exactly. The same method applies to the Paggahakathā (Discourse on Exertion).
## Niggahakathāvaṇṇanā.
## 3. Sukhānuppadါnakathāvaṇṇanā
747-748. Now begins the Sukhānuppadānakathā (Discourse on Bestowing Happiness). In this Sukhānuppadānakathā, based on the Sutta passage, "The Blessed One is indeed the bringer of many happy states to us," it is the view of the Hetuvādins and others that one person can bestow happiness upon another accordingly. With reference to them, the Sakavādī asks the question and the opponent affirms. When asked, "Can one bestow suffering accordingly?", the opponent rejects it because they do not see such a Sutta passage. In the problem of "one's own happiness" and so on, one cannot give that happiness which belongs to oneself or to another. Thinking, "In the happiness that belongs only to that person, how can there be such a thing as bestowing?", the opponent rejects it. In the problem of "neither one's own" and so on, the opponent affirms according to their own view, thinking that such a kind of happiness does not deserve to be called "bestowed." The Sakavādī says the words "No ca vata re" because of the non-existence of such happiness. The statement "bringer of happy states" (sukhadhammānaṃ upahattā) merely demonstrates that the Blessed One is the condition (paccaya) for the arising of happiness in others; it does not mean bestowing happiness in the same way as giving rice and so on. Therefore, it does not serve as proof.
## Sukhānuppadါnakathāvaṇṇanā.
251:
## 4. Adhigayhamanasikārakathāvaṇṇanā
749-753. Now begins the commentary on the Adhigayhamanasikārakathā (Discourse on Comprehensive Attention). In this context, attention (manasikāra) is of two kinds: by way of method (naya) and by way of object (ārammaṇa). Of these two, when the impermanence of a single formation (saṅkhāra) is seen, attention by way of method occurs regarding the remaining formations, thinking, "All formations are impermanent." One who is attending to past formations is unable to attend to future formations. Attending to any one of the past, etc., is attention by way of object. In thus attending by way of object, one who is attending to present formations cannot, at that same present moment, attend back to the very mind with which they are attending to those formations. In this regard, based on the statement "All formations are impermanent," etc., the Pubbaseliyas and Aparaseliyas hold the view that "attending means comprehensively grasping and including all formations to attend to them as a whole." With reference to them, the Sakavādī asks the question and the opponent affirms.

Then, for one who attends to all as a whole, the mind with which they attend to those formations must also be an object of attention. Therefore, to examine the existence of that mind, the Sakavādī said, "with that mind." The opponent rejects it, intending that it cannot be known by making it an object. Then, the opponent affirms again, intending that since the mind is already known as having such characteristics, that mind is also already known. Or else, they reject it, thinking that the mind itself cannot be the object of that same mind. They affirm by the power of the view that has arisen based on the Pali, "All formations are impermanent; when one sees with wisdom," and so on. In the remaining two problems, the method is the same. However, in "with that contact" (phassa) and so on, the opponent simply rejects it because they do not find such a Sutta. In the problems concerning the past, etc., the rejection and affirmation should be understood according to the method stated below. The remaining text follows the Pali exactly. The statement "all formations," etc., is spoken with reference to seeing by way of method, not with reference to seeing by way of object in a single moment. Therefore, it does not serve as proof.
## Adhigayhamanasikārakathāvaṇṇanā.
## 5. Rūpaṃ Hetūtikathāvaṇṇanā
754-756. Now begins the commentary on the Rūpaṃ Hetūtikathā (Discourse on "Matter is a Cause"). In this context, "cause" (hetu) is the name for an actual root cause such as a wholesome root (kusalāmūla), and it is also the name for any condition (paccaya) whatsoever.
252:
However, without making this distinction, relying merely on the statement "The four great essentials are causes," those like the Uttarāpathakas hold the view that "Matter is a cause" without qualification. With reference to them, the Sakavādin asks and the other (Paravādin) accepts. When it is said "Non-greed is a cause," the question is asked: "According to your view, is matter the cause called non-greed?" The other denies it. The same method applies to the remaining questions. In the passage "The great essentials are the causal basis (upādāya-hetu) for derived matter," the state of being a cause is spoken of in the sense of a condition (paccaya), not in the sense of a root (mūla). Therefore, it does not prove [their position].

## Commentary on the Discussion: Matter is a Cause (Rūpaṃ hetūti).

757-759. In the discussion on "Having a cause" (Sahetuka-kathā), the meaning should be understood in this same way.

## Commentary on the Discussion: Matter has a Cause (Rūpaṃ sahetukanti).

## 7. Commentary on the Discussion: Matter is Wholesome or Unwholesome (Rūpaṃ kusalākusalanti)

760-764. Now comes the discussion: Matter is Wholesome or Unwholesome. Therein, relying on the statement "Bodily action and vocal action are wholesome and unwholesome," those like the Mahīśāsakas and Sammitīyas hold the view that bodily intimation and vocal intimation, called bodily and vocal action, are wholesome and unwholesome. With reference to them, the Sakavādin asks "Is matter wholesome?" and the other accepts. Then, to examine him [with the thought], "If, according to your view, matter is wholesome, it should be of such a nature as having an object (sārammaṇa), etc.," [the Buddha] said "Sārammaṇaṃ," etc. The same method applies to the question on "unwholesome" that follows. The remaining words here have an obvious meaning.

## Commentary on the Discussion: Matter is Wholesome or Unwholesome.

## 8. Commentary on the Discussion: Matter is a Result (Rūpaṃ vipākoti)

765-767. Now comes the discussion: Matter is a Result. Therein, those like the Andhakas and Sammitīyas hold the view that just as consciousness and mental factors arise because of having performed kamma, so too that matter which arises because of having performed kamma is a result (vipāka)...
253:
With reference to them, there is the question of the Sakavādin and the acceptance of the other. Then, to examine him [with the thought], "If, according to your view, matter is a result, it should have such a nature as being associated with pleasant feeling (sukhavedanīya), etc.," [the Buddha] said "Sukhavedanīyaṃ," etc. The rest proceeds according to the Pali text itself.

## Commentary on the Discussion: Matter is a Result.

## 9. Commentary on the Discussion: Matter belongs to the Fine-material and Immaterial Spheres (Rūpaṃ rūpāvacara-arūpāvacaranti)

768-770. Now comes the discussion: Matter belongs to the Fine-material and Immaterial Spheres. Therein, those like the Andhakas hold the view that just as matter produced by kamma of the sense sphere is of the sense sphere (kāmāvacara), so too matter produced by kamma of the fine-material and immaterial spheres must be of the fine-material and immaterial spheres. With reference to them, the Sakavādin asks "Does matter belong to the fine-material and immaterial spheres?" and the other accepts. The rest here is according to the method already mentioned previously.

## Commentary on the Discussion: Matter belongs to the Fine-material and Immaterial Spheres.

## 10. Commentary on the Discussion: Inclusion in the Fine-material and Immaterial Elements (Rūpārūpadhātu-pariyāpanna-kathā)

771-775. Now comes the discussion: Lust for the fine-material sphere is included in the fine-material element, and lust for the immaterial sphere is included in the immaterial element. Therein, those like the Andhakas hold the view that just as lust for the sense sphere is included in the sense element, so too lust for the fine-material and immaterial spheres must be included in the fine-material and immaterial elements. With reference to them, there is the question of the Sakavādin and the acceptance of the other. The rest should be understood by the method already mentioned previously. Specifically, in that discussion, the phrase "lies latent in the fine-material element, lies latent in the immaterial element" is the only distinction. That view belongs to the Andhakas and Sammitīyas. [But] this view belongs only to the Andhakas.

Commentary on the discussion: Lust for the fine-material sphere is included in the fine-material element, and lust for the immaterial sphere is included in the immaterial element.

## Commentary on the Discussion: Inclusion in the Fine-material and Immaterial Elements.
