## 17. Chapter Seventeen (Sattarasama Vagga)

## 1. Commentary on the Discussion: The Arahant has Accumulation of Merit (Atthi arahato puññūpacaya-kathā)

776-779. Now comes the discussion: The Arahant has Accumulation of Merit. Therein, seeing the Arahant's acts such as giving, sharing, and worshipping a shrine, those like the Andhakas hold the view that "The Arahant has accumulation of merit." With reference to them, the Sakavādin asks and the other (Andhaka) accepts. Then, to challenge him [with the thought], "An Arahant is one who has abandoned both merit and evil; if he were to perform merit, he would also perform evil," [the Sakavādin] says "There is no accumulation of evil." The other denies it, as he does not see acts such as killing. In the problems such as "meritorious formations" (puññābhisaṅkhāra), he denies it, considering that the Arahant has no kamma that leads to [future] existence. In the problems such as "He would give a gift," the Sakavādin accepts because the occurrence of giving, etc., with functional consciousness (kiriyacitta) is evident. The other establishes his view merely by seeing the occurrence of the action, without taking the consciousness (as an indeterminate functional mind) into account. However, because that view is established improperly, it is as if it were not established at all.

## Commentary on the Discussion: The Arahant has Accumulation of Merit.

## 2. Commentary on the Discussion: The Arahant has no Untimely Death (Natthi arahato akālamaccū-kathā)

Now comes the discussion: The Arahant has no Untimely Death. Therein, improperly grasping the meaning of the Sutta, "Monks, I do not say that there is an ending of volitional kammas that have been performed and accumulated without having experienced [their results]" (A. Ni. 10.217), those like the Rājagirikas and Siddhatthikas hold the view that "An Arahant must attain Parinibbāna only after experiencing the results of all kamma; therefore, the Arahant has no untimely death." With reference to them, the Sakavādin asks and the other accepts. Then, to challenge him [with the thought], "If that Arahant has no untimely death, there should be no such thing as a killer of an Arahant," [the Sakavādin] says "There is no killer of an Arahant." The other denies it because of the existence of heinous crimes (ānantariya-kamma) and such persons. 

In the problem "Poison would not affect him," he denies it with the view: "As long as previously performed kamma is not yet exhausted, so long [poison] cannot affect him; it can only affect him when that kamma is exhausted." The rest proceeds according to the Pali text itself.
255:
Monks, this sutta, 'I [do not say]...', was spoken with reference to the following meaning: I do not say that there is an ending of volitional actions (sañcetanika kamma) that have been performed and accumulated without having experienced, attained, or undergone their results. Among those actions, kamma to be experienced in the present life (diṭṭhadhammavedanīya) gives its result in the present life itself, and not beyond that. Kamma to be experienced in the next life (upapajjavedanīya) gives its result only after arising in the next life, and not beyond that. Kamma to be experienced in subsequent lives (aparāpariyavedanīya) gives its result whenever it finds an opportunity, or in such successive rounds of rebirth. Thus, in all respects, as long as the cycle of saṃsāra continues, when kamma finds its turn to give results, there is no place in this world where one can stand and be free from evil kamma. While this is the truth, the establishment of the view that 'there is no untimely death (akālamaraṇa) for Arahants' based on the speculation that 'even kamma that has not yet found its turn to result must certainly be experienced by an Arahant' is indeed a wrong action.

## The Explanation of the Discourse on 'There is no Untimely Death for an Arahant' is finished.

## 3. Explanation of the Discourse on 'All this is due to Kamma'

Now comes the discourse known as 'All this is due to Kamma' (Sabbāmidaṃ kammato). In this discourse, based on the sutta 'The world revolves through kamma' (Kammunā vattati loko), the members of the Rājagirika and Siddhatthika sects hold the view that 'this entire round of kamma, round of defilements, and round of results (kammavaṭṭa, kilesavaṭṭa, vipākavaṭṭa) occurs only because of kamma.' With reference to them, the Sakavādin asks, 'Is all this [due to kamma]?' and the other (Paravādin) affirms it. Then, to challenge him with 'If so, then kamma must also arise from kamma,' the Sakavādin asks, 'Is kamma also due to kamma?' The other denies it, thinking that if kamma were also due to kamma, then that kamma would merely be a result (vipāka).

To challenge him with 'If all this is due to kamma, then it must be due to the cause of what was done in the past (pubbekatahetu),' the Sakavādin asks [about it]. The other denies it, fearing the doctrine of past-action determinism (pubbekatahetuvāda).

[The Sakavādin] asks to challenge: 'If all this is due to kamma, then the kamma that was the cause occurring in a past life must also be due to kamma in a previous life, thus becoming a result of kamma (kammavipāka). Therefore, according to your view, does it not follow that all this is a result of kamma?' The other denies it, referring to the arising of kamma occurring in the present, just as a sprout arises from a seed. When asked a second time, he affirms that just as a seed arises from a previous seed, so too that kamma arises from previous kamma.

The words 'One might kill a living being...' etc. [were spoken]. This is stated to challenge: 'If all is due to the result of kamma, then actions such as killing (pāṇātipāta) would be performed only through the result of kamma.' The other affirms this view, thinking that the volition of an immoral person also arises from previous kamma and is thus, in a way, only a result (vipāka). Then, to challenge him, [the Sakavādin] asks, 'Is there a fruit (phala)?' meaning, 'If your act of killing arises from the result of kamma, then like the act of killing, would the result not also become a thing that has a fruit?' The other affirms that there is a fruit, seeing that killing leads to hell, etc. However, he denies it regarding the result (vipāka) of kamma because he does not see any Pali passage stating 'this is the fruit' of a result. The same method applies to stealing (adinnādāna) and so on. In the passages concerning the sick (gilāna), etc., the question 'Is there a fruit?' asks about the fruit of giving (dāna) in relation to the articles to be offered. The sutta 'Kammunā vattati'...
256:
...affirms it because that kamma arises from previous kamma, just as a seed arises from a previous seed. The words 'One might kill a living being' etc., are stated to challenge: 'If all is due to the result of kamma, then one would perform killing etc., only by the result of kamma.' The other affirms this view, as even the volition of immorality is produced by previous kamma and is thus, in one sense, only a result. Then, to challenge him, [the Sakavādin] says, 'Is it fruitful?' meaning, 'If your act of killing is produced from the result of kamma, then like killing, the result would also become fruitful.' The other affirms it, seeing the fruitfulness of killing in its leading to hell, etc. But he denies it for the result of kamma, not seeing any place where such a fruit of a result is mentioned. The same method applies to stealing and so on. By 'Is the medicinal requisites for the sick fruitful?', he asks about the fruit of giving in terms of the objects to be given. The sutta 'The world revolves through kamma' rejects the doctrine of non-action (akammavāda) which says 'there is no kamma,' and demonstrates the doctrine of kamma (kammavāda) that 'there is kamma' and that kamma is one's own property (kammassakata). It does not show that everything arises from kamma; therefore, it does not prove [the opponent's point].

## The Explanation of the Discourse on 'All this is due to Kamma' is finished.

## 4. Explanation of the Discourse on 'Bound to the Faculties'

786-787. Now comes the discourse known as 'Bound to the Faculties' (Indriyabaddha). In that discourse, suffering (dukkha) is of two kinds: that which is bound to the faculties (indriyabaddha) and that which is not bound to the faculties (anindriyabaddha). The 'bound to the faculties' is called suffering because it is the basis for painful feeling. The 'not bound to the faculties' is called suffering because it is included in the statement 'whatever is impermanent is suffering' (yadaniccaṃ taṃ dukkhaṃ) in the sense of being oppressed by rise and fall. Without grasping this distinction, the Hetuvādins hold the view that 'only that which is bound to the faculties is the suffering for the full understanding of which the holy life is lived under the Blessed One, and not the other.' To show them the nature of suffering in the other [insentient] things, the Sakavādin asks, 'Is only that which is bound to the faculties [suffering]?' and the other affirms it. Then, to challenge him, 'Since the Blessed One said "whatever is impermanent is suffering," should not that impermanent thing be only that which is bound to the faculties?', [the Sakavādin] says, 'Is only that which is bound to the faculties impermanent?' and so on. The meaning is: are not the earth, mountains, rocks, etc., which are not bound to the faculties, also impermanent?

To the question 'Should it not be said that only that which is bound to the faculties is suffering?', the Sakavādin affirms with 'Yes' (āmantā). For even that which is not bound to the faculties becomes an object for suffering and grief. Indeed, in hot weather, fire, and in cold weather, wind, become objects of suffering.
257:
At all times, the destruction of wealth and so forth are objects of grief (domanassa). Therefore, because it is associated with the sense of impermanence, even insentient matter (anindriyabaddha) should be called suffering (dukkha). However, because it is not produced by kamma and defilements, it should not be called 'the noble truth of suffering' (dukkha-ariya-sacca); likewise, because it is not to be fully understood by the Noble Path. Since the cessation of grass, wood, and so forth, or the cessation of climate (utu), seeds, and so forth, is not called the noble truth of the cessation of suffering, therefore sentient existence (indriyabaddha) is both suffering and a noble truth, while the other (insentient) is merely suffering. To show this distinction, the Sakavādin admits [the point]. The phrase "Just as for the sentient..." (yatha indriyabaddhassa) shows the practice of the holy life (brahmacariya) for the full understanding of sentient existence and the non-recurrence of sentient existence that has been fully understood. Therefore, the Sakavādin makes a rejection here. The suffering nature of insentient matter, which is included by the statement "Whatever is impermanent is suffering" (yad-aniccaṃ taṃ dukkhaṃ), cannot be rejected; therefore, that statement cannot serve as a proof.

## Explanation of the Discourse on Sentient Existence (Indriyabaddha).

## 5. Explanation of the Discourse on 'Excluding the Noble Path' (Thapetvā Ariyamaggaṃ)

789-790. Now there is the discourse named 'Excluding the Noble Path'. Therein, because the Noble Path is called 'the practice leading to the cessation of suffering' (dukkha-nirodha-gāminī-paṭipadā), therefore some hold the view (such as the Hetuvādins) that, excluding the Noble Path, the remaining formations (saṅkhāra) are suffering. With reference to them, there is the question of the Sakavādin and the admission of the other. Then, to object that "If so, the nature of suffering would also apply to the Truth of Origination (samudaya-sacca)", he says "Is the origin of suffering also...?" (dukkha-samudayo pi). The other (Paravādin) rejects it with reference to the characteristic of being the cause of suffering. When asked again, he admits it with reference to its inclusion in the suffering of the three-planed round of existence (tebhūmaka-vaṭṭa-dukkha). In the questions "Only three" (tīṇeva) and so forth, he rejects out of fear of contradicting the Suttas, but admits according to his own view. The rest of the meaning here is clear.

## Explanation of the Discourse on 'Excluding the Noble Path'.

## 6. Explanation of the Discourse: 'It should not be said that the Sangha accepts offerings'

791-792. Now there is the discourse named 'It should not be said that the Sangha accepts offerings'. Therein, [the view is that] in the ultimate sense, only the Paths and Fruits are the Sangha; there is no Sangha other than the Paths and Fruits. The Paths and Fruits cannot accept any material object. Therefore, it should not be said that the Sangha, which is the Noble Path, accepts offerings. This is the view of the Vetullakas, who are now called Mahāpuññavādins. With reference to them, there is the question of the Sakavādin and the admission of the other. Then, to object that "If the Sangha does not accept anything, the Teacher would not have praised the Sangha with attributes such as 'worthy of offerings' (āhuneyya)", he says "Is it not that...?" (nanu) and so forth. In the statement "They give gifts to the Sangha", the Sakavādin says this to object: "If those donors give to the Sangha, to whom would they give if there were no recipients?" The Sutta "Or like the fire (jātaveda) [accepting] the oblation (āhutiṃ)" is a Sutta that comes from the scriptures of those with other views.
258:
In the ultimate sense, only the Paths and Fruits are the Sangha; there is no Sangha other than the Paths and Fruits. The Paths and Fruits cannot accept any material object. Therefore, the view that "It should not be said that the Sangha accepts offerings" is the view of the Vetullakas, who are now called Mahāpuññavādins. With reference to them, the question "It should not be said" is the Sakavādin's question, and the admission is the other's answer. Then, to object that "If the Sangha does not accept offerings, the Teacher would not have praised that Sangha with attributes such as 'worthy of offerings' (āhuneyya)", he said "The Sangha is worthy of offerings" and so forth. The statement "They give offerings to the Sangha" is intended to object: "Those donors give to the Sangha; to whom would they give if there were no recipients?" The Sutta "Or like the fire (jātaveda) [accepting] the oblation (āhutiṃ)" is a Sutta from another school. In that Sutta, the word "great cloud" (mahāmegha) refers to the rain. Indeed, the earth accepts only the rain, not the cloud itself. The statement "The Path accepts" is said with the view that "The Paths and Fruits are the Sangha". In reality, the Paths and Fruits alone are not the Sangha. Rather, the eight noble persons, designated based on the aggregates purified by the manifestation of the Paths and Fruits, are the Sangha. Therefore, this statement cannot serve as a proof.

## Explanation of the Discourse: 'It should not be said that the Sangha accepts offerings'.

## 7. Explanation of the Discourse: 'It should not be said that the Sangha purifies offerings'

793-794. Now the discourse 'It should not be said that the Sangha purifies offerings' arises. Therein, the view that "Only the Paths and Fruits are the Sangha, and those Paths and Fruits are not able to purify offerings, therefore it should not be said that the Sangha purifies offerings" is the view of those same people. With reference to them, the question is the Sakavādin's and the admission is the other's. The words "worthy of offerings" (āhuneyya) and so forth are said to show that "If the Sangha were not able to purify offerings, the Teacher would not have praised the Sangha in this way". "Purifies" (visodheti) means making it of great fruit. Indeed, even a small gift given to the Sangha becomes great; a large gift becomes even greater. "Worthy of offerings" (dakkhiṇeyya) means deserving of offerings, suitable for offerings, and capable of purifying offerings. "They fulfill the offering" (ārādhenti) means that even through a small offering, they reach a great result. The rest of the explanation follows the method mentioned below.

## Explanation of the Discourse: 'It should not be said that the Sangha purifies offerings'.
259:
## 8. Commentary on the Discourse: "It Should Not Be Said That the Saṅgha Eats"

795-796. Now there is the discourse titled "It should not be said that the Saṅgha eats." In this discourse, those who hold the view: "Only the Paths and Fruits are called the Saṅgha, and those Paths and Fruits do not eat anything; therefore, it should not be said that the Saṅgha eats, drinks, chews, or tastes," are the Seyyathāpivādins. With reference to them, the Sakavādī (proponent of our own school) asks the question, and the other (Paravādī/opponent) admits. Then, to object, "If the Saṅgha does not eat, the preparation of food for the Saṅgha (saṅghabhatta) and so forth would be useless," the statement beginning with "Do not some people prepare food for the Saṅgha?" is made. The statement beginning with "group meal" (gaṇabhojana) is made to object: "If the Saṅgha does not eat, for whom would there be group meals and so forth?" This statement "eight kinds of drinks" is also made to object: "If the Saṅgha does not drink, for whom would the Teacher have allowed these drinks?" The rest in this discourse should be understood in the same manner as mentioned below.

## The Commentary on the Discourse: "It Should Not Be Said That the Saṅgha Eats" is finished.

## 9. Commentary on the Discourse: "It Should Not Be Said That a Gift Given to the Saṅgha is of Great Fruit"

797-798. Now there is the discourse titled "It should not be said that a gift given to the Saṅgha is of great fruit." In this discourse, those who hold the view: "Only the Paths and Fruits are called the Saṅgha; it is not possible to give anything to those Paths and Fruits, nor can they receive anything, nor is any beneficial service accomplished by giving to them; therefore, it should not be said that a gift given to the Saṅgha is of great fruit," are the Seyyathāpivādins. With reference to them, the Sakavādī asks, and the Paravādī admits. The statement beginning with "āhuneyyo" (worthy of offerings) is made for the purpose of showing: "If a gift given to the Saṅgha were not of great fruit, the Teacher would not have praised that Noble Saṅgha in this way as āhuneyyo and so forth." The rest follows according to the Pāḷi text.

## The Commentary on the Discourse: "It Should Not Be Said That a Gift Given to the Saṅgha is of Great Fruit" is finished.

## 10. Commentary on the Discourse: "It Should Not Be Said That a Gift Given to the Buddha is of Great Fruit"

Now there is the discourse titled "It should not be said that a gift given to the Buddha is of great fruit." In that discourse, [the view is]: "The Blessed Buddha does not consume anything; he only shows himself as if consuming for the sake of conforming to the world; therefore, because of the absence of beneficial service, it should not be said that a gift given to him is of great fruit."
260:
is the view of those [Seyyathāpivādins]. With reference to them, there is the question of the Sakavādī and the admission of the other. The statement beginning with "The foremost among bipeds" is made to show: "Even a gift given to immoral humans has a thousandfold benefit; what then need be said [of the greatness of fruit] regarding such a Supreme Person?" The rest here follows according to the Pāḷi text.

## The Commentary on the Discourse: "It Should Not Be Said That a Gift Given to the Buddha is of Great Fruit" is finished.

## 11. Commentary on the Discourse on the Purification of the Offering (Dakkhiṇāvisuddhi)

800-801. Now there is the discourse titled "Purification of the Offering." In that discourse, those who hold the view: "If the offering were purified by the recipient, it would be of great fruit. [But if] the donor gives the gift and the recipient produces the result, then one would be the doer for another; one would undergo the happiness or suffering created by another; one would act and another would experience [the result]. Therefore, the gift is purified only by the donor, not by the recipient; only the donor's purity of mind is the giver of the result," are the Uttarāpathakas. With reference to them, there is the question of the Sakavādī and the admission of the other. The statement beginning with "āhuneyya" is made to show: "If the gift were not purified by the recipient, what could the recipient's state of being āhuneyya and so forth do?" The statement "one would be the doer for another" would be appropriate if the donor's volition of giving (dānacetanā) were created by the recipient. However, that pure volition of giving of the donor is purified by being of great result depending on the object known as the recipient. Therefore, this objection, "Is the gift purified by the recipient?" does not constitute a valid objection.

## The Commentary on the Discourse on the Purification of the Offering is finished.

## The Seventeenth Chapter.

## 18. The Eighteenth Chapter

## 1. Commentary on the Discourse on the Human World (Manussaloka)

802-803. Now there is the discourse titled "The Human World." In that discourse, "The Tathāgata was born in the world, grew up in the world, and having overcome the world..."
261:
“Though born in the world, he dwells unsullied by the world” (Saṃ. Ni. 3.94). Having incorrectly grasped this Sutta, those such as the Vetullakas of the present time hold the view: “The Blessed One was reborn in the Tusita heaven and dwells only there; he does not come to the human world, but merely displays a created form (nimmitarūpa) here.” With reference to them, the Proponent (Sakavādī) asks the question, and the other (Paravādī) gives his assent. Then, in order to make him understand by way of the place of dwelling and by citing the Sutta, [the Proponent] said “Nanu atthi” and so forth. Regarding the phrase “Born in the world,” the Paravādī speaks with reference to the Tusita heaven. However, the Teacher (the Commentator) says that this was said with reference only to the human world. Regarding the phrase “Having overcome the world,” the Paravādī speaks according to his own view, meaning “having overcome the human world.” But the Teacher says that [the Buddha] dwelt having overcome the world of sense-objects (ārammaṇaloka). Regarding the phrase “Unsullied by the world,” the Paravādī speaks with reference only to being unsullied by the human world. But the Teacher says that he dwelt unsullied by the defilements (kilesas) among the worldly conditions (lokadhammas). Therefore, this evidence is not established [for the Paravādī].

## Commentary on the Discussion of the Human World (Manussalokakathāvaṇṇanā).

## 2. Commentary on the Discussion of the Teaching of the Dhamma (Dhammadesanākathāvaṇṇanā)

804-806. Now follows the Discussion of the Teaching of the Dhamma. Therein, those such as the Vetullakas hold the view: “The Blessed One, staying in the Tusita heaven, sent a created form (nimmitarūpa) for the purpose of teaching the Dhamma; having received the teaching from that created form and of that [form], the Venerable Ānanda taught the Dhamma, not the Blessed One himself.” With reference to them, the Sakavādī asks the question, and the Paravādī gives his assent. Then, to challenge him, “If the Dhamma was taught by that created form, then that form itself would be the Teacher,” [the Proponent] said “Abhinnimmito jino” and so forth. The other (Paravādī) does not accept this and rejects it. The rest of the meaning here is clear.

## Commentary on the Discussion of the Teaching of the Dhamma (Dhammadesanākathāvaṇṇanā).

## 3. Commentary on the Discussion of Compassion (Karuṇākathāvaṇṇanā)

807-808. Now follows the Discussion of Compassion. Therein, seeing the occurrence of what resembles compassion through the power of lust (rāga) in those with lust, due to the ruin of beloved objects—
262:
“Lust (rāga) alone is called compassion (karuṇā); that lust does not exist in the Blessed One; therefore, the Blessed One has no compassion.” Such is the view of those like the Uttarāpathakas. With reference to them, the Sakavādī asks the question, and the other (Paravādī) gives his assent. Then, for the purpose of challenging him—“This compassion, because of its state of being free from defilements, because of its state of having beings as its object, because of its state of being a liberation of mind (cetovimutti), and because of its state of having eleven advantages, is of the same class as loving-kindness (mettā) and so forth; therefore, if the Blessed One has no compassion, then loving-kindness and so forth would also not exist for that Blessed One”—[the Proponent] said “The Blessed One has no loving-kindness” and so forth. Regarding the problem of “one without compassion (akāruṇika),” [the Paravādī] rejects it as such a term is not found. The rest of the meaning here is very clear.

## Commentary on the Discussion of Compassion (Karuṇākathāvaṇṇanā).

## 4. Commentary on the Discussion of Perfumes (Gandhajātakathāvaṇṇanā)

Now follows the Discussion of Perfumes. Therein, due to the power of improper affection for the Blessed Buddha, some such as the Andhakas and Uttarāpathakas hold the view: “The excrement and urine of the Blessed One excel other kinds of perfumes; there is no perfume more fragrant than that.” With reference to them, the Sakavādī asks the question, and the other gives his assent. The rest of the words here follow the Pāḷi text.

## Commentary on the Discussion of Perfumes (Gandhajātakathāvaṇṇanā).

## 5. Commentary on the Discussion of a Single Path (Ekamaggakathāvaṇṇanā)

810-811. Now follows the Discussion of a Single Path. Therein, also due to the power of improper affection for the Blessed Buddha, they hold the view: “The Blessed One, having become a Stream-enterer (Sotāpanna), became a Once-returner (Sakadāgāmī); having become a Once-returner, he became a Non-returner (Anāgāmī); having become a Non-returner, he realized Arahantship; however, he realized the four fruits with only a single Noble Path.” With reference to them, the Sakavādī asks the question, and the other gives his assent. Then, to him, regarding the four factors such as contact (phassa) which arise together with the four fruits...
263:
He said the words beginning with "catunnam phassānam" to challenge by way of the combination of the four states beginning with contact that occur along with the four fruits. He said the words beginning with "Sotāpattimaggena" for the purpose of asking, "By which path does one realize?" When "Arahattamaggena" is said, he challenges by way of the fact that the Path of Arahantship does not abandon identity view and so on. In the question "Is the Blessed One a Stream-enterer?", he rejects it, saying that for one who has become a Buddha, the state of being a Stream-enterer does not exist. The same method applies to the two subsequent questions (regarding the Once-returner and Non-returner). The rest of the text here follows the Pali exactly.

## Commentary on the Discourse on a Single Path.

## 6. Commentary on the Discourse on Transition between Jhanas

813-816. Now follows the Discourse on Transition between Jhanas (Jhānasaṅkantikathā). In that discourse, based on the sequential teaching, "Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu, secluded from sensual pleasures... enters and dwells in the first jhana... with the subsiding of initial and sustained thought, the second jhana, the third jhana, the fourth jhana" (SN 5.923-934), the Mahīśāsakas and some Andhakas hold the view that "one transitions from one jhana to another without the arising of access concentration (upacāra-bhāvanā) for each respective jhana." With reference to them, the proponent (Sakavādī) asks and the opponent (Paravādī) affirms.

Then, to challenge him, "If one transitions from the first jhana to the second jhana in a non-sequential manner without reaching the access of the second jhana, could one also transition from the first to the third, or from the second to the fourth?", he said "pathamā jhānā" etc. The words beginning with "yā pathamassa" were said for the purpose of challenging, "If one enters the second jhana immediately after the first, or the third etc. after the second etc., would one enter them with a single adverting (āvajjana)?"

"Kāme ādīnavato" means the first jhana arises later in the continuum of a person who contemplates the disadvantages of sensual pleasures. However, at the moment of jhana, this person contemplates only the sign (nimitta). By the Pali "taññeva pathamam", he asks to challenge, "If the subsequent impulsion (javana) arises immediately after the preceding impulsion, then setting aside the state of being preceding and subsequent, would that first jhana be the same as that second jhana by way of characteristic?" In this way, the meaning should be understood in all places. By the Pali beginning with "vivicceva kāmehi", he shows only that the jhanas are taught in sequence, not that they arise in immediate succession. Therefore, it is not a valid reason.

## Commentary on the Discourse on Transition between Jhanas.
264:
## 7. Commentary on the Discourse on the Interval between Jhanas

817-818. Now follows the Discourse on the Interval between Jhanas (Jhānantarikakathā). In that discourse, although five jhanas are analyzed in the fivefold method (pañcakanaya), only three types of concentration (samādhi) are specifically mentioned. In such a presentation, because they do not know the opportunity for the concentration that is without initial thought but with sustained thought only (avitakka-vicāramatta-samādhi), the Sammitīyas and some Andhakas hold the view that "this concentration between the first and second jhanas is called the intermediate jhana (jhānantarika)." With reference to them, the Sakavādī asks and the Paravādī affirms. Then, to challenge the Paravādī, "Jhanas are mental states (cetasika dhamma), and contact (phassa) and so on are also mental states. Therefore, if there is such a thing as an intermediate jhana, there should also be intermediate contact (phassantarika) and so on," he said "atthi phassantarikam" etc.

The phrase beginning with "dutiyassa ca jhānassa" is said for the purpose of challenging, "If there is such a thing as an intermediate jhana, the second and third jhanas etc. are also jhanas; there should also be an intermediate concentration between those jhanas." That Paravādī denies (when asked if there is an interval between the second and third) because it is not in his own view, and affirms (when asked if there is not). When asked "pathamassa ca", he affirms by the power of his own view.

The phrase beginning with "savitakko savicāro" is said for the purpose of challenging, "While all three concentrations are equal in being concentration, why is it that only the concentration without initial thought but with sustained thought only is an intermediate jhana, and the other concentrations are not? What is the specific reason for this distinction?"

820-822. With the phrase "dvinnam jhānānam paccuppannānam" etc., he asks with reference to the first and second jhanas. The other (Paravādī) affirms according to his view, "The concentration without initial thought but with sustained thought only, occurring between those jhanas which are presently occurring, is called the intermediate jhana." When asked "Has the first jhana ceased?", he affirms, considering that the simultaneous occurrence of the three concentrations is not appropriate. He asks by way of the fourfold method (catukkanaya), "Is the concentration without initial thought but with sustained thought only the first jhana?" The Sakavādī denies because that concentration does not exist in that fourfold method. In the phrase "nanu tayo samādhī", the meaning is: Just as among those three concentrations, two concentrations are jhanas only and not intermediate jhanas, so too the remaining concentration should be a jhana only and not an intermediate jhana.

## Commentary on the Discourse on the Interval between Jhanas is finished.
265:
## 8. Samāpanno Saddaṃ Suṇātīti Kathāvaṇṇanā

823-825. Now, the discussion known as 'Samāpanno Saddaṃ Suṇāti' (The one in attainment hears sound) arises. In that discussion, the Pubbaseliyas hold the view: "The Blessed One stated that sound is a thorn to the first jhāna. If one in attainment did not hear that sound, how could it be a thorn? Therefore, one in attainment hears sound." With reference to them, the Sakavādī asks, and the other (Pubbaseliya) affirms. The statement beginning with "sees form with the eye" is said for the purpose of objection: "For one in attainment, there is no occurrence of mental states at the five doors (pañcadvāra-pavattī) in the first place. In the absence of that, if that person were to hear sound, they should also see form." The statement "sound is a thorn" is spoken because it causes distraction (vikkhepa). Indeed, when a coarse sound strikes the ear-sensitivity, emergence (vuṭṭhāna) from the first jhāna occurs; that is why this was said. Therefore, that statement does not serve as evidence (for the view that one hears while in attainment). The statement beginning with "is [a thorn] to the second jhāna" is said for the purpose of making it known that "just as other thorns do not exist within the attainment, so too the hearing of sound does not exist within the attainment." All of that is clear in meaning.

## Samāpanno Saddaṃ Suṇātīti Kathāvaṇṇanā.

## 9. Cakkhunā Rūpaṃ Passatīti Kathāvaṇṇanā

826-827. Now, the discussion known as 'Cakkhunā Rūpaṃ Passati' (One sees form with the eye) arises. In that discussion, based on the words "having seen form with the eye," the Mahāsaṃghikas hold the view: "The eye-sensitivity (cakkhu-pasāda) itself sees form." With reference to them, the Sakavādī asks, and the other (Mahāsaṃghika) affirms. Then, in order to object to him, "If one sees form with the eye-sensitivity, one would see form with matter (rūpa)," [the Sakavādī] says, "Does one see form with matter?" The other rejects it with reference to the form-base (rūpāyatana), but when asked again, affirms it with reference only to the eye-sensitivity matter. Regarding the word 'paṭivijānāti' (cognizes), this is the intended meaning: In saying "sees," we ask with reference to cognition (knowing), not with reference to the mere directing of the eye-sensitivity towards the form. Therefore, say first: "According to your view, does the one with eyes cognize form with the matter of eye-sensitivity?" The other both rejects (regarding rūpāyatana) and affirms (regarding cakkhu-pasāda) just as in the previous method. Then, in order to object to him, "If that is so, matter (eye-sensitivity) would become mind-consciousness, for only that mind-consciousness is what is called cognizing," [the Sakavādī] says, "Is matter mind-consciousness?" The other, finding no opening (for an argument), simply rejects it. The statement beginning with "Does the eye have adverting (āvajjanā)?" is asked as an objection: "If the eye-sensitivity sees in the sense of cognizing, then just as there is adverting for eye-consciousness, there should also be adverting for that eye-sensitivity." The other rejects it with "It is not so," because the eye-sensitivity is not connected with adverting, and because that eye-consciousness does not arise immediately after adverting [of the eye itself]. In the statements beginning with "hears sound with the ear," the method is the same.

In this context, the word "sees" is [explained] by the method of description including the apparatus (sasambhārakathānaya)...
266:
...to object that "if the eye sees in the sense of cognizing, just as there must be adverting for eye-consciousness, there must also be adverting for that eye." The other (the proponent) rejects it with "It is not so," because the eye is not associated with adverting, and because that eye does not arise immediately after adverting. In the phrases such as "hears sound with the ear," the method is the same. "Monks, in this Dispensation, a monk sees form with the eye"—this statement is spoken by way of the method of description including the apparatus (sasambhārakathānaya). Just as one who shoots with an arrow is said to "shoot with a bow," so too, one who sees with eye-consciousness is said to "see with the eye." Therefore, this statement cannot prove [the view that the eye itself sees]. In the remaining phrases, the method is the same.

## Cakkhunā Rūpaṃ Passatīti Kathāvaṇṇanā.

## Eighteenth Group (Aṭṭhāramo Vaggo).

## 19. Nineteenth Group (Ekūnavīsatimo Vaggo)

## 1. Kilesapajahana Kathāvaṇṇanā

828-831. Now, it is the discussion on the abandoning of defilements (Kilesapajahana Kathā). Therein, because there is such a thing as the abandoning of defilements, and for a person who has abandoned defilements, past defilements are indeed abandoned, as are future and present ones, some Uttarāpathakas hold the view: "Therefore, one abandons past defilements, future defilements, and present defilements." With reference to them, the question beginning with "In the past?" is the Sakavādī's question, and the affirmation is the other's (Paravādī's). The rest is to be understood according to the Pali text. Regarding this question of the Paravādī, "Does one not abandon defilements?", just as there is effort in discarding for one who abandons rubbish, there is no effort in the defilements distinguished as past, etc., for one who abandons defilements. However, when the Noble Path (ariya-magga) having Nibbāna as its object is processed, defilements, being unarisen, simply do not arise, and thus are called "abandoned." Therefore, [the Sakavādī] rejects it with "It is not so." As for the statement "one abandons past defilements," etc., because it should not be said that "there is no abandoning of defilements," it is said by way of a pretext (chala) that one abandons defilements distinguished as past, etc.

## Kilesapajahana Kathāvaṇṇanā.
267:
## 2. Suññatākathāvaṇṇanā
Now comes the Suññatākathā. In this Suññatākathā, emptiness (suññatā) is of two kinds: the characteristic of non-self (anattalakkhaṇa) of the aggregates and Nibbāna. Among these two, the characteristic of non-self, in a certain sense and by one method, may be included in the aggregate of mental formations (saṅkhārakkhandha), while Nibbāna is definitely not included in any of the five aggregates. Without making this distinction, those like the Andhakas hold the view that "Emptiness is included in the aggregate of mental formations." Referring to them, the Sakavādī asks the question and the other (Paravādī) admits it. "Signless" (animitta) means Nibbāna, which is free from all signs. "Undirected" (appaṇihita) is also a name for that same Nibbāna. Why is this statement brought forward? It is to point out the fault in the doctrine of the non-distinctionist (avibhajjavādī). For if one holds the view without making a distinction that "Emptiness is partially included in the aggregate of mental formations," then for him, it follows that Nibbāna is also included in the aggregate of mental formations. To point out this fault, the words "signless" and "undirected" are brought forward. The other (Paravādī) rejects the inclusion of Nibbāna in the aggregate of mental formations as he does not desire it. The statement beginning with "The aggregate of mental formations is not impermanent" is said to show the fault of Nibbāna, which is called emptiness, becoming impermanent.

The phrase "emptiness of the aggregate of mental formations" is said for the purpose of challenging: "If the emptiness of another aggregate is included in another aggregate, should the emptiness of the aggregate of mental formations also be included in the remaining aggregates?" The statement beginning with "The emptiness of the aggregate of mental formations should not be said" is stated to show the opposite: "If the emptiness of the aggregate of mental formations is not included in the remaining aggregates, then the emptiness of the remaining aggregates is also not included in the aggregate of mental formations."

The sutta "Monks, these formations are empty" is brought forward from the views of the other schools. In that sutta, "formations" (saṅkhārā) refers to the five aggregates, as in the passage "All formations are impermanent." Since those aggregates are empty of self and what belongs to self, they are called "emptiness" (suññatā); this is a meaning that accords with the Teaching and is not contradictory, thus it is accepted. However, since this sutta does not show that emptiness is included in the aggregate of mental formations, it is inconclusive (asādhaka) and cannot serve as proof.

## Suññatākathāvaṇṇanā.

## 3. Sāmaññaphalakathāvaṇṇanā
835-836. Now comes the Sāmaññaphalakathā. In this Sāmaññaphalakathā, the resultant consciousness (vipākacitta) of the Noble Path, whether in the process of the Path (maggavīthi) or in the process of the attainment of fruition (phalasamāpattivīthi), is called the fruit of recluseship (sāmaññaphala).
268:
The term "fruit of recluseship" is the conclusion in one's own school (Sakasamaya). However, some opponents, such as the Pubbaseliyas, do not hold this view but believe that "Only the abandonment of defilements and the arising of fruition is the fruit of recluseship; therefore, it is unconditioned (asaṅkhata)." Referring to them, the Sakavādī asks and the Paravādī admits. The remaining words here follow the method mentioned below, according to the Pali text.

## Sāmaññaphalakathāvaṇṇanā.

## 4. Pattikathāvaṇṇanā

837-840. Now comes the Pattikathā. Therein, some like the Pubbaseliyas hold the view: "Whatever object one obtains, the obtaining of that object is called attainment (patti), and that attainment is unconditioned." Referring to them, the Sakavādī asks and the Paravādī admits. Here too, the remaining words follow the method mentioned below, according to the Pali text.

The statement beginning with "It should not be said" is spoken by the Paravādī to clarify the view by which he thinks "Attainment is unconditioned." Therein, the Sakavādī, while rejecting it by saying "It should not be said so," does not accept that attainment is merely matter (rūpa) and so on. In truth, there is no such thing as a dhamma called "attainment," yet he does not concede that it is unconditioned. The Paravādī, however, establishes his view that "it is unconditioned" merely by the rejection. Since that view is established improperly, it is indeed not established.

## Pattikathāvaṇṇanā.

## 5. Tathatākathāvaṇṇanā

841-843. Now comes the Tathatākathā. Therein, some like certain Uttarāpathakas hold the view: "There exists what is called suchness (tathatā), which is the nature of all phenomena such as matter (rūpa) and so on; and that suchness is unconditioned because it is not included in conditioned things like matter and so on." Referring to them, the Sakavādī asks and the Paravādī admits. Here too, the remaining words are clear according to the method mentioned below.

## Tathatākathāvaṇṇanā.
269:
## 6. Commentary on the Discourse on the Wholesome (Kusalakathāvaṇṇanā)

844–846. Now comes the Discourse on the Wholesome (Kusalakathā). In this discourse, a state that is blameless is called wholesome (kusala), and a state that has a desirable result is also called wholesome. "Blameless" (anavajja) refers to states dissociated from the defilements (kilesa). This method, excluding the unwholesome, encompasses all states. "Having a desirable result" (iṭṭhavipāka) refers to merit (puñña) that produces desirable fruit in the future, both at the moment of rebirth-linking (upapatti) and during the course of existence (pavatti). This method pertains only to the first term (kusalā dhammā) of the Wholesome Triad (Kusalattika). For those who, without making this distinction, hold the view that Nibbāna is wholesome merely because of its blameless nature (for example, the Andhakas), the Proponent (Sakavādin) asks to demonstrate that Nibbāna is not wholesome in the sense of having a desirable result, and the other (Paravādin) concedes according to his own view. The remaining text here is also clear in meaning, following the method already stated below.

## Commentary on the Discourse on the Wholesome.

## 7. Commentary on the Discourse on Absolute Finality (Accantaniyāmakathāvaṇṇanā)

Now comes the Discourse on Absolute Finality (Accantaniyāmakathā). Therein, based on the Sutta, "Once submerged, he is submerged indeed" (AN 7.15), some (for example, certain Uttarāpathakas) hold the view that "A worldling has absolute finality (accantaniyāmatā)." Referring to them, the Proponent asks and the other concedes. The mention of "matricide" (mātughātaka) etc., is stated for the purpose of challenging: "If the fixedness of wrongness (micchattaniyāma) is the same for one with fixed wrong view and for a matricide etc., then matricides etc., should also be absolutely fixed." The other rejects this with "Na hevaṃ" (Not so), based on the view that "One with fixed wrong view is like a stump in the cycle of rebirth (saṃsārakhāṇuka) and is fixed even in another life, whereas these matricides etc., are fixed only in a single existence."

"Would doubt arise?" (vicikicchā uppajjeyya) is a question asking whether doubt such as "Am I fixed or not?" would arise. The other, not seeing the reason for its non-arising, concedes. However, when asked "Would it not arise?" (nuppajjeyya), he concedes with reference to the non-arising of doubt regarding that very view which he has entered into by frequenting it. When asked "Is it abandoned from that?" (tato pahīnā), he rejects it because it has not been abandoned by the Path (Magga); yet he concedes it with reference to the non-occurrence of doubt regarding that view. Then, because abandonment does not exist apart from the Noble Path (Ariyamagga), the Buddha said "By the path of stream-entry" (sotāpattimaggena) etc., to challenge him by way of that Path. He rejects it because it has not been abandoned even by a single Path.
270:
(The Paravādī) denies it because (doubt, vicikicchā) has not yet been abandoned by the Noble Path. When asked again, "By which path is it abandoned?", referring to the wrong path (micchāmagga), he says "By the unwholesome path (akusalamagga)," etc.

With the words "Would annihilationism (ucchedadiṭṭhi) arise?", he asks about the occurrence of a second certainty (niyāma). The other (Sakavādī) affirms it because, according to the statement "Even those people of Ukkala, Vaya and Bhañña, who hold the doctrine of nothingness (natthikavāda), the doctrine of non-action (akiriyavāda), and the doctrine of non-causality (ahetukavāda)" (M. iii. 143), all three fixed wrong views (niyata-micchādiṭṭhi) can arise in a single individual. Then, to challenge him, "Is that view not indeed an absolute certainty?", he says "Hañci" (If), etc. For one with an absolutely fixed eternalist view, a second certainty (annihilationism) is useless. In the question "Would it not arise?", considering that the very five aggregates held as "eternal" by eternalism (sassatadiṭṭhi) will be "annihilated," he affirms it, referring to the non-arising of annihilationism. When asked "Is it abandoned?", he denies it because it has not been abandoned by the Path. He affirms it because it does not arise according to the stated method. The same method applies to questions such as "Would eternalism arise?". The rest should be understood as stated in the section on doubt (vicikicchā-vāra).

851-852. The question "It should not be said" is the Paravādī's question, and the affirmation due to the existence of the Sutta is the Sakavādī's affirmation. However, that person is not submerged even in another life. The intention here is that he is unable to give up that wrong view in this very life; therefore, this Sutta does not prove (the Paravādī's point). It is stated to show that one should seek the meaning without being attached to the mere words "emerging and then submerging for all time," etc.

## Commentary on the Discourse on Absolute Certainty (Accantaniyāmakathā).

## 8. Commentary on the Discourse on Faculties (Indriyakathā)

853-856. Now follows the Discourse on Faculties. Therein, the view of the Hetuvādīs and Mahīsāsakas is that mundane faith is merely called faith, not the faculty of faith (saddhindriya). Similarly, mundane energy, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom are merely called energy, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom, but not the faculty of energy (viriyindriya), the faculty of mindfulness (satindriya), the faculty of concentration (samādhindriya), or the faculty of wisdom (paññindriya). Referring to them, the question is by the Sakavādī, and the affirmation...
271:
To the opponent: "Mundane faith does not exist," etc. Because mundane faith and other such states are faculties (indriya) in the sense of predominance (adhipati), and there is no other "faith faculty" (saddhindriya) etc. apart from faith itself, the proponent (Sakavādī) says this to show that mundane faith etc. are indeed the faith faculty etc. "Mundane mind exists," etc. Just as those mundane mind etc. are the mind faculty (manindriya) etc., so too mundane faith etc. are the faith faculty etc. This is said to clarify that meaning by way of an analogy. The rest here should be understood according to the Pali text.

## Commentary on the Discussion of Faculties (Indriyakathāvaṇṇanā).
## The Nineteenth Chapter (Ekūnavīsatimo Vaggo).
## 20. The Twentieth Chapter (Vīsatimavagga)
## 1. Commentary on the Discussion of the Unintentional (Asañciccakathāvaṇṇanā)

857-862. Now is the discussion of the unintentional (asañcicca). In this discussion of the unintentional, some, such as the Uttarāpathakas, hold the view: "The objects of immediate retribution (ānantariya-vatthu) are grave and heavy; therefore, even if those objects are violated unintentionally, one becomes an offender of immediate retribution." With reference to them, the question "Unintentionally?" is the proponent's question, and the affirmation based on their view is the opponent's affirmation.

Then, to challenge them: "Because an act of immediate retribution is a path of action (kammapatha). If there were a breach of the path of action unintentionally, then the remaining acts like killing living beings (pāṇātipāta) etc. would also occur unintentionally." Thus, "Having killed a living being unintentionally," etc. is said. The opponent denies this because they do not hold such a view. The rest should be understood according to the Pali text.

"Should it not be said 'matricide' (mātughātaka)?" is the opponent's question. The proponent's affirmation is with reference to unintentional killing during medical treatment etc. Even in the problem "Is a mother not deprived of life?", the proponent's affirmation is only with reference to unintentional deprivation of life. However, without taking the proponent's intention, the opponent establishes their own view with "If (hañci)". That view is not established because it is established improperly. The same applies to the problems of parricide (pitughātaka) etc.

Regarding the schism of the Sangha (saṅghabheda), however, for one who perceives it as Dhamma (dhammasaññī), the question "Is schism of the Sangha an act of immediate retribution?" is the proponent's question. "Having split the harmonious Sangha..."
272:
The opponent affirms by improperly taking the words "He is boiled in hell for an aeon (kappaṃ nirayamhi paccati)." Again, when asked "Do all (schismatics incur immediate retribution)?", the proponent denies regarding the dhammasaññī (one who perceives it as Dhamma) in their own side, but affirms regarding the dhammasaññī in the opponent's side. In both questions about dhammasaññī, this is the method. The Sutta "Was it not said by the Blessed One?" etc. is said by the proponent to show that a dhammavādī (one who speaks according to Dhamma) does not incur immediate retribution. In the verse "Destined for the state of loss, destined for hell (āpāyiko nerayiko)", only the adhammavādī (one who speaks contrary to Dhamma) is intended. However, the other party (the opponent) establishes their view without taking that intention. That established view is not truly established because it is established improperly.

## Commentary on the Discussion of the Unintentional (Asañciccakathāvaṇṇanā).

## 2. Commentary on the Discussion of Knowledge (Ñāṇakathāvaṇṇanā)
863-865. Now is the discussion of knowledge (ñāṇa). In this discussion of knowledge, knowledge is of two kinds: mundane (lokiya) and supramundane (lokuttara). Mundane knowledge is knowledge in attainments (samāpatti) and knowledge of the ownership of deeds (kammassakatā-ñāṇa) occurring through giving (dāna) etc. Supramundane knowledge is path knowledge (magga-ñāṇa) and fruition knowledge (phala-ñāṇa) which distinguishes the Four Noble Truths. However, without making this distinction, some (like the Hetuvādins) hold the view: "Only the knowledge that distinguishes the Four Noble Truths is called knowledge; other knowledge is not knowledge. Therefore, a worldling (puthujjana) has no knowledge." The proponent asks with reference to them, and the other affirms. The word "wisdom" (paññā) etc. is said to show synonyms of knowledge. This shows: If a worldling has no knowledge, they also have no wisdom etc. If they have wisdom etc., they also have knowledge. Why? Because wisdom etc. are not different from knowledge. "The first jhāna" etc. is said to show knowledge in attainments. "One should give a gift" etc. is said to show knowledge of the ownership of deeds. "He understands suffering" shows only supramundane path knowledge, but it does not show that only supramundane knowledge is knowledge.

## Commentary on the Discussion of Knowledge (Ñāṇakathāvaṇṇanā).

## 3. Commentary on the Discussion of Hell-wardens (Nirayapālakathāvaṇṇanā)
Now is the discussion of hell-wardens. In this discussion of hell-wardens, some hold the view: "In hell, only the unwholesome kamma of the denizens of hell punishes them in the form of hell-wardens; there are no beings called hell-wardens (nirayapāla)." Or, if there were no hell-wardens in hell, there would be no punishment. Indeed, only when there are hell-wardens who inflict punishment does punishment occur. To ask this, "There are none in the hells" etc. is said.

867-868. "There are among humans" is said by the proponent to make it known through direct observation. Indeed, just as among humans, punishment occurs only when there are those who inflict it, so too in hell (punishment occurs only when there are punishers). This is the proponent's intention here. "There are in the hells" etc. is the opponent's question and the other's affirmation. The Sutta "Neither Vessabhū nor the King of Petas" etc. is a Sutta cited by the opponent from their own view. However, since that Sutta is included in the Dispensation (Sāsana), the proponent accepts it. In that verse, "Vessabhū" is a certain deity. "Pettirājā" is a peta of great power in the realm of petas. King Yama, the Makhā deities, etc., are indeed well-known. The meaning is: a man who is cast down from this life by his own deeds and reaches another world, these deities like Vessabhū...
273:
The Sakavādin asks, and the Paravādin admits, referring to those like the Andhakas who hold the view that "There are no hell-wardens in hell." Then, to ask, "If there were no hell-wardens in that hell, there would also be no punishments. For it is only when there are hell-wardens who inflict punishment that punishment can occur," he said the words beginning with "Natthi nirayesu" (There are none in hells).

867-868. The phrase "Are there [such] among humans?" is intended to make it known through direct observation. Just as among humans, punishment occurs only when there are those who inflict it, so it is in that hell as well—this is the intention of the Sakavādin here. The question "Are there [such] in hell?" is the Paravādin's question, and the Sakavādin admits it. The Paravādin brings forward a sutta from his own tradition, beginning with "Neither the god Vessabhū nor the King of the Petas." However, since that sutta is included in the Teaching (Sāsana), the Sakavādin accepts it. In that verse, "Vessabhū" refers to a certain deity. "Pettirājā" refers to a peta of great psychic power in the realm of the petas. Deities such as King Yama and the Magha deity are indeed well-known. The meaning is this: These deities like Vessabhū do not kill the man who has reached another world, having been cast out from here by his own kamma. It is the very kamma of his own, by which he was cast into hell, that kills him there—this is to show that kamma is one's own property (kammassakatā), not to show the non-existence of hell-wardens. The Sakavādin, however, says that the sutta passages brought forward, such as "Tamenaṃ bhikkhave" (Him, O monks), have a direct meaning (nītattha) that has been extracted.

## Commentary on the Discussion of Hell-wardens (Nirayapālakathāvaṇṇanā)

## 4. Commentary on the Discussion of Animals (Tiracchānakathāvaṇṇanā)

869-871. Now is the Discussion of Animals. In that discussion, among the devas, young devas (devaputta) like Erāvaṇa and others manifest the form of an elephant or the form of a horse. There are no actual animals among those devas. The Sakavādin asks, and the Paravādin admits, referring to those like the Andhakas who, seeing the young devas in animal forms, hold the view that "There are animals among the devas." Then, to ask, "If there were animals in the deva-birth, there would also be devas in the animal-birth," he said the words beginning with "Atthi tiracchānagatesu" (Are there among animals). The words beginning with "Kīṭā" (insects) were said to show things like caterpillars, which the Paravādin intends to say do not exist [among devas]. In the problem of "Erāvaṇa," the admission is due to the existence of that elephant Erāvaṇa.
274:
In the problem of the elephant Erāvaṇa and others, the admission is due to the existence of that elephant Erāvaṇa and the vehicles of those devas; it is not an admission due to the existence of actual animal elephants or animal horses. For the purpose of the objection, "If there were elephants and so on in that place, there would also be elephant-keepers and so on," the words beginning with "Hatthibandhā" (elephant-keepers) were said. In that passage, "Yāvasikā" means those who give grass (fodder). "Kāraṇikā" means elephant-masters and others who would perform various kinds of training (punishment) on those elephants. "Bhattakāraka" means those who cook rice for the elephants and others. With the words "Na hevaṃ" (Not so), he rejects it, not desiring the existence of such elephant-keepers and so on.

## Commentary on the Discussion of Animals (Tiracchānakathāvaṇṇanā)

## 5. Commentary on the Discussion of the Path (Maggakathāvaṇṇanā)

872-875. Now is the Discussion of the Path. In that discussion, referring to those like the Mahīsāsakas who hold the view that "In a literal sense, the Path is only five-fold," based on this sutta: "Even before [attaining the Path], his bodily action, vocal action, and livelihood are very pure," and also based on the fact that right speech, right action, and right livelihood are dissociated from the mind (citta-vippayutta), the Sakavādin asks, "Is it five-fold?" and the other admits it. The statements "Right speech is a factor of the Path, but that right speech is not the Path" and so on are said according to the view of the Paravādin. In the Paravādin's view, right speech and others appear as factors of the Path. However, they are explained as not being the Path because they are material (rūpa). The statements "Right view is a factor of the Path" and so on were said to show that there is no such thing as being a factor of the Path but not being the Path. In the sutta beginning with "Pubbeva kho panassa," it is taught that "bodily action, vocal action, and livelihood are very pure" to show the purity of the practice leading to the Path—that the development of the Path (magga-bhāvanā) can occur only in the continuity of one who has pure virtue, and not in another. It was not taught to show a five-fold nature excluding these factors. Therefore, he said: "Thus, this Noble Eightfold Path reaches fulfillment in development." The sutta brought forward by the Sakavādin has a direct meaning (nītattha).

## Commentary on the Discussion of the Path (Maggakathāvaṇṇanā)

## 6. Commentary on the Discussion of Knowledge (Ñāṇakathāvaṇṇanā)

876-877. Now is the Discussion of Knowledge. In that discussion, referring to those who hold the view that "Knowledge with twelve bases is supramundane," referring to the twelve-fold knowledge mentioned in the Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta. To object that "If that supramundane knowledge has twelve bases, the Path-knowledges would also be twelve," he said the words beginning with "Dvādasa" (Twelve). The Paravādin rejects this, referring to the singleness of the Path. Because there are three kinds of knowledge—knowledge of the truth (sacca-ñāṇa), knowledge of the task (kicca-ñāṇa), and knowledge of completion (kata-ñāṇa)—for each of the [four] truths, it is said to be knowledge with twelve bases.
275:
Just like the view of the Pubbaseliyas, the Sakavādin asks with reference to them, and the other (the Paravādin) accepts. Then, to challenge him with "If that knowledge has twelve bases, there must be twelve path-knowledges," he says "Dvādasa" (twelve), etc. The other (the Paravādin) rejects it with reference to the unity of the Path, but accepts it with reference to the diversity of knowledges by way of the knowledge of the truth (sacca-ñāṇa), the knowledge of the function (kicca-ñāṇa), and the knowledge of accomplishment (kata-ñāṇa) in each of the truths. This same method applies to the questions "Twelve paths of stream-entry," etc. The Sutta beginning with "Nanu vuttaṃ bhagavatā" (Has it not been said by the Blessed One?) shows the diversity of knowledges along with the preceding and succeeding knowledges; it does not show that the Ariyan Path has twelve knowledges. Therefore, it cannot be proven.

## Commentary on the Discussion of Knowledge (Ñāṇakathāvaṇṇanā).

## The Twentieth Chapter (Vīsatimo Vaggo).

## The Fourth Fifty (Catutthapaṇṇāsaka) is finished.

## 21. The Twenty-first Chapter (Ekavīsatimavagga)

## 1. Commentary on the Discussion of the Dispensation (Sāsanakathāvaṇṇanā)

Now follows the Discussion of the Dispensation. Therein, with reference to the three Councils (saṅgīti), some Uttarāpathakas hold the view that "The Dispensation has been made new," "Is there anyone who makes the Dispensation of the Tathāgata new?" and "Is it possible to make the Dispensation of the Tathāgata new?" With reference to them, the Sakavādin asks in the three discussions, and the other (the Paravādin) accepts. By "satipaṭṭhāna," etc., the Dispensation means the Ariyan Dhamma such as the foundations of mindfulness and the teaching of wholesome states, etc. Among those two, if one were to make the Dispensation new by creating other foundations of mindfulness, etc., apart from those taught by the Blessed One, or by making unwholesome states into wholesome states, etc., would it be said that the Dispensation is made new? Has anyone done so, or is there anyone who does so, or is it possible to do so? This is stated to challenge him in the three questions. In all the remaining discourse, it should be understood according to the Pali text.

## Commentary on the Discussion of the Dispensation (Sāsanakathāvaṇṇanā).
276:
## 2. Commentary on the Discussion of Non-seclusion (Aviwittakathāvaṇṇanā)

879-880. Now follows the Discussion of Non-seclusion. Therein, for whatever person whatever state is present, he is said to be "not secluded" (aviwitta) from that state; this is the conclusion in our own (Sakavādin) doctrine. However, because a worldling (puthujjana) has not fully understood the states belonging to the three realms (tedhātuka), some hold the view that at one and the same moment, he is not secluded from all the states belonging to the three realms (i.e., they still exist in his continuum). With reference to them, the Sakavādin asks, and the other accepts. The words "Phassehi," etc., are stated to show the fault of the occurrence of all states like contact (phassa) in a single moment. In all the remaining discourse, the meaning is clear.

## Commentary on the Discussion of Non-seclusion (Aviwittakathāvaṇṇanā).

## 3. Commentary on the Discussion of Fetters (Saññojanakathāvaṇṇanā)

881-882. Now follows the Discussion of Fetters. Therein, because an Arahant cannot know the entire range of a Buddha, some (like the Mahāsaṅghikas) hold the view that "The attainment of Arahantship occurs without abandoning certain fetters," thinking that for that Arahant, ignorance (avijjā) and doubt (vicikicchā) regarding the Buddha's range must remain unabandoned. With reference to them, the Sakavādin asks, and the other accepts. The words "Atthi kiñci sakkāyadiṭṭhi," etc., are stated to show the abandonment of all fetters by an Arahant. In the two questions "The entire range of a Buddha," etc., the denial is made because of the absence of omniscience (sabbaññuta-ñāṇa) in an Arahant, not because of the non-abandonment of ignorance and doubt. The other (the Paravādin), however, establishes his view by saying "If that is so," referring to their non-abandonment. Since that view is established improperly, it remains without foundation.

## Commentary on the Discussion of Fetters (Saññojanakathāvaṇṇanā).

## 4. Commentary on the Discussion of Psychic Power (Iddhikathāvaṇṇanā)

883-884. Now follows the Discussion of Psychic Power. Therein, this so-called psychic power (iddhi) succeeds in some cases and does not succeed in others. It absolutely does not succeed in making the impermanent, etc., permanent, etc. However, in changing a similar continuity (sabhāga-santati) and making it a dissimilar continuity, or...
277:
By the power of a similar continuity (sabhāgasantati) or by its long-lasting occurrence, it succeeds in some places depending on the causes such as the merit of those for whose benefit it is performed. This is like the turning of drinking water into ghee, milk, etc., for the benefit of the monks, or like the long-lasting continuity of lamps, etc., in the enshrinement of the Great Relics. This is the conclusion in our own tradition (sakasamaya). Based on the fact that the Venerable Pilindavaccha resolved upon the King's palace, "Let it be gold," some like the Andhakas hold the view that "there is psychic power of achieving according to one's wish (abhippāyiddhi)." With reference to them, the question "Is there psychic power of achieving according to one's wish?" is the question of the proponent (sakavādī). Here, abhippāyiddhi means the psychic power of succeeding as one wishes. The affirmation "Yes" is the affirmation of the opponent (paravādī) who stands merely on that view. Then, in order to examine him regarding the permanence of impermanent things, [the proponent] said, "Let the trees have ever-green leaves," and so on. The remaining words here are clear in meaning. Regarding the establishment of the view, the statement "And it became gold" happened due to King Bimbisāra's supportive force of merit (puññūpanissaya), and not solely by the Elder's wish. Therefore, this example is insufficient.

## Commentary on the Discourse on Psychic Power (Iddhikathāvaṇṇanā).

## 5. Commentary on the Discourse on the Buddha (Buddhakathāvaṇṇanā)

Now comes the Discourse on the Buddha (Buddhakathā). In that regard, setting aside the differences in physical size, lifespan, and radiance at various times, there is no such thing as inferiority or superiority among the Buddhas in terms of the remaining Buddha-qualities (buddhadhamma). With reference to those like the Andhakas who hold the view that there is [inferiority or superiority] without distinction, the question "Is there [inferiority or superiority] among the Buddhas?" is the question of the proponent, and the affirmation is that of the opponent. Then, in order to examine him regarding the Buddha-qualities, [the proponent] said, "Is it because of the foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna)?" and so on. The opponent rejects it because he does not see inferiority or superiority by way of those foundations of mindfulness and other qualities.

## Commentary on the Discourse on the Buddha (Buddhakathāvaṇṇanā).

## 6. Commentary on the Discourse on All Directions (Sabbadisākathāvaṇṇanā)

Now comes the Discourse on All Directions (Sabbadisākathā). Therein, regarding the existence of the world systems all around, described as the four directions, below, and above, in all world systems...
278:
Those who, having developed their own various imaginative skills, hold the view that "Buddhas exist in all world systems" and "Buddhas stand in all directions," such as the Mahāsaṅghikas; it is with reference to them that the question is of the Sakavādī and the affirmation is of the other (Paravādī). When asked, "In the East?", he denies it with reference to the Buddha Sakyamuni. When asked again, he affirms it with reference to a Buddha situated in another world system according to his own view. The words beginning with "What is the name of that Blessed One?" are spoken for the purpose of challenging: "If you know, tell me his name and so forth." In this way, the meaning should be understood in all such problems.

## Commentary on the Discourse on All Directions (Sabbadisākathāvaṇṇanā)

## 7. Commentary on the Discourse on Phenomena (Dhammakathāvaṇṇanā)

887-888. Now there is the discourse named Dhammakathā. Therein, because phenomena such as matter (rūpa) are fixed by their nature as matter and do not abandon that nature, those who hold the view that "all phenomena are fixed," such as the Andhakas and some Uttarāpathakas; it is with reference to them that the question "Are all phenomena (fixed)?" is of the Sakavādī and the affirmation is of the other. Then, in order to challenge him, "If they are fixed, they must be either fixed in wrongness (micchatta-niyata) or fixed in rightness (sammatta-niyata); there is no other such thing as 'fixed' (niyāma) apart from these," he said the words beginning with "fixed in wrongness."

In that context, the denial and the affirmation belong to the Paravādī. The words beginning with "Is matter (fixed) in the sense of matter?" are spoken to challenge him according to the sense in which he says they are fixed. Herein, this is the intention: "Matter is fixed in the sense of matter" means matter is only matter, not of the nature of feeling (vedanā) and so forth; it should be stated with this intention, and not otherwise. Why? Because there is no matter other than the sense of being matter (rūpaṭṭha). Indeed, the nature of matter is the sense of matter, and the nature of matter is matter itself, not something other than matter. However, this conventional usage exists for the purpose of making known its distinction from feeling and so forth. Therefore, one who says "matter is fixed in the sense of matter" is saying "matter is fixed." And that which is called "fixed" must be either fixed in wrongness or fixed in rightness; there is no other such thing as 'fixed' apart from these. Then why does he affirm it? Because of a different sense. For in the statement "matter is fixed in the sense of matter," the meaning is that matter is only matter, not of the nature of feeling and so forth. Therefore, he affirms it. But otherwise, there is no such thing as its being fixed; thus, to challenge again by that same method...
279:
The teacher said the words beginning with "fixed in wrongness" (micchattaniyata). All those words have an obvious meaning. Therefore, the view that "form (is fixed)" is also unstable because it is established in an improper way (ayoniso).

## Commentary on the Discussion on Phenomena (Dhammakathāvaṇṇanā)

## 8. Commentary on the Discussion on Kamma (Kammakathāvaṇṇanā)

889-891. Now there is the discussion named Kammakathā. Therein, because kammas such as those to be experienced in this very life (diṭṭhadhammavedanīya) are fixed by their state of being experienced in this very life and so on, those who hold the view that "all kammas are fixed," for example, the view of those very same people; with reference to them, the question is of the Sakavādī and the admission is of the other. In this text, "fixed by the state of being experienced in this very life," the kamma to be experienced in this very life is just the state of being experienced in this very life. If it is able to give its result in the very life seen, it gives it; if not, it becomes what is called lapsed kamma (ahosikamma). With reference to this meaning, it is the admission of the Sakavādī. But by way of fixity in wrongness and fixity in rightness, this kamma is indeed not fixed; thus, everything should be understood by the method already stated below.

## Commentary on the Discussion on Kamma (Kammakathāvaṇṇanā)

## 1. Commentary on the Discussion on Final Nirvana (Parinibbānakathāvaṇṇanā)

Now there is the discussion named Parinibbānakathā. Therein, because an Arahant passes away (parinibbāyati) while still having fetters (saṃyojana) that are unabandoned within the scope of the Omniscient One, those who hold the view that "there is final nirvana without abandoning some fetters," such as the Andhakas; with reference to them, the question is of the Sakavādī and the admission is of the other. The rest here is just the method already stated below.
