## 2. Commentary on the Discussion on the Wholesome Mind (Kusalacittakathāvaṇṇanā)

894-895. Now there is the discussion named Kusalacittakathā. Therein, because an Arahant, having reached the abundance of mindfulness, passes away while being mindful and clearly comprehending, those who hold the view that "he passes away with a wholesome mind," such as the Andhakas; with reference to them, the question is of the Sakavādī and the admission is of the other. Furthermore, because that which is called a wholesome mind occurs by way of the performance of meritorious formations (puññābhisaṅkhāra) and so on, the teacher said the words beginning with "Does an Arahant (perform) meritorious formations..." in order to challenge him with that meaning. The rest here follows the Pali text itself. The words "mindful and clearly comprehending" are spoken for the purpose of illustrating death without confusion by way of functional (kiriya) mindfulness and clear comprehension at the moment of javana, not for the purpose of illustrating a wholesome mind. Therefore, it does not prove the view (the evidence is not valid).

## Commentary on the Discussion on the Wholesome Mind (Kusalacittakathāvaṇṇanā)

## 3. Commentary on the Discussion on the Imperturbable (Āneñjakathāvaṇṇanā)

Now there is the discussion named Āneñjakathā. Therein, having noted that the Blessed One passed away while staying in the fourth jhāna, those who hold the view that "an Arahant passes away while staying in the imperturbable (the fourth jhāna)," such as some Uttarāpathakas; with reference to them, the question is of the Sakavādī and the admission is of the other. "In the natural mind" (pakaticitte) means in the life-continuum mind (bhavaṅga-citta). Indeed, all sentient beings with perception stay in the life-continuum mind and pass away with the death-consciousness (cuti-citta) which is the end of the life-continuum. Thus, the teacher spoke in this way to challenge him with this meaning. Therein, although the natural mind of an Arahant in the four-constituent existence (catuvokāra-bhava) is also imperturbable (āneñja), this problem is raised by way of the five-constituent existence (pañcavokāra-bhava). Therefore, he said, "One should certainly not say that, friend." The rest here has an obvious meaning.

## Commentary on the Discussion on the Imperturbable (Āneñjakathāvaṇṇanā)

## 4. Commentary on the Discussion on the Realization of Dhamma (Dhammābhisamayakathāvaṇṇanā)

Now there is the discussion named Dhammābhisamayakathā. Therein, having seen a person who had become a Stream-enterer (sotāpanna) in a past life dwelling in and emerging from the mother's womb, (the view is held) that "there is the realization of the Four Noble Truths (dhammābhisamaya) by dwelling in the mother's womb"...
281:
## Commentary on the Discussion of Dhamma-realization (Dhammābhisamayakathāvaṇṇanā)

"Dhamma-realization" (dhammābhisamaya) is the doctrine of some members of the Uttarāpathaka sect. With reference to them, the Sakavādī questions and the other (Paravādī) affirms. Then, to refute him, saying, "If there is Dhamma-realization in the womb, must there not be the causes of Dhamma-realization, such as the preaching of the Dhamma?", he said, "Is there preaching of the Dhamma in the womb?" and so on. The term "one who is asleep" (suttassa) and so forth is said with reference to the occurrence of the life-continuum (bhavaṅga). This is because, while staying in the womb, for the most part, only the bhavaṅga-consciousness occurs. Because of the occurrence of that bhavaṅga-consciousness, the being is called "one who is asleep" due to the absence of the occurrence of impulsion (javana) that produces bodily and vocal actions; "one who is negligent" (pamatta) due to the absence of the practice of meditation (bhāvanā); and "one of muddled mindfulness and lacking clear comprehension" (muṭṭhassatī asampajāna) due to the absence of mindfulness and clear comprehension that grasp the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna). How could there be Dhamma-realization for one of such a nature?

## 5–7. Commentary on the Three Discussions (Tissopikathāvaṇṇanā)

898–900. Now, the Three Discussions (Tissopikathā) will be presented. Therein, seeing the attainment of Arahantship by those who have recently become Stream-enterers (sotāpanna), and seeing the seven-year pregnancy of the laywoman Suppavāsā, they hold the view that "There is the attainment of Arahantship in the womb." Also, seeing such things as flying through the air in dreams, they hold the views that "There is Dhamma-realization [in dreams]" and "There is the attainment of Arahantship therein." These are also the doctrines of those same people. With reference to them, the Sakavādī questions and the other affirms. The rest of the discourse here is just the same as the previous discussion (Dhammābhisamayakathā).

## Commentary on the Three Discussions.

## 8. Commentary on the Discussion of the Indeterminate (Abyākatakathāvaṇṇanā)

901–902. Now, the Discussion of the Indeterminate (Abyākatakathā) will be presented. Therein, based on the word of the Buddha, "Monks, there is this intention, and that [in a dream] is indeed negligible (abbhohārika)" (Pārājika 235), some members of the Uttarāpathaka sect alone hold the view that "All consciousness in a dream is indeterminate (abyākata)." With reference to them, the Sakavādī questions and the other affirms. The rest here proceeds according to the Pāḷi text itself. The statement "The consciousness of one who is dreaming is negligible (abbhohārika)" is spoken with reference to an offense (āpatti). If an unwholesome consciousness, such as that of taking life, arises in one who is dreaming, since there is no actual destruction of the object, an offense cannot be prescribed for that dream. For this reason, that consciousness is called "negligible" (abbhohārika), but not because it is indeterminate (abyākata).

## Commentary on the Discussion of the Indeterminate.
282:
This statement was made with reference to the [Vinaya] offense. Even if an unwholesome consciousness such as killing a living being occurs to one who is dreaming, since there is no destruction of the object (actual killing), it is not possible to prescribe an offense for it. For this reason, it is negligible (avvohārika), not because it is indeterminate (abyākata).

## Commentary on the Discussion of the Indeterminate.

## 9. Commentary on the Discussion of the Condition of Repetition (Āsevanapaccayakathāvaṇṇanā)

903-905. Now, there is the discussion of the condition of repetition (Āsevanapaccaya-kathā). In that discussion, since all phenomena are momentary, there is no phenomenon that lasts even for a moment to repeat (āsevati) the condition of repetition. Therefore, there is no such thing as the state of being a condition of repetition. Some hold the view that there is no phenomenon produced by the power of the condition of repetition (this refers to the Pubbaseliyas and Aparaseliyas). With reference to them, the Sakavādī asks and the other (Paravādī) admits. Then, in order to make the condition of repetition known by the power of the Sutta, the Sakavādī cites, "Is it not said by the Blessed One, 'Killing living beings...' and so on?" All those Suttas have a clear meaning.

## Commentary on the Discussion of the Condition of Repetition.

## 10. Commentary on the Discussion of Momentariness (Khaṇikakathāvaṇṇanā)

906-907. Now, there is the discussion of momentariness (Khaṇika-kathā). In that discussion, since all conditioned phenomena (saṅkhata-dhamma) are impermanent, they last only for a single thought-moment. While the state of impermanence is the same, what rule is there to say that one perishes quickly and another perishes after a long time? Such is the view of the Pubbaseliyas and Aparaseliyas. With reference to them, the Sakavādī asks, "Do they last only for a single thought-moment?" and the other admits it. In the problems such as "The great earth in a [single] mind," the Sakavādī rejects it because he does not see the earth and so on existing for only such a thought-moment. The statement "The eye-base (cakkhāyatana)" and so forth was said by the Sakavādī for the purpose of challenging: "If all phenomena were to last for only a single thought-moment, would the eye-base and so forth arise and cease together with eye-consciousness and so forth?" The other (Paravādī), however, with reference to the arising of consciousness of a being that has entered the mother's womb...
283:
(That person) denies it because he does not see the persistence of earth and so forth in that manner of a thought-moment. He affirms it with reference to the period of occurrence (pavatti) according to the power of his own view. The rest of the words here have an obvious meaning. Therefore, he states the reason according to his own preference: "Because they are not permanent, therefore they exist for a single thought-moment." That reason is just like a reason that has not been stated.

## Commentary on the Discourse on Momentariness (Khaṇikakathāvaṇṇanā)

## 3-7. Commentary on the Discourse on Acting According to One's Will (Issariyakāmakārikākathāvaṇṇanā)

910-914. Now follows the Discourse on Acting According to One's Will (the view that things happen because of the power to act as one desires). With reference to the Chaddanta Jātaka and others, some, such as the Andhakas, hold the view: "Because of the cause of acting according to his will, the Bodhisatta goes to a state of loss (animal birth), enters a mother's womb, performed difficult practices (dukkara-cariyā), performed the self-tormenting practice (aparantapa), and designated another teacher." Regarding them, there is the question of the Sakavādī and the assent of the other. The remaining text in the first discourse has a clear meaning.

In the second discourse, the word "iddhimā" (one with psychic power) [should be connected to the question]. If he were to enter a womb because of the cause of acting according to his will, would he go by psychic power, or would he go without the influence of kamma? This is stated for the purpose of objection. The other (Paravādī), however, rejects the first question with reference to psychic power born of meditation (bhāvanāmaya-iddhi). In the second question, he assents with reference to the power of merit (puññiddhi).

In the third discourse, what is called "the cause of acting according to his will" is performed with wrong view when performing difficult practices (dukkara-kārikā). If that Bodhisatta were to perform that practice, would he also hold views such as eternalism? For the purpose of objection, it is stated: "The world is eternal," and so on. In the fourth discourse, the method is the same.

## Commentary on the Discourse on Acting According to One's Will.

## 8. Commentary on the Discourse on Counterfeits (Patirūpakathāvaṇṇanā)

915-916. Now follows the Discourse on the Counterfeit of Lust (the view regarding states resembling lust). Therein, with reference to loving-kindness (mettā), compassion (karuṇā), and appreciative joy (muditā), they hold: "There is a state that is not lust but resembles lust." With reference to envy (issā), stinginess (macchariya), and remorse (kukkucca), they hold: "There is a state that is not hatred but resembles hatred." With reference to the smile-producing consciousness (hasituppāda), they hold: "There is a state that is not delusion but resembles delusion." With reference to the rebuking of unruly persons, the supporting of virtuous monks, the blaming of evil, the praising of good, the use of the word "outcaste" (vasala) by the Venerable Pilindavaccha, and the use of the words "spittle-eater" (kheḷāsaka) and "vain man" (moghapurisa) by the Blessed One, some, such as the Andhakas, hold the view: "There is a state that is not a defilement but resembles a defilement." Regarding them, in all these discourses, there is the question of the Sakavādī and the assent of the other.

Then, because there are no such things as "non-contacts" that resemble contact and so on, it is stated: "Is there a state that is not lust but resembles lust?" and so on, in order to object that there are no states that are not lust but resemble lust. The other rejects it because of the non-existence of those counterfeits of contact and so on. In all places, the remaining text has a clear meaning.
285:
To challenge that it does not exist, he said the words beginning with "There is no counterfeit of contact which is not contact." The other (Paravādī) denies it because those counterfeits do not exist. In all the remaining problems, the meaning is very clear.

## Commentary on the Discourse on Counterfeits (Patirūpakathāvaṇṇanā)

## 9. Commentary on the Discourse on the Unproduced (Aparinipphannakathāvaṇṇanā)

917-918. Now there is the discourse on the Unproduced. In that discourse—

"Only suffering (dukkha) comes to be, suffering stands and passes away;
Nothing other than suffering comes to be, nothing other than suffering ceases."

Based on this statement, those who hold the view that "only the truth of suffering is produced (parinipphanna) by causes, while the remaining aggregates, bases, elements, and faculties are unproduced (aparinipphanna) by causes," such as some Uttarāpathakas and Hetuvādins; it is with reference to them that the Sakavādī asks, "Is matter unproduced?" and the other (Paravādī) affirms it. Then, in order to challenge him, "If matter were unproduced, it would not have the nature of impermanence and so forth," he said the words beginning with "Is matter not impermanent?" The other denies it, not seeing such matter that has the nature of impermanence. The Sakavādī, having refuted one view of his with the words "Is matter not impermanent?" and wishing to ask a second time, said the words beginning with "Is only suffering produced?" Then, to refute that view of his as well, he said the words beginning with "That which is impermanent (is that not suffering?)."

In this statement, this is the intention: Not only the first truth (the truth of suffering) is suffering. Whatever is impermanent, that is suffering. Matter is also impermanent; therefore, that matter is also produced. This being so, your statement "Matter is unproduced, only suffering is produced" should not be said as "Only suffering is produced." In the sequences of sentences where feeling (vedanā) and so forth are the basis, the method should be understood in this same way. In the case of the base of phenomena (dhammāyatana) and the element of phenomena (dhammadhātu), impermanence should be understood by way of the remaining phenomena, excluding Nibbāna. The faculties (indriya) are indeed impermanent.

## The Commentary on the Discourse on the Unproduced ends.

## Twenty-third Chapter.
288:
Among those sections, the Enumeration Section (Uddesavāra) is first because it must be explained in detail according to the order of the summary. The beginning of that Uddesavāra is this Yamaka (pair): "Whatever states are wholesome, are all those wholesome roots? Or rather, whatever states are wholesome roots, are all those states wholesome?" The nature of this Yamaka should be understood in three ways: as Attha-yamaka (Meaning-pair) by way of the two meanings known as wholesome and wholesome roots; as Dhamma-yamaka (Text-pair) by way of the Pāḷi text proceeding in forward and reverse order based on those same meanings; or as Pucchā-yamaka (Question-pair) by way of the questions proceeding in forward and reverse order. The same method applies to the remaining Yamakas.

Now, in this Mūlayamaka taught by way of these Yamakas, the definition of the Pāḷi text of the Uddesavāra should be understood by way of the divisions of methods (naya), pairs (yamaka), questions (pucchā), and meanings (attha). In the Wholesome Triad (Kusala-tika) Matika, based on this first term "Kusala dhammā" (wholesome states), there are these four methods: Mūla-naya, Mūlamūla-naya, Mūlaka-naya, and Mūlamūlaka-naya. In each of these methods, there are three Yamakas: Mūlayamaka, Ekamūlayamaka, and Aññamaññamūlayamaka. Thus, in the four methods, there are twelve Yamakas. In each Yamaka, there are two questions by way of forward and reverse order, making twenty-four questions. In each question, there are two meanings by way of the established meaning (sanniṭṭhāna) and the doubtful meaning (saṃsaya), making forty-eight meanings.

Among those established and doubtful meanings, in the phrase "Whatever states are wholesome" (Ye keci kusalā dhammā), the established meaning should be understood because there is no doubt such as "Are they wholesome or are they not wholesome?" In the phrase "Are all those wholesome roots?" (sabbe te kusalamūlā), the doubtful meaning should be understood because it is asked by way of doubt: "Are all those wholesome states called wholesome roots or not?" That doubt is stated for the purpose of showing the point of doubt in those to be taught (veneyya); for the Tathāgata, however, there is no such thing as doubt. The same method applies to the subsequent question phrases.

Just as there are these four methods based on the term "wholesome" (kusala), twelve Yamakas by way of three Yamakas in each method, twenty-four questions by way of two questions in each Yamaka, and forty-eight meanings by way of two meanings in each question; so it is based on the term "unwholesome" (akusala) and the term "indeterminate" (abyākata). It is also the same based on the term "name" (nāma), which is indicated by combining the three terms. Thus, in the four terms of the Wholesome Triad Matika, there are sixteen methods in total, and forty-eight...
289:
The Yamakas, the ninety-six questions, and the one hundred and ninety-two meanings are stated by way of the Summary (Uddesa). By this extent of the sequence of words, that which is called the Root Section (Mūlavāra) is first indicated.

Following that Mūlavāra, nine sections starting with "Whatever states are wholesome, all those have wholesome roots" (Ye keci kusalā dhammā, sabbe te kusalahetū) are indicated by way of synonyms of that very Mūlavāra. Thus, there are ten sections in all: the Root Section (Mūlavāra), the Condition Section (Hetuvāra), the Source Section (Nidānavāra), the Origin Section (Sambhavavāra), the Genesis Section (Pabhavavāra), the Origination Section (Samuṭṭhānavāra), the Nutriment Section (Āhāravāra), the Object Section (Ārammaṇavāra), the Condition Section (Paccayavāra), and the Arising Section (Samudayavāra). Among these, the methods (naya) and so forth in the remaining sections should be understood according to the definition given in the Mūlavāra. Thus, it should be understood that in all ten sections, one hundred and sixty methods, four hundred and eighty Yamakas, nine hundred and sixty questions, and one thousand nine hundred and twenty meanings are taught. In this way, first, in the Summary Section (Uddesavāra), the definition of the Pāḷi should be understood by way of the divisions of methods, Yamakas, questions, and the section on meanings.

The verse beginning with "Mūlaṃ hetu nidānañca" is called the Summary Verse (Uddānagāthā) of the ten sections. In that summary verse, all terms such as 'mūla' are merely synonyms for the word 'cause' (kāraṇa). A cause is called 'mūla' (root) in the sense of being a foundation. It is called 'hetu' (condition) because it proceeds to produce its own fruit. It is called 'nidāna' (source) because it bestows its own fruit, as if pointing out, "Here, take this fruit." It is called 'sambhava' (origin) because the fruit arises well from it. It is called 'pabhava' (source/genesis) because it originates. It is called 'samuṭṭhāna' (origination) because the fruit arises well in it, or the fruit arises because of it. It is called 'āhāra' (nutriment) because it brings its own fruit. It is called 'ārammaṇa' (support/object) because its own fruit, which should not be rejected, depends on it. It is called 'paccaya' (condition) because, depending on this and without rejection, the fruit arises. It is called 'samudaya' (arising) because the fruit well emerges from it. Thus, the word-meaning (vacanattha) of these terms should be understood.

## Explanation of the Summary Section (Uddesavāravaṇṇanā)

## Explanation of the Exposition Section (Niddesavāravaṇṇanā)

Now, the Exposition Section (Niddesavāra) is commenced with the method beginning with "Whatever states are wholesome" (Ye keci kusalā dhammā). Therein, the words "Ye keci" (Whatever) are words expressing "without exception". "Kusalā dhammā" (Wholesome states) refers to those states of a wholesome nature that have the characteristics stated in the Word-Analysis (Padabhājanī) of the Wholesome Triad (Kusalatika), being faultless and having pleasant results. "Are all those wholesome states wholesome roots?" (Sabbe te kusalamūlā?) is the question asked.
290:
## "There are only three wholesome roots" means that not all those wholesome states are wholesome roots; only the three states beginning with non-greed (alobha) are wholesome roots. "The remaining wholesome states are not wholesome roots" means that wholesome states such as contact (phassa) and so forth, which remain after the three wholesome roots, are not called wholesome roots. Alternatively, it means that the remaining states like contact are indeed wholesome states, but they are not wholesome roots.

Furthermore, in the phrase "Whatever wholesome roots" (Ye vā pana kusalamūlā), the three states beginning with non-greed, which were called "wholesome roots" in the second part of the first question, are taken. By the Pāḷi "Are all those states wholesome?" (Sabbe te dhammā kusalā?), He asks whether all those three states beginning with non-greed are wholesome. He says "Yes" (Āmantā) to affirm the wholesome nature of all wholesome roots. This is the meaning of the Root Yamaka (Mūlayamaka) in the Root Method (Mūlanaya). By this means, the method of answering in all questions should be understood. Whatever slight distinction exists in any Yamaka, that alone we shall explain.

In the Single-Root Yamaka (Ekamūlayamaka), in the Pāḷi "Do all those states have one root with a wholesome root?" (Sabbe te kusalamūlena ekamūlā?), the term "one root" (ekamūla) should be taken in the sense of "same" (samāna) rather than in the sense of the number "one". The meaning here is: "Do all those wholesome states have the same root as a wholesome root?" The question is: "Is that which is the root of contact the very same root of feeling (vedanā) and so forth?" Then, wishing to affirm that those wholesome states have such a same root, He says "Yes" (Āmantā). By the term "wholesome-originated" (kusalasamuṭṭhāna), matter (rūpa) originated by wholesome consciousness is shown. "Having one root" (ekamūla) means having the same root as a wholesome root such as non-greed. Just as non-greed and so forth are roots for contact and so forth because they are root-conditions (hetupaccaya), so too are they roots for that wholesome-originated matter. However, because it lacks the characteristic of being wholesome, that matter is not called "wholesome".

In the Mutual Yamaka (Aññamaññayamaka), instead of asking "Whatever wholesome states", the question is made as "Whatever states have one root with a wholesome root". Why? Because by this phrasing (byañjana) also, that very meaning of "Whatever wholesome states" is possible. The term "wholesome roots" (kusalamūlāni) is a qualifier (visesana) of the preceding term "Whatever roots". For it is said, "Roots that arise together"; those can be wholesome roots, unwholesome roots, or indeterminate roots. Here, this is said for the purpose of showing the distinction as "wholesome roots". In "and are mutual roots" (aññamaññamūlāni ca), the meaning is that they are conditions for each other by way of root-condition (hetupaccaya). In the reverse question (paṭilomapucchā) of that very Yamaka, instead of saying "Do all those states have one root with a wholesome root?", it is said "Are all those states wholesome?". Why? Because there is no distinction in meaning. If the question were made as "Do all those states have one root with a wholesome root?", the answer would have to be given by the method already stated below, "Roots that arise together", and in that case, there would be no distinction in meaning. Therefore, in that way...
291:
Because there is no such distinction in meaning, the Buddha did not state it [as in the direct order] but posed the question in this way. By this method, the distinction of the question in the Aññamaññamūlayamaka should also be understood in the Mūlamūlanaya and so forth.

53-55. In the Mūlamūlanaya, "Are all those roots of wholesome roots?" (sabbe te kusalamūlamūlā) means asking whether all those wholesome states are roots known as wholesome roots. "Having the same root of roots" (ekamūlamūlā) means they are called so because they have a root of roots that is identical in the sense of being the same. "Having mutual roots of roots" (aññamaññamūlamūlā) means the root of each other is a mutual root; because that mutual root is a root in the sense of root-condition (hetupaccaya), they are called "having mutual roots of roots."

In the Mūlakanaya, "rooted in wholesome roots" (kusalamūlakā) means they are called so because they have wholesome states as their root in the sense of root-condition.

57-61. In the Mūlamūlakanaya, "rooted in the root of wholesome roots" (kusalamūlamūlakā) means the root of wholesome states is called the wholesome root. Because that very root of wholesome states is a root in the sense of root-condition, they are called "rooted in the root of wholesome roots." This is the specific meaning in the questions of the Nayamaka based on the term "wholesome" (kusala).

62-73. The same method applies to the term "unwholesome" (akusala) and others. However, this distinction—"rootless unwholesome" (ahetukaṃ akusalaṃ)—is stated with reference to delusion (moha) associated with doubt (vicikicchā) and restlessness (uddhacca).

74-85. "Rootless indeterminate" (ahetukaṃ abyākataṃ) refers to the eighteen rootless arisings of consciousness (cittuppāda), matter (rūpa), and Nibbāna. In this context, "not of the same root as the indeterminate root" (abyākatamūlena na ekamūlaṃ), matter produced by indeterminate states with roots (sahetuka-abyākata) is excluded, and the remainder (rootless cittuppāda, matter, Nibbāna) is obtained. Although matter produced by indeterminate states with roots is of the same root as the indeterminate root, this answer is given based on the states obtained together, treating that matter as if the term "rootless" (ahetuka) does not apply to it.

86-97. "Mental phenomena" (nāmā dhammā) refers to states called "name" (nāma). In terms of meaning, these are the four formless aggregates (arūpī-khandha) and Nibbāna. "Only nine mental roots" (naveva nāmamūlāni) refers to the nine roots by way of wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate roots. "Rootless mental phenomena are not of the same root as the mental root" (ahetukaṃ nāmaṃ nāmamūlena na ekamūlaṃ) means the mental phenomena called the eighteen rootless arisings of consciousness, delusion associated with doubt and restlessness, and Nibbāna are not of the same root as the mental root. This is because they do not arise together with that mental root.
292:
In the phrase "mental phenomena with roots [are of the same root] as the mental root" (sahetukaṃ nāmaṃ nāmamūlena), it means that mental phenomena with roots have a root identical to the mental root. The remaining phrases in all places have meanings that are clear.

98-99. In the Section on Causes (Hetuvāra) and so forth, the meaning should be understood by this very method. The verses beginning with "Root, cause, and source" (mūlaṃ hetu nidānañca) are stated again by way of a summary (uddāna) of the ten sections already explained in detail.
