## 2. Pairs of Aggregates (Khandhayamaka)

## 1. Description of the Brief Exposition of the Section on Designations (Paṇṇatti-uddesavāravaṇṇanā)

Now follows the description of the Khandhayamaka, which is taught immediately after the Mūlayamaka, by grouping the wholesome and other states already taught in the Mūlayamaka according to the aggregates (khandha). Therein, the divisions of the Pali text should first be understood as follows: In this Khandhayamaka, there are three Great Sections (Mahāvāra)—the Section on Designations (Paṇṇattivāra), the Section on Occurrence (Pavattivāra), and the Section on Full Understanding (Pariññāvāra).

Among them, the Section on Designations is so called because it proceeds solely by way of clarifying the names and designations of the aggregates. The Section on Occurrence proceeds by clarifying the occurrence of those aggregates, whose names and designations were clarified in the previous section, by way of their arising and cessation; therefore, it is called the Section on Occurrence. The Section on Full Understanding proceeds by illustrating, in brief, the three types of full understanding regarding the aggregates that occur in this sequence; therefore, it is called the Section on Full Understanding.

Among those sections, the Section on Designations is established in two modes: by way of brief exposition (uddesa) and detailed exposition (niddesa). In the other sections, there is no separate Section of Brief Exposition. From the beginning, they are established in a single way by way of question and answer (pucchāvissajjana).

Therein, from the term "five aggregates" (pañcakkhandhā) up to the term "not aggregates, not formations" (na khandhā na saṅkhārā), it should be understood as the Brief Exposition of the Section on Designations. "Section of Questions" (pucchāvāra) is also a name for that same Brief Exposition. In that Brief Exposition, this Pali text "five aggregates" is the heading (uddesa) of the aggregates to be questioned by way of pairs (yamaka). The words "aggregate of matter ... aggregate of consciousness" are the establishment of the names of those very aggregates by way of their classification.
293:
2-3. Now, by way of these aggregates, there are four methods: the Section on the Purification of Terms (Padasodhana-vāra), the Section on the Wheel of the Root of Purification of Terms (Padasodhanamūla-cakkavāra), the Section on the Pure Aggregates (Suddhakkhandha-vāra), and the Section on the Wheel of the Root of Pure Aggregates (Suddhakkhandhamūla-cakkavāra). Among these, the section that proceeds by purifying only the terms in the manner of 'Is matter the aggregate of matter? Is the aggregate of matter matter?' is called the Section on the Purification of Terms. This Section on the Purification of Terms is twofold by way of the forward (anuloma) and reverse (paṭiloma) orders. Therein, in the forward order, there are five pairs (yamakas) such as 'Is matter the aggregate of matter? Is the aggregate of matter matter?' In the reverse order as well, there are exactly five pairs such as 'Is it not matter, not the aggregate of matter? Is it not the aggregate of matter, not matter?' Following that, the section that proceeds by forming wheels of four each, taking each aggregate as a root from among the aggregates already purified in that Section on the Purification of Terms, in the manner of 'Is matter the aggregate of matter? Are the aggregates the aggregate of feeling?' is called the Section on the Wheel of the Root of Purification of Terms, because of the existence of wheels having the purification of terms as their root. This section is also twofold by way of the forward and reverse orders. Therein, in the forward order, there are twenty pairs, having made four pairs for each aggregate as a root, in the manner of 'Is matter the aggregate of matter? Are the aggregates the aggregate of feeling?' In the reverse order as well, there are exactly twenty pairs such as 'Is it not matter, not the aggregate of matter? Are they not aggregates, not the aggregate of feeling?'

Following that, the section that proceeds by way of the pure aggregates alone, in the manner of 'Is matter an aggregate? Are the aggregates matter?' is called the Section on the Pure Aggregates. In that Section on the Pure Aggregates, among terms such as 'Are the aggregates matter?', the meaning should be taken as 'Is the aggregate the aggregate of matter? Is the aggregate the aggregate of feeling?' Why? Because it is analyzed in this way in the Exposition Section (Niddesa-vāra). For therein, when it is asked 'Is matter an aggregate?', the answer is 'Yes' (āmantā). When it is asked 'Are the aggregates the aggregate of matter?', the meaning is analyzed by extracting the term in the manner of 'The aggregate of matter is both an aggregate and the aggregate of matter; the remaining aggregates are not the aggregate of matter,' and so on for 'Are the aggregates matter?' and 'Are the aggregates the aggregate of matter?' For this very reason, this is called the Section on the Pure Aggregates. Here, the word itself is not the standard as in the purification of terms. Rather, in whatever way the pure aggregates are obtained, in that way the meaning alone is the standard. This same method applies to the Pairs on the Bases (Āyatana-yamaka) and so on later. This Section on the Pure Aggregates is also twofold by way of the forward and reverse orders. Therein, in the forward order, there are five pairs such as 'Is matter an aggregate? Are the aggregates matter?' In the reverse order as well, there are exactly five pairs such as 'Is it not matter, not an aggregate? Are they not aggregates, not matter?'

Following that, the section that proceeds by forming wheels of four each, taking each aggregate as a root from among those very pure aggregates, in the manner of 'Is matter an aggregate? Are the aggregates feeling?' is called the Section on the Wheel of the Root of Pure Aggregates, because of the existence of wheels having the pure aggregates as their root.
294:
In that Section on the Wheel of the Root of Pure Aggregates, the meaning should be understood in the manner of 'Are the aggregates the aggregate of feeling?' and so on for terms such as 'Are the aggregates feeling?' Otherwise, there would be a contradiction with the Exposition Section (Niddesa-vāra). This Section on the Wheel of the Root of Pure Aggregates is also twofold by way of the forward and reverse orders. Among those forward and reverse orders, in the forward order, there are twenty pairs, having made four pairs for each aggregate as a root, in the manner of 'Is matter an aggregate? Are the aggregates feeling?' In the reverse order as well, there are exactly twenty pairs such as 'Is it not matter, not an aggregate? Are they not aggregates, not feeling?' Thus, the Summary Section (Uddesa-vāra) of the Chapter on Designations (Paṇṇatti-vāra) should be understood as being adorned with one hundred pairs, two hundred questions, and four hundred meanings, by making two meanings for each question according to the distinction of the thesis (sanniṭṭhāna) and the doubt (saṃsaya).

## Commentary on the Summary of Designations

## 1. Commentary on the Exposition of Designations
Now, the Blessed One has begun the Exposition Section (Niddesa-vāra) in the manner of 'Is matter the aggregate of matter?' and so on. Therein, in the Exposition Section, with the Pali 'Is matter the aggregate of matter?', He asks for the purpose of purifying the term: 'Whatever is called matter without distinction, is all that matter the aggregate of matter?' In the passage 'Piyarūpaṃ sātarūpaṃ, rūpaṃ, na rūpakkhandho' (Pleasant matter, agreeable matter is matter, but not the aggregate of matter), the meaning is: 'That which is called matter in this passage "pleasant matter, agreeable matter" is indeed matter, but it is not the aggregate of matter.' In the passage 'Rūpakkhandho rūpañceva rūpakkhandho ca' (The aggregate of matter is both matter and the aggregate of matter), the meaning is: 'That which is the aggregate of matter is fit to be called both matter and the aggregate of matter.' However, in this passage 'Is the aggregate of matter matter?', because the aggregate of matter is invariably called matter, He said 'Yes' (āmantā). By this method, the meaning should be understood in all answers. Whatever distinction occurs in a particular Pali passage, I shall explain that specific meaning right there. In the Pairs on Perception (Saññā-yamaka), the term 'perception of views' (diṭṭhi-saññā) refers to that perception of views which appears in Pali passages such as 'perception of proliferation' (papañca-saññā). In the Pairs on Formations (Saṅkhāra-yamaka), the term 'remaining formations' (avasesā saṅkhārā) refers to the conditioned phenomena (saṅkhata-dhamma) remaining from the aggregate of formations, which appear in Pali passages such as 'Formations are indeed impermanent' (aniccā vata saṅkhārā). In the reverse order as well, this is the very method.

## The Section on the Purification of Terms is Finished.
In the Section on the Wheel of the Root of Purification of Terms, with the passage 'Are the aggregates the aggregate of feeling?', He asks: 'Whatever things are called aggregates without distinction, are all those aggregates the aggregate of feeling?' In the remaining questions as well, this is the very method. In the reverse order, in this passage 'Are they not aggregates, not the aggregate of feeling?', those things called designations (paññatti) and Nibbāna...
295:
States (dhammā) are not aggregates; since those states are also not the aggregate of feeling (vedanākkhandha), therefore He said, "Āmantā" (Yes). In the remaining answers, this same method applies.

## The Word-cleansing Root-cycle Section (Padasodhana-mūlacakkavāra) is finished.

In the Pure Aggregates Section (Sudda-khandha-vāra), by the term "Is matter (rūpa) an aggregate (khandha)?", it is asked whether all that is called matter is an aggregate. In that question, whether it be matter that is pleasant and agreeable (piyarūpa-sātarūpa) or primary and derived matter (bhūta-upādārūpa), all matter is included within the five aggregates; therefore, He affirms with "Āmantā". In the second term, although it should be asked "Are aggregates matter?", because only the aggregate of matter (rūpakkhandha) is intended by the word "matter", He asks "Are aggregates the aggregate of matter?", disregarding the literal word and focusing on the meaning. In this way, the meaning should be understood in all terms. This same method applies in the Exposition Section (Niddesa-vāra) of the Yamaka of Bases (Āyatana-yamaka) and others that follow. Regarding "Is perception (saññā) an aggregate?", whether it be perception associated with wrong view (diṭṭhi-saññā) or just perception, He said "Āmantā" because all perception is an aggregate. The same method applies to the term "Are formations (saṅkhāra) an aggregate?". For there is no such thing as a formation that is liberated from the aggregates.

In the Reverse Section (Paṭiloma-vāra), by the text "Is that which is not matter also not an aggregate?", He asks whether a state that is not matter is also not an aggregate. In the answer to that question, it means that, excluding matter, the remaining aggregates are not matter, but they are aggregates. Aggregates such as feeling (vedanā) and others, which are different from matter, are not matter, but they are indeed aggregates. The states remaining after excluding matter and aggregates are Nibbāna and concepts (paññatti), which are liberated from the five aggregates. In the subsequent terms "the rest" (avasesā), this same method should be understood.

## The Pure Aggregates Section (Sudda-khandha-vāra) is finished.

40-44. In the Root-cycle of Pure Aggregates (Sudda-khandha-mūlacakkavāra), the meaning of the terms "Is matter an aggregate?" etc., should be understood in the same way as the method stated below.

## The Root-cycle of Pure Aggregates (Sudda-khandha-mūlacakkavāra) is finished.

## The Commentary on the Designation Exposition Section (Paṇṇatti-niddesa-vāra-vaṇṇanā) is finished.
296:
## 2. Commentary on the Occurrence Section (Pavatti-vāra-vaṇṇanā)

50-205. Now, the Occurrence Section (Pavatti-vāra) is undertaken by the method "To whom the aggregate of matter...", etc. Why is the Summary Section (Uddesa-vāra) not stated here? Because the method has already been shown below (in the Designation Section). Indeed, the method was shown in the Summary Section of the Designation Section (Paṇṇatti-vāra). Since it is possible to know it by that method even if it is not stated here in this Occurrence Section, He did not state that Summary Section but undertook only the Exposition Section (Niddesa-vāra). In this Great Section (Mahā-vāra) known as the Occurrence Section, there are three internal sections (antara-vāra): the Section on Arising (Uppāda-vāra), the Section on Cessation (Nirodha-vāra), and the Section on Arising and Cessation (Uppāda-nirodha-vāra). Among these three, the first is called the Section on Arising because it illustrates the characteristic of the arising of states. The second is called the Section on Cessation because it illustrates the characteristic of the cessation of those same states. The third is called the Section on Arising and Cessation because it illustrates both characteristics. Here, by the Section on Arising, only the mode of arising of states is illustrated. By the Section on Cessation, the impermanence (aniccatā) of those same states is illustrated, as in "That which has arisen is never permanent". By the Section on Arising and Cessation, both are illustrated.

In that Section on Arising, first, there are six divisions of time by way of the three periods: the present, the past, the future, the present with the past, the present with the future, and the past with the future. Among those six, the present time should be understood by way of the designation of the present as "To whom the aggregate of matter arises (uppajjati)". That present time is stated first because it is extremely easy to understand, as present states are to be grasped through direct perception. The past time should be understood by way of the designation of the past as "To whom the aggregate of matter arose (uppajjittha)". That past time is stated second because it is easier to understand than the future through inference of past states previously experienced through direct perception. The future time should be understood by way of the designation of the future as "To whom the aggregate of matter will arise (uppajjissati)". That future time is stated third because it is to be grasped through inference of states already grasped by way of direct perception and previous experience, thinking "In the future also, states of such nature will arise".

The present-past time should be understood by way of the designation of the past together with the present as "To whom the aggregate of matter arises, to him the aggregate of feeling arose". That time is stated fourth because it is the easiest to understand among the three mixed times. The present-future time should be understood by way of the designation of the future together with the present as "To whom the aggregate of matter arises, to him the aggregate of feeling will arise". That time is stated fifth because it is easier to understand in terms of meaning due to the existence of states to be grasped through direct perception. As for "To whom the aggregate of matter arose, to him the aggregate of feeling will arise"...
297:
The past-and-future time (atītenānāgata-kāla) should be understood by the power of designating the future together with the past. This past-and-future time is taught as the sixth because it is more difficult to understand than the preceding times.

Among these six divisions of time mentioned, there is the first, which is the present time (paccuppanna-kāla). In that present time, there are three sections (vāra): the section on persons (puggalavāra), the section on locations (okāsavāra), and the section on persons and locations (puggalokāsavāra). Among these three sections, the section that illustrates the arising of the aggregates by the power of the person using the term 'yassa' (to whom) is called Puggalavāra. The section that illustrates the arising of the aggregates by the power of the location using the term 'yattha' (where) is called Okāsavāra. The section that illustrates the arising of the aggregates by the power of both person and location using the term 'yassa yattha' (to whom, where) is called Puggalokāsavāra. These three sections are first shown by the method of direct order (anuloma-naya) and subsequently by the method of reverse order (paṭiloma-naya). Among these, the method that illustrates the state of arising through the words 'uppajjati' (arises), 'uppajjittha' (arose), and 'uppajjissati' (will arise) is called the Anuloma method. The method that illustrates the state of non-arising through the words 'nuppajjati' (does not arise), 'nuppajjittha' (did not arise), and 'nuppajjissati' (will not arise) is called the Paṭiloma method.

Between these two methods, first, in the Anuloma method of the Puggalavāra in the present time: 'To whom the aggregate of matter arises, to him the aggregate of feeling arises. Or else, to whom the aggregate of feeling arises, to him the aggregate of matter arises.' In this manner, there are four Yamakas (pairs) rooted in the aggregate of matter (rūpakkhandha). By the method beginning with 'To whom the aggregate of feeling arises, to him the aggregate of perception arises,' there are three Yamakas rooted in the aggregate of feeling (vedanākkhandha), two Yamakas rooted in the aggregate of perception (saññākkhandha), and one Yamaka rooted in the aggregate of mental formations (saṅkhārakkhandha). Thus, by taking the subsequent aggregates not yet taken (or by not repeating the preceding aggregates already taken), there are ten Yamakas.

Among those ten Yamakas, in the four Yamakas rooted in the aggregate of matter, only the first one, the aggregate of feeling Yamaka, is fully answered. The remaining Yamakas are abbreviated for the sake of the lightness of the Pali text (tanti), as their answers are similar to that of the aggregate of feeling Yamaka. In the Yamakas rooted in the aggregate of feeling and so on, there is only the identical answer 'Āmantā' (Yes). Therefore, those Yamakas are also abbreviated for the sake of the lightness of the Pali text. Thus, it should be understood that by answering a single Yamaka in the Anuloma method of the Puggalavāra in the present time, all ten Yamakas are considered answered. Just as there are ten in the Puggalavāra, there are ten in the Okāsavāra and ten in the Puggalokāsavāra; thus, there are thirty Yamakas in the Anuloma method among the three sections of the present time. As in the Anuloma method, so also in the Paṭiloma method there are thirty; therefore, in the present time, the total is...
298:
...sixty Yamakas. Among those sixty Yamakas, it should be understood that there are 120 questions (pucchā) and 242 meanings (attha). In the same way, in the remaining five divisions of time, there are six sections each by way of the distinctions of person and so on, through the power of the Anuloma and Paṭiloma methods. By making ten Yamakas for each section, there are sixty Yamakas each, totaling 300 Yamakas. When these 300 Yamakas are combined with the previously mentioned Yamakas, there are 360 Yamakas, 720 questions, and 1440 meanings. This is the definition of the Pali text in the Section on Arising (Uppādavāra) first.

As in the Uppādavāra, so also in the Section on Cessation (Nirodhavāra) and the Section on Arising and Cessation (Uppāda-nirodhavāra); therefore, in the entire Great Section on Occurrence (Pavatti-mahāvāra), it should be understood that there are 1080 Yamakas, 2160 questions, and 4320 meanings.

In the Pali text, however, in the three unmixed divisions of time within the Uppādavāra and Nirodhavāra, only one Yamaka is answered in each respective section and then abbreviated. In the three mixed divisions of time, by the method beginning with 'To whom the aggregate of feeling arises, to him the aggregate of perception has arisen,' only one Yamaka is answered even among the Yamakas rooted in the aggregate of feeling and so on. In the Uppāda-nirodhavāra, however, that Yamaka is already answered in all six divisions of time. The remaining Yamakas are abbreviated because they have answers identical to the one already answered. This is the definition of the Pali text in the entire Pavatti-mahāvāra.

For the purpose of determining the meaning, this characteristic should be understood: in this Pavatti-mahāvāra, the determination of meaning should be understood by applying five types of answers to four types of questions in twenty-seven instances. Therein, the four types of questions are: the prior question (purepañhā), the posterior question (pacchāpañhā), the complete question (paripuṇṇapañhā), and the void question (moghapañhā). In each Yamaka, there are two questions. In each question, there are two terms (pada). Among them, the question in whose answer the arising or cessation of the aggregate is obtained by only one term is called a prior question (purepañhā). The question in whose answer the arising or cessation of the aggregates is obtained by both terms is called a posterior question (pacchāpañhā). The question in whose answer the arising or cessation of the aggregate is obtained by one term as well as the arising or cessation of the aggregates is obtained by both terms is called a complete question (paripuṇṇapañhā). The question in whose answer a rejection or a prohibition is obtained is called a void question (moghapañhā). Since these cannot be understood without being demonstrated, we shall demonstrate them.
299:
In the question 'Where the aggregate of matter does not arise, does the aggregate of feeling not arise there?', in this answer 'It arises' first, the arising of the aggregate of feeling, which is taken by only one term, is obtained. Thus, this question and other such questions should be known as Purepañhā (Prior Question). In the question 'To whom the aggregate of matter has arisen, has the aggregate of feeling arisen to him?', in this answer 'Yes' (āmantā), the arising in the past for any being whatsoever of the aggregates of matter and feeling, which are taken by two terms, is obtained. Thus, this question and other such questions should be known as Pacchāpañhā (Posterior Question).

In this first question 'To whom the aggregate of matter is arising, is the aggregate of feeling arising to him?', in this answer beginning with 'To those attaining the non-percipient realm...', in this portion (koṭṭhāsa) 'To those attaining the non-percipient realm, the aggregate of matter is arising to them, but the aggregate of feeling is not arising to them', the arising of the aggregate of matter, which is taken by only one term, is also obtained. In this portion 'To those attaining the five-constituent existence, the aggregate of matter is arising to them and the aggregate of feeling is arising', the arising of both the aggregates of matter and feeling, which are included by two terms, is also obtained. Thus, this question and other such questions should be known as Paripuṇṇapañhā (Complete Question). Purepacchāpañhā is also a name for this very question. The reason is that in the answer to this question, in the first portion, only the arising of the aggregate of matter, included by one term, is shown. In the second portion, the arising of the aggregates of matter and feeling, included by two terms, is shown. By this very characteristic, in whatever question the arising or cessation of an aggregate included by one term is obtained, that question is called Purepañhā. In whatever question the arising or cessation of aggregates included by two terms is obtained, that question is called Pacchāpañhā.

In this question 'To whom the aggregate of matter has not arisen, has the aggregate of feeling not arisen to him?', in this answer 'No' (natthi), rejection (paṭikkhepa) is obtained. In the question 'To whom the aggregate of matter is arising, is the aggregate of feeling ceasing to him?', in this answer 'No' (no), prohibition (paṭisedha) is obtained. Therefore, these two types of questions and other such questions should be known as Moghapañhā (Vain Question). It is also called Tucchapañhā. Thus, first, the four types of questions should be known.

There are these five types of answers (vissajjanā): answering according to the course of the Pali, answering by way of response, answering by showing the specific nature, answering by rejection, and answering by prohibition.
300:
There are five types of answers (vissajjanā): Pāḷigativissajjanā, Paṭivacanavissajjanā, Sarūpadassanavissajjanā, Paṭikkhepavissajjanā, and Paṭisedhavissajjanā. Among these answers, that which becomes the very term of the question Pali (without the 'not') and answers the meaning is called answering according to the course of the Pali (Pāḷigativissajjanā). That Pāḷigativissajjanā is obtained in the Prior Question (Purepañhā). For in the question 'Where the aggregate of matter does not arise, does the aggregate of feeling not arise there?', this answer 'It arises' becomes the very term of the question Pali and proceeds answering the meaning; therefore, in such places, it should be known as answering according to the course of the Pali.

The answer that answers the meaning by way of response is called answering by way of response (Paṭivacanavissajjanā). That Paṭivacanavissajjanā is obtained in the Posterior Question (Pacchāpañhā). For in the question 'To whom the aggregate of matter has arisen, has the aggregate of feeling arisen to him?', this answer 'Yes' (āmantā) proceeds answering the meaning only by the power of response; therefore, in such places, it should be known as Paṭivacanavissajjanā.

The answer that answers the meaning by showing the specific nature is called answering by showing the specific nature (Sarūpadassanavissajjanā). That Sarūpadassanavissajjanā is obtained in the Complete Question (Paripuṇṇapañhā). For in the question 'To whom the aggregate of matter is arising, is the aggregate of feeling arising to him?', this answer 'To those attaining the non-percipient realm...' proceeds answering the meaning only by showing the specific nature, such as 'To these, the aggregate of matter is arising, but not the aggregate of feeling; to these, both the aggregate of matter and the aggregate of feeling are arising'. Therefore, in such places, it should be known as Sarūpadassanavissajjanā.

The answer that answers the question by rejection of the meaning (atthapaṭikkhepa) because such a meaning does not exist is called answering by rejection (Paṭikkhepavissajjanā). The answer that answers the question by prohibition of the meaning (atthapaṭisedha) because such a meaning is not obtained in a single moment is called answering by prohibition (Paṭisedhavissajjanā). These (Paṭikkhepa and Paṭisedha) answers are obtained in the Vain Question (Moghapañhā). For in the question 'To whom the aggregate of matter has not arisen, has the aggregate of feeling not arisen to him?', this answer 'No' (natthi) proceeds answering the question by rejection of the meaning, saying that there is no such being; therefore, in such places, it should be known as Paṭikkhepavissajjanā. But in the question 'To whom the aggregate of matter is arising, is the aggregate of feeling ceasing to him?', this answer 'No' (no) proceeds answering the question by prohibition of the meaning, saying that cessation cannot be obtained along with arising in a single moment of rebirth-linking; therefore, in such places, it should be known as Paṭisedhavissajjanā.

Now, these four types of questions and these five types of answers should be inserted into twenty-seven locations, which should be known as follows: 'To those attaining the non-percipient realm' is one location; 'There in the non-percipient realm' is one location; 'Of those in the non-percipient realm' is one location; 'To those passing away from the non-percipient realm' is one location; 'To those attaining the formless realm' is one location; 'There in the formless realm' is one location; 'Of those in the formless realm' is one location; 'To those passing away from the formless realm' is one location; In the formless realm...
301:
One for those in their last birth; one for those attaining Parinibbāna in the immaterial realm; one for those who, having been reborn in the immaterial realm, will attain Parinibbāna; one for those entering the five-constituent existence; one for those existing there in the five-constituent existence; one for those of the five-constituent existence; one for those passing away from the five-constituent existence; one for those in their last birth in the five-constituent existence; one for those attaining Parinibbāna in the five-constituent existence; one for those entering the Pure Abodes; one for those existing there in the Pure Abodes; one for those of the Pure Abodes; one for those attaining Parinibbāna in the Pure Abodes; one for all those who are being reborn (upapajjanta); one for all those who are passing away (cavanta); one for those in their last birth by way of being common to all; one for those attaining Parinibbāna; one for those entering the four-constituent and five-constituent existence; one for those passing away. Thus, these five answers to these four questions should be inserted into these twenty-seven locations, and the determination of the meaning in this Great Chapter on the Course of Existence (Pavatti Mahāvāra) should be understood. Indeed, one who answers the question having understood this is said to have answered well; one who determines the meaning is said to have determined it well.

In that insertion, this is the method: "Does the aggregate of form arise for such a person?" means the aggregate of form is arising for such a person because of being endowed with the moment of arising (uppādakkhaṇa). "Does the aggregate of feeling arise for that person?" means the question asks whether the aggregate of feeling also arises for that person at that very same moment. "For those entering the unconscious realm (Asaññasatta)" means for those entering the unconscious existence by way of rebirth-linking without consciousness. For them, the aggregate of form is certainly arising. For those who have already arisen in the course of existence (pavatti), the aggregate of form both arises and ceases. Therefore, instead of saying "for those of the unconscious realm," it is said "for those entering the unconscious realm." "The aggregate of feeling does not arise for them" means that because of being without consciousness, the aggregate of feeling certainly does not arise for them. This is the explanation by demonstrating the specific nature of the first part of the complete question in the first of the twenty-seven locations.

"For those entering the five-constituent existence" means for those entering the five-constituent existence by way of rebirth-linking mixed with matter and mind. For them, both aggregates, namely the aggregate of form and the aggregate of feeling, are certainly arising. However, for those who have already arisen there in the course of existence, those aggregates both arise and cease. Therefore, instead of saying "for those of the five-constituent existence," it is said "for those entering the five-constituent existence." This is the explanation by demonstrating the specific nature of the latter part of the complete question in the location "for those entering the five-constituent existence." In this manner, all answers should be understood.

The defining characteristic in arising and ceasing here is: In this entire Yamaka of the Aggregates, for those who have arisen in various existences, during the course of existence until death, the aggregates are without limit...
303:
The Victorious Buddha, having contemplated the person (puggala), the location (okāsa), and both person and location together, taught the Yamakas in the circumstances that arose. I have shown in due order the specific arrangement of the Pali texts (pāḷivavatthāna) of those Yamakas. For the purpose of determining the meaning, I have fully shown the five kinds of answers and the twenty-seven locations of those answers, and I have also explained the connection of the meaning in a single problem. In this detailed sequence of questions and answers of the Pavattivāra of the Khandha Yamaka, what more could one who explains the meaning achieve beyond showing this arrangement of the Pali? Therefore, let the wise understand the meaning according to this stated method.

## Commentary on the Great Chapter of Occurrence (Pavattimahāvāravaṇṇanā)

## 3. Commentary on the Chapter of Full Understanding (Pariññāvāravaṇṇanā)

206-208. In the Pariññāvāra (Chapter of Full Understanding), which immediately follows that Pavattivāra, there are also six divisions by way of time. There are only two methods: the affirmative (anuloma) and the negative (paṭiloma). Among these three sections—the section on persons (puggalavāra), the section on locations (okāsavāra), and the section on both persons and locations (puggalokāsavāra)—only the section on persons is applicable; the other two are not. Why? Because the answers are identical. Indeed, if a certain person fully understands the aggregate of matter (rūpakkhandha) in a certain place, they also fully understand the aggregate of feeling (vedanākkhandha). If they fully understand the aggregate of feeling, they also fully understand the aggregate of matter. If they do not fully understand the aggregate of matter, they also do not fully understand the aggregate of feeling. If they do not fully understand the aggregate of feeling, they also do not fully understand the aggregate of matter. Therefore, in those okāsavāra and puggalokāsavāra as well, having raised the question such as "Where one fully understands the aggregate of matter, does one there fully understand the aggregate of feeling?", the answer must be given only as "Āmantā" (Yes). It should be understood that because the answers are identical, these sections are not included here in the Pariññāvāra.

Alternatively, what is called the function of full understanding (pariññākicca) is the function of the person only, not of the location (okāsa). Only the person is capable of full understanding, not the location. Therefore, in this Pariññāvāra, the Blessed One took only the puggalavāra and did not take the okāsavāra. Because the okāsavāra was not taken, the puggalokāsavāra which follows it, though obtainable, was also not taken. In the puggalavāra that was taken, in the present time, there are 4 Yamakas with the aggregate of matter as the root, 3 Yamakas with the aggregate of feeling as the root, 2 Yamakas with the aggregate of perception as the root, and 1 Yamaka with the aggregate of mental formations as the root...
304:
By the same method mentioned below, by taking what has not yet been taken in the affirmative method (anulomanaya), there are 10 Yamakas, and in the negative method (paṭilomanaya), there are 10, making 20. Likewise, in the remaining times, making 20 for each time, in the 6 times there are 120 Yamakas, 480 questions (pucchā), and 480 meanings (attha). This is the determination of the Pali text (pāḷivavatthāna) in this context.

In determining the meaning, the three times called past, future, and present in this Pariññāvāra are not obtained by way of death and rebirth as in the Pavattivāra. They are obtained only by way of the thought-moment (cittakkhaṇa) at the time of occurrence. Because they are obtained in connection with the thought-moment, in this Pariññāvāra, the answer "Āmantā" (Yes) is given to questions such as "Does he who fully understands the aggregate of matter fully understand the aggregate of feeling?" At the moment of the supramundane path (lokuttaramagga), because the function of full understanding (pariññākicca) regarding the five aggregates is accomplished by the mind that has Nibbāna as its object, when any one aggregate is fully understood, it is said that the remaining aggregates are also fully understood. Thus, it should be understood that in the questions "parijānāti" (fully understands) in this Pariññāvāra, in the affirmative method, "Āmantā" is said with reference to the person endowed with the highest path (aggamaggasamaṅgī), who has reached the peak of the function of full understanding. In the negative method, however, in the questions "na parijānāti" (does not fully understand), "Āmantā" is said with reference to worldlings (puthujjana) and so forth. In the past time section "parijānitthā" (fully understood), one who stands in the fruit of Arahantship (arahattaphala) immediately following the path is also said to have fully understood, because the function of full understanding is completed.

By the question "Does he who fully understands the aggregate of matter fully understand the aggregate of feeling?", the person endowed with the path of Arahantship is asked. Although that person is currently fully understanding the five aggregates, because the function of full understanding is not yet completed, the answer "No" (no) is given as a negation. In the second question, the Arahant is asked by the term "parijānitthā". Because the Arahant has completed the function of full understanding and there is no longer any dhamma to be fully understood by him, the answer "No" is given as a negation. In the answer to the negative method of this present-past section (paccuppannātītavāra), the statement "The Arahant does not fully understand (is not currently fully understanding) the aggregate of matter" is said because there is no full understanding in the Arahant. The statement "The one endowed with the path of Arahantship did not fully understand (has not already fully understood) the aggregate of feeling" is said because the function of full understanding of the person established in the path of Arahantship is not yet completed. Not only the aggregate of feeling, but that person has not yet fully understood even a single dhamma. This is stated by way of the question. The statement "Nor the aggregate of matter" is also said only in connection with the question. In reality, however, that person is currently fully understanding the other aggregates as well.

210-211. In the case of "Does he who fully understands the aggregate of matter fully understand the aggregate of feeling in the future?", because the person established in the path (maggaṭṭha) exists for only a single thought-moment, he does not come to be designated as "one who will fully understand." Therefore, "No" is said. Those [persons]... the aggregate of matter also...
305:
The phrase "na parijānittha" is stated in accordance with the question. In reality, however, it carries the meaning "na parijāniṃsu" in this context. By this method, the determination of meaning in all instances should be understood.

## Commentary on Pariññā-vāra.

## The Commentary on Khandha Yamaka is finished.

## 3. Āyatana Yamaka

## 1. Commentary on Paṇṇatti-uddesa-vāra

1-9. Now, I shall explain the commentary on the Āyatana Yamaka, which is taught immediately after the Khandha Yamaka, by encompassing the same dhammas such as wholesome (kusala) etc., already taught in the Mūla Yamaka, according to the bases (āyatana). In that Āyatana Yamaka, the definition of the Pali text should be understood by the same method as stated in the Khandha Yamaka. Indeed, just as there are three great chapters (mahā-vāra)—Paṇṇatti-vāra, Pavatti-vāra, and Pariññā-vāra—in that Khandha Yamaka, so too are there in this Āyatana Yamaka. The word-meanings of these chapters should also be understood by the same method as stated in that Khandha Yamaka. Furthermore, in this Āyatana Yamaka, the Paṇṇatti-vāra is distinguished into two parts by way of Uddesa (Enumeration) and Niddesa (Exposition). The remaining Pavatti-vāra and Pariññā-vāra are distinguished by way of Niddesa only. From the term "Tattha dvādasāyatanāni" up to the term "nāyatanā na mano", it should be understood as the Uddesa-vāra of the Paṇṇatti-vāra. In that Paṇṇatti-uddesa-vāra, the expression "dvādasāyatanāni" is a brief indication of the bases to be questioned by way of the Yamaka. The sentence "cakkhāyatanaṃ ...pe... dhammāyatanaṃ" is the definition of the names of those very bases by way of their divisions. Moreover, in this Paṇṇatti-vāra, for the sake of ease in questioning in connection with the Yamaka, the internal physical bases (ajjhatta-rūpāyatana) are taught first in order. Afterwards, the external physical bases (bāhira-rūpāyatana) are taught. At the end, the mind base (manāyatana) and the dhamma base (dhammāyatana) are taught.

Just as it was by way of the aggregates (khandha) in the Khandha Yamaka below, so too in this Āyatana Yamaka, by way of these bases, there are only four methods (naya-vāra): Padasodhana-vāra, Padasodhanamūlacakka-vāra, Suddhāyatana-vāra, and Suddhāyatanamūlacakka-vāra. Each of these methods is twofold by way of Anuloma (Forward) and Paṭiloma (Reverse). The meaning of these should be understood by the same method as stated in that Khandha Yamaka. Furthermore, just as there are five pairs (yamaka) such as "rūpaṃ rūpakkhandho, rūpakkhandho rūpaṃ" in the Anuloma-vāra of the Padasodhana-vāra in the Khandha Yamaka, so too in this Āyatana Yamaka, there are twelve pairs such as "cakkhu cakkhāyatanaṃ, cakkhāyatanaṃ cakkhu". In the Paṭiloma-vāra also, "na cakkhu na cakkhāyatanaṃ, na cakkhāyatanaṃ na cakkhu" and so on...
306:
...there are twelve. In the Anuloma-vāra of the Padasodhanamūlacakka-vāra in this Paṇṇatti-vāra, however, taking each base as the root (mūla) with eleven pairs each, there are one hundred and thirty-two pairs. In the Paṭiloma-vāra also, there are exactly one hundred and thirty-two. In the Suddhāyatana-vāra also, there are twelve in the Anuloma-vāra and twelve in the Paṭiloma-vāra. In the Suddhāyatanamūlacakka-vāra also, in the Anuloma-vāra, taking each base as the root with eleven pairs each, there are one hundred and thirty-two pairs. In the Paṭiloma-vāra also, there are exactly one hundred and thirty-two. Thus, in this Paṇṇatti-vāra, the Uddesa-vāra of the Paṇṇatti-vāra should be understood as being adorned with five hundred and seventy-six pairs (yamaka), one thousand one hundred and fifty-two questions (pucchā), and two thousand three hundred and four meanings (attha).

## Commentary on Paṇṇatti-uddesa-vāra.

## 1. Commentary on Paṇṇatti-niddesa-vāra

10-17. In the Niddesa-vāra, however, the meaning should be understood by the same method as stated in the Paṇṇatti-vāra-niddesa of the Khandha Yamaka below. It should be understood by excluding the specific terms. In that Paṇṇatti-vāra-niddesa, the following are the distinctions. "Dibba-cakkhu" (divine eye) means the second knowledge (vijjā-ñāṇa). "Paññā-cakkhu" (eye of wisdom) means the third knowledge (vijjā-ñāṇa). "Dibba-sota" (divine ear) means the second higher power (abhiññā-ñāṇa). "Taṇhā-sota" (stream of craving) means craving (taṇhā) itself. "The remaining body" (avaseso kāyo) means the mental group (nāma-kāya), the physical group (rūpa-kāya), the elephant group (hatthi-kāya), the horse group (assa-kāya), and so on. "The remaining form" (avasesaṃ rūpaṃ) means the primary elements (bhūta-rūpa), derived form (upādā-rūpa), pleasant form (piya-rūpa), and agreeable form (sāta-rūpa) remaining from the rūpāyatana. Names such as "sīla-gandha" (fragrance of virtue) are only names for virtue (sīla) etc., because of the sense of spreading. Names such as "attha-rasa" (taste of meaning) are also only names for meaning (attha) etc., because of the sense of being good and sweet. "The remaining dhamma" (avaseso dhammo) means the many types of dhamma such as the Pariyatti-dhamma. This is the distinction in this Āyatana-paṇṇatti-vāra.

## Commentary on Paṇṇatti-niddesa-vāra.

## 2. Commentary on Pavatti-vāra

18-21. In this Āyatana Yamaka also, among the three internal cycles (antara-vāra) such as Uppāda-vāra of the Pavatti-vāra, there are six divisions of time in each cycle. Among those six times, there are three cycles such as Puggala-vāra in each time. All those cycles, by way of the Anuloma and Paṭiloma methods...
307:
These sections are of only two kinds. Therein, in the forward method of the section on individuals (puggalavāra) in the present time, just as in the Khandha Yamaka there are 10 pairs by taking what has not yet been taken—namely, 4 pairs with the root of the aggregate of matter (rūpakkhandha), 3 with the root of the aggregate of feeling (vedanākkhandha), 2 with the root of the aggregate of perception (saññākkhandha), and 1 with the root of the aggregate of mental formations (saṅkhārakkhandha).

Similarly, there are 11 pairs with the root of the eye base (cakkhāyatana), such as: "To whom the eye base arises, does the ear base also arise for that person? Or else, to whom the mental object base (dhammāyatana) arises, does the eye base also arise for that person?" By taking what has not yet been taken, there are 66 pairs in total: 10 pairs with the root of the ear base (sotāyatana), 9 with the root of the nose base (ghānāyatana), 8 with the root of the tongue base (jivhāyatana), 7 with the root of the body base (kāyāyatana), 6 with the root of the visible object base (rūpāyatana), 5 with the root of the sound base (saddāyatana), 4 with the root of the odour base (gandhāyatana), 3 with the root of the flavour base (rasāyatana), 2 with the root of the tangible object base (phoṭṭhabbāyatana), and 1 with the root of the mind base (manāyatana).

Among those 11 pairs with the root of the eye base, only these five are answered: "To whom the eye base arises, does the ear base, nose base, visible object base, mind base, or mental object base arise for that person?" Among these five, the first pair is answered because it is worthy of being answered first. Although the second pair has the same answer as the first, it is answered to prevent doubt as to "How should this pair be answered?" because the nose base does not definitely occur in the place where the eye and ear bases occur. The three pairs involving the visible object base, mind base, and mental object base are answered because their answers are not the same.

Among the remaining pairs, the two pairs involving the tongue base and body base have the same answers as the two preceding pairs. Since the sound base does not occur at the moment of rebirth, there is no answer for the pair involving the sound base. The three pairs involving the odour base, flavour base, and tangible object base also have the same answers as the two preceding pairs; therefore, they are abbreviated for the sake of brevity in the Pāḷi text.

Among the pairs with the root of the ear base, all available pairs have the same answers as the preceding pairs with the root of the eye base; therefore, not even one enters the Pāḷi text. Among the pairs with the root of the nose base, three pairs enter the Pāḷi text: one involving the visible object base and two involving the mind and mental object bases. The remaining pairs do not enter the Pāḷi text because they have the same answers as the nose base pair. The same applies to the pairs with the roots of the tongue base and body base.
308:
Among the pairs with the root of the visible object base (rūpāyatana), only two pairs involving the mind base (manāyatana) and mental object base (dhammāyatana) are answered. The three pairs involving the odour base, flavour base, and tangible object base have the same answers as the pairs of the visible object base and mind base. Just as it was stated in this pair of the visible object base and mind base as "sarūpakānaṃ acittakānaṃ" (for those with matter but without mind), etc., so too in these pairs of odour, etc., the application of terms should be understood as "sarūpakānaṃ agandhakānaṃ, arasakānaṃ, aphoṭṭhabbakānaṃ" (for those with matter but without odour, without flavour, without tangible objects). Here, regarding odour, etc., only those that have become bases (āyatana) are intended. Therefore, the meaning here should be noted by way of bases as "sarūpakānaṃ sagandhāyatanānaṃ" (for those with matter and with the odour base).

The pairs with the root of the sound base (saddāyatana) do not enter the Pāḷi text at all because they lack meaning (i.e., they cannot be established). The four, three, and two pairs with the roots of odour, flavour, and tangible objects respectively also do not enter the Pāḷi text because they have the same answers as the pairs mentioned below. The pair with the root of the mind base is directly answered. Thus, it should be understood that in the forward method of the section on individuals (puggalavāra) in the present time, by answering only a few pairs, these sixty-six pairs are said to be answered. Just as in the section on individuals, there are sixty-six pairs each in the section on planes (okāsavāra) and the section on individuals and planes (puggalokāsavāra). Thus, in the forward method among the three sections in the present time, there are 198 pairs. As in the forward method, so it is in the reverse method (paṭilomanaya). Thus, in the present time, there are 396 pairs in total. Among those 396 pairs, it should be understood that there are 792 questions (pucchā) and 1,584 meanings/answers (attha).

Similarly, this applies to the remaining five divisions of time. Thus, there are 2,376 pairs in total. There are twice as many questions as those pairs, and twice as many meanings as those questions. What has been stated is the determination of the Pāḷi text in the section on arising (uppādavāra) of this Āyatana Yamaka. The same method applies to the section on cessation (nirodhavāra) and the section on arising and cessation (uppāda-nirodhavāra). Thus, in the entire section on the occurrence of processes (pavattivāra), there are 7,128 pairs. Twice as many questions as those pairs and twice as many meanings as those questions should be understood. In the Pāḷi text, the mind base and mental object base are identical; there is no difference. Above, however, the words "vāra-saṅkhepo hoti" (there is an abbreviation of sections), etc., are spoken, and they are abbreviated in various places. Therefore, whatever pairs are abbreviated in various places, all of them should be noted without confusion.

In deciding the meaning in this section on the occurrence of processes, the following is the introductory method. The phrase "sacakkhukānaṃ asotakānaṃ" (for those with eyes but without ears) is spoken with reference to those with spontaneous rebirth (opapātika) who are born deaf (jātibadhira) in the woeful states. Indeed, that person of spontaneous rebirth who is born deaf arises with the eye base but without the ear base. How is it stated? "At the moment of rebirth in the sense sphere (kāmadhātu), for some individuals, ten bases other than the ear base and sound base appear"—thus it is stated (in the Dhammahadayavibhaṅga Pāḷi). For those with spontaneous rebirth...
309:
At the moment of rebirth for spontaneously reborn petas, asuras, animals, and hell-beings, and for those born deaf, ten bases appear: the eye base, the visible-form base, the nose base, the odor base, the tongue base, the flavor base, the body base, the tangible-object base, the mind base, and the mental-object base. The phrase "for those with eyes and those with ears" is spoken with reference to spontaneously reborn beings in happy and unhappy destinations who have complete bases, and to the fine-material Brahmās. Indeed, they are reborn possessing eyes and ears. As it is said: "At the moment of rebirth in the sense sphere, for some, eleven bases appear: for devas of the sense sphere, for humans of the first aeon, and for spontaneously reborn petas, asuras, animals, and hell-beings who have complete bases. At the moment of rebirth in the fine-material sphere, five bases appear: the eye base, the visible-form base, the ear base, the mind base, and the mental-object base."

The phrase "for those without the nose base" is spoken with reference to Brahmās such as those of the Great Brahma's retinue (Brahmapārisajja). They are reborn with eyes but without the nose base. In the sense sphere, however, there are no spontaneously reborn beings without the nose base. If there were, it would have been said, "for some, eight bases appear." Although there may be womb-born beings without the nose base, they are not intended here because of the phrase "for those with eyes." The phrase "for those with eyes and with the nose base" is spoken with reference to spontaneously reborn beings who are born deaf but have other bases complete. The phrase "for those with the nose base but without eyes" is spoken with reference to spontaneously reborn beings who are born blind or born deaf. The phrase "for those with the nose base and with eyes" is spoken only with reference to spontaneously reborn beings with complete bases.

In the phrase "for those with bodies but without eyes," one may find either spontaneously reborn beings who are born blind or born deaf, or womb-born beings. In the phrase "for those with mind but without eyes," one finds immaterial Brahmās along with the three types mentioned above, such as those born blind. In the phrase "for those without eyes," one finds non-percipient beings along with the four types mentioned in the previous term. In the phrase "for those with bodies but without the nose base," one finds womb-born beings, non-percipient Brahmās, and the remaining fine-material Brahmās. In the phrase "for those with mind but without the nose base," one finds womb-born beings, fine-material Brahmās, and immaterial Brahmās. In the terms "for those without mind" and "for those without bodies," only one-constituent beings and four-constituent beings are found. In this manner, the classification of persons in all sections on persons (Puggala-vāra) should be understood.

## 22-254. In the Section on Locations (Okāsa-vāra), the question is asked, "In which place does the eye base arise?" Therefore, it is answered, "Yes" (āmantā). In that plane, those bases invariably...
310:
...bases arise at the moment of rebirth. This which has been stated is the methodological summary (nayammukha) for this Section on Occurrence (Pavatti-vāra). By this methodological summary, the meaning in the entire Section on Occurrence should be understood. The Section on Full Understanding (Pariññā-vāra) is the same as the method stated in the Khandha Yamaka.
