## 4. Dhātu Yamaka (The Pairs of Elements)

1-19. Now follows the commentary on the Dhātu Yamaka, which was taught immediately after the Āyatana Yamaka, by grouping those same states such as the wholesome, which were taught in the Mūla Yamaka, by way of elements (dhātu). In that Dhātu Yamaka, the structure of the Pali text should be understood according to the method already stated in the Āyatana Yamaka. For here too, the three great sections (Mahā-vāra) such as the Section on Designations (Paṇṇatti-vāra), and the remaining intermediate sections (Antara-vāra), along with the divisions of time, etc., are just like those that appeared in the Āyatana Yamaka. Also in this Dhātu Yamaka, for the sake of ease in the Yamaka questions, the material elements, which are internal and external elements, are stated in order before the consciousness elements are stated. However, because of the multiplicity of elements, there are more pairs (yamakas) here than in the Āyatana Yamaka; there are twice as many questions as pairs, and twice as many meanings as questions. Among them, the determination of the meaning of the pairs found in the pairs starting with the eye element as the root should be understood according to the method already stated in the Āyatana Yamaka. For the course of the meaning here is similar to that in the Āyatana Yamaka; for that very reason, the Pali text is also abbreviated. The Section on Full Understanding (Pariññā-vāra) is just as usual.

## The Commentary on the Dhātu Yamaka is finished.

## 5. Sacca Yamaka (The Pairs of Truths)

## 1. Commentary on the Section on Designations

1-9. Now follows the commentary on the Sacca Yamaka, which was taught immediately after the Dhātu Yamaka, by grouping those same states such as the wholesome, which were taught in the Mūla Yamaka, by way of truths (sacca). In that Sacca Yamaka also, according to the method stated below, the three sections such as the Section on Designations...
312:
In determining that meaning, this is the brief method (naya-mukha): "For all those being reborn" (sabbesaṃ upapajjantānaṃ) refers to those being reborn even in the Pure Abodes (Suddhāvāsa) at the very least. This is because those individuals in the Pure Abodes are also reborn with the suffering-truth itself. "Of a mind dissociated from craving" (taṇhā-vippayutta-cittassa)—this statement was made for the purpose of showing the arising of one group, namely the suffering-truth, out of the two groups of the suffering-truth and the origin-truth. Therefore, it should be taken only by way of the five-constituent existence (pañcavokāra). In the four-constituent existence (catuvokāra), however, at the moment of arising (uppāda-kkhaṇa) of the fruition-attainment mind (phalasamāpatti-citta) which is dissociated from craving, not even a single truth arises. This fruition-attainment mind in the four-constituent existence should not be taken here when speaking of the arising of these truths. "And for them the suffering-truth" (tesaṃ dukkhasaccañca)—this statement was made with the intention that, at that moment of the arising of craving, excluding craving, the remaining phenomena are called the suffering-truth. The same method applies to the moment of arising of the path. At that moment of the arising of the path, however, only matter (rūpa) is called the suffering-truth. The remaining phenomena associated with the path are free from the truths. For that very reason, it was said: "In the immaterial sphere (arūpa), at the moment of arising of the path, for them the path-truth arises, but the suffering-truth does not arise for them."

In the phrase "For all those being reborn... there" (sabbesaṃ upapajjantānaṃ... tattha), the location (okāsa) should be understood by way of the moment, both at the moment of rebirth for those individuals and at the moment of the arising of the mind dissociated from craving. In other such answers (vissajjanā), the same method applies. "For those who have not realized" (anabhisametāvīnaṃ) refers to beings who have not yet reached the realization (abhisamaya) known as the penetration of the four truths. "For those who have realized" (abhisametāvīnaṃ) refers to noble ones (ariya) who have penetrated the truths. By this brief method, the determination of meaning should be understood in all answers.

## Commentary on the Chapter on Occurrence (Pavatti-vāra-vaṇṇanā).

## 3. Commentary on the Chapter on Full Understanding (Pariññā-vāra-vaṇṇanā)

165–170. In the Chapter on Full Understanding (Pariññā-vāra), these three types of full understanding are obtained in this Sacca Yamaka: full understanding as the known (ñāta-pariññā), full understanding as investigation (tīraṇa-pariññā), and full understanding as abandoning (pahāna-pariññā). Since there is no such thing as full understanding in supramundane phenomena (lokuttara-dhamma), only two truths are taken in this Chapter on Full Understanding. Therein, the statement "He fully understands the suffering-truth" (dukkhasaccaṃ parijānāti) was made only by way of full understanding as the known and full understanding as investigation. The statement "He abandons the origin-truth" (samudayasaccaṃ pajahati) was made by way of full understanding as the known and full understanding as abandoning. Thus, the meaning should be understood in all terms by way of these three types of full understanding.

## Commentary on the Chapter on Full Understanding (Pariññā-vāra-vaṇṇanā).

## The Commentary on the Book of Pairs on Truths (Sacca Yamaka) is finished.
313:
## 1. Paṇṇattivāravaṇṇanā
## 6. Saṅkhārayamaka

Now, among the states such as the wholesome (kusala) taught in that very Mūlayamaka, having collected a portion according to what is obtainable, there follows the commentary (vaṇṇanā) on the Saṅkhārayamaka, which was taught immediately after the Saccayamaka. In this Saṅkhārayamaka as well, the three great chapters (Mahāvāra) such as the Paṇṇattivāra, and the remaining divisions such as the Antaravāra, should be understood in the same manner as previously stated. However, there is this distinction here: In the Paṇṇattivāra, whereas previously states like the aggregates (khandha) were pointed out and the Padasodhanavāra (word-purification section) was undertaken with such phrases as "Is matter the aggregate of matter? Is the eye the eye-base? Is the eye the eye-element? Is suffering the truth of suffering?", here, without such an undertaking, the three formations are first shown by way of classification, starting with "In-breaths and out-breaths are the body-formation (kāyasaṅkhāra)."

In that text, it is called "body-formation" (kāyasaṅkhāra) because it is the cause of the body's conditioning (or its result). According to the teaching, "In-breaths and out-breaths are bodily; these states are bound up with the body," it is called kāyasaṅkhāra because it is the formation that is the result of the physical body (karajakāya), which acts as the cause. Another way: it is called saṅkhāra because it is conditioned (saṅkhariyatīti). By what is it conditioned? It is conditioned by the body. Just as air is conditioned by a bellows, this breath is conditioned by the physical body; thus, being that which is conditioned by the body, it is called kāyasaṅkhāra. The meaning is: the in-breath and out-breath air produced by the body. According to the teaching, "Friend Visākha, having first applied thought and sustained thought, one subsequently breaks into speech; therefore, applied thought and sustained thought are the speech-formation (vacīsaṅkhāra)," it is called saṅkhāra because it conditions (saṅkharotīti). What does it condition? It conditions speech. Because it is the cause of the conditioning of speech, it is called vacīsaṅkhāra. This is the name for the pair of applied thought (vitakka) and sustained thought (vicāra) which originate the breaking into speech. According to the teaching, "Perception and feeling are mental; these states are bound up with the mind," in the third phrase as well, it is called saṅkhāra because it is conditioned. By what is it conditioned? It is conditioned by the mind. Using the genitive case (sāmivibhatta) in the sense of the instrumental (karaṇa), it is called mind-formation (cittasaṅkhāra) because it is a state conditioned by the mind. This is a designation for all mental factors (cetasika) that originate from the mind. However, because applied thought and sustained thought are taken separately as speech-formations, it is stated, "excluding applied thought and sustained thought."
314:
## 2-7. Now, the Padasodhanavāra beginning with "Is the body the body-formation?" (Kāyo kāyasaṅkhāro) is commenced. In the forward method (anulomanaya) of that Padasodhanavāra, there are 3 pairs, and in the reverse method (paṭilomanaya), there are 3 pairs, making 6 pairs in total. In the Padasodhana-mūlacakkavāra, by taking each formation as a root and forming 2 pairs each, there are 6 pairs in the forward method and 6 in the reverse, making 12 pairs in total.

In the Suddhasaṅkhāravāra, however, just as in the Suddhakhandhavāra and others, pairs were taught in the manner of "Is matter the aggregate? Is the aggregate matter? Is the eye the base? Is the base the eye?", here it is not taught as "Is the body the formation? Is the formation the body?" Instead, it is taught in the manner of "Is the body-formation the speech-formation? Is the speech-formation the body-formation?", with 2 pairs having the body-formation as the root and 1 pair having the speech-formation as the root, making 3 pairs in the forward order and 3 in the reverse, totaling 6 pairs in the Suddhikavāra. For what reason? Because there is no intended meaning by way of each individual term in its pure form (suddhika).

Indeed, in the Khandha Yamaka and others, there is an intended meaning by way of each individual term in its pure form, such as "Is matter the aggregate? Is the aggregate matter? Is the eye the base? Is the base the eye?", because the aggregates are specified by matter and so on, and the bases are specified by the eye and so on. In this Saṅkhārayamaka, however, there is no such meaning as "Is the body the formation? Is the formation the body?" In fact, only through both words together as "body-formation" (kāyasaṅkhāro) is the single meaning of in-breath or out-breath obtained. Because there is no intended meaning by way of each individual term in its pure form, it is not taught as "Is the body the formation? Is the formation the body?"

Furthermore, the statement "Is the body the body-formation?" might be expected to be taught. However, that statement is also inappropriate because the formations intended here cannot be grasped by the terms "body," "speech," and "mind" alone. This is because this chapter is the Suddhasaṅkhāravāra (Section on Pure Formations). In the Padasodhanavāra, however, the statement is appropriate even without the specific technical meaning because it is linguistically sound; therefore, that method is adopted there. But in this Suddhasaṅkhāravāra, because the body-formation is distinct from the speech-formation and others, and the speech-formation is distinct from the mind-formation and others, and the mind-formation is distinct from the body-formation and others, the 6 pairs formed by taking each formation as a root, such as "Is the body-formation the speech-formation? Is the speech-formation the body-formation?", are appropriate. Among those pairs, by not repeating those already taken, only 3 are obtained. Therefore, to show those three, 6 pairs are taught: 3 in the forward method and 3 in the reverse method. The Suddhasaṅkhāramūlacakkavāra is not included here. Thus, the Uddesavāra (Summary Section) of the Paṇṇattivāra should be understood.

## 8-18. In the Niddesavāra (Exposition Section), in the forward order, since the body and so on are not the names of the body-formation and so on, the negation "No" (no) is made. In the reverse order, with the text "Is that which is not the body not the body-formation?" (Na kāyo na kāyasaṅkhāro), it asks whether what is not the body is also not the body-formation. By the text "The body-formation is not the body" (Kāyasaṅkhāro na kāyo), the meaning is that the body-formation is not the body; rather, this body-formation is only the body-formation. By the text "the rest" (avasesā), it means that only the group of the other two—speech-formation and mind-formation—remaining from the body-formation is neither the body nor the body-formation. In fact, the entire group of states—conditioned, unconditioned, and designations—that are free and remaining from the body-formation are neither the body nor the body-formation. In this manner, it should be understood in all answers. The commentary on the Paṇṇattivāra is finished.

## 19. In the Pavattivāra (Occurrence Section) of this Saṅkhārayamaka, in the forward method of the section on persons in the present time, only 3 pairs are obtained: 2 pairs with the body-formation as the root, such as "For whom the body-formation arises, does the speech-formation arise for him?", and 1 pair with the speech-formation as the root. These pairs are indeed taken. In the reverse method of that section on persons, and in the section on locations (okāsavāra) and so on, it is the same. Thus, in all sections of this Pavattivāra, the number of pairs should be understood by way of 3 pairs each. Furthermore, in determining the meaning in this Pavattivāra, the following statement is a noteworthy characteristic. Indeed, in this Saṅkhārayamaka, because of the words 'in-breath and out-breath'...
315:
Bodily formation (kāyasaṅkhāra) means that the bodily formation is not the body (kāya); the meaning is that this phenomenon is merely the bodily formation. 'The remainder' (avasesa) does not mean only the remaining two formations. Rather, it should be understood that in all answers (vissajjanā), the meaning is that the entire collection of phenomena—comprising the conditioned (saṅkhata), the unconditioned (asaṅkhata), and designations (paṇṇatti)—which is distinct from the bodily formation, is neither the body nor the bodily formation.

## Explanation of the Chapter on Designations (Paṇṇatti-vāra-vaṇṇanā)

## 2. Explanation of the Chapter on Occurrence (Pavatti-vāra-vaṇṇanā)

In this Chapter on Occurrence (pavatti-vāra), in the forward order (anuloma-naya) of the classification of persons (puggala-vāra) in the present time, only three pairs (yamaka) are obtained: two with bodily formation as the root—'For whom the bodily formation arises, for him the verbal formation arises'—and one with verbal formation as the root. These are indeed the ones taken. The same method applies to the reverse order (paṭiloma-naya) of that classification of persons, as well as to the classification of locations (okāsa-vāra) and so forth. Thus, in all sections of this Chapter on Occurrence, the count of pairs should be understood by way of these three pairs each.

In determining the meaning here, the following characteristic is noteworthy: because of the words in this Saṅkhāra Yamaka such as 'at the moment of arising of inhalation and exhalation' and 'at the moment of arising of initial and sustained thought,' the distinction of times such as the present should be taken by way of occurrence (pavatti), and not solely by way of death and rebirth-linking. Also, because of the words 'in the second jhāna, in the third jhāna, there the bodily formation arises,' it should be understood that jhāna is also taken by way of location (okāsa). Thus, in this Chapter on Occurrence, whatever meaning is obtained, the determination of the meaning should be understood by way of that specific meaning.

This is the introduction to the method of determining that meaning: the phrase 'without initial and sustained thought' is spoken by way of the second and third jhānas. The phrase 'of those' refers to those individuals possessed of the second and third jhānas. The phrase 'of those of the sensuous sphere' refers to beings born in the sensuous sphere (kāmāvacara-bhūmi). For the deities of the fine-material sphere (rūpāvacara), there is no inhalation and exhalation. For those of the immaterial sphere (arūpāvacara), even matter (rūpa) does not exist. The phrase 'without inhalation and exhalation' is spoken with reference to the arising of initial and sustained thought in beings born in the fine-material and immaterial planes of existence.

'In the first jhāna of the sensuous sphere' means the first jhāna that has arisen in the sensuous plane. Here, the first jhāna should be taken by way of its factors (aṅga) only, and not solely by way of absorption (appanā). For even in a mind that has not reached absorption but is accompanied by initial and sustained thought, these two formations certainly arise.
316:
'At the moment of dissolution of the mind': this is stated because the bodily formation is definitely mind-produced (cittasamuṭṭhāna). Indeed, only the arising mind produces matter or mentality; the dissolving mind cannot produce them.

'When the second mind of the Suddhāvāsa beings occurs' means the occurrence in the second life-continuum mind (bhavaṅga-citta) after rebirth-linking. Even if the rebirth-linking mind occurs for those beings, those formations have never arisen before in that realm. However, this is stated to show that as long as the resultant mind (vipāka-citta), unmixed with others, continues, it is called 'not having arisen before.' Alternatively, for those beings who are reborn by the resultant mind of a certain jhāna, even if that resultant mind arises hundreds or thousands of times, it is considered only the first mind. The adverting mind (āvajjana-citta) of the craving for existence (bhavanikanti), which is dissimilar to the resultant mind, is called the second mind. It should be understood that this is stated with reference to that second mind.

'To those possessed of the final mind' refers to the Arahants who are possessed of the final death-consciousness (cuti-citta) which is not followed by rebirth-linking. 'The final mind without initial and sustained thought' is stated by way of the death-consciousness of the second jhāna and so forth for those of the fine-material sphere, and by way of the death-consciousness of the fourth jhāna for those of the immaterial sphere. 'To those' refers to those individuals possessed of the final mind and so forth.

In the question, 'For whom the bodily formation ceases, does the mental formation cease for him?', the answer 'Yes' (āmantā) is given because the bodily formation always ceases at the same moment as the mental formation. The mental formation does not always cease together with the bodily formation. Why? Because the mental formation arises and ceases even without the bodily formation. The bodily formation, however, is the inhalation and exhalation wind produced by the mind. Mind-produced matter arises at the moment of the mind's arising and lasts as long as sixteen other minds arise. It ceases together with the very last of those sixteen minds. Therefore, it ceases together with the seventeenth mind, counting from the mind with which it arose. It does not cease at the moment of arising or the moment of presence (ṭhitikkhana) of any mind, nor does it arise at the moment of presence or the moment of dissolution. Since this is the nature (dhammatā) of mind-produced matter, it is stated 'Yes' because it always ceases at the same moment as the mental formation. The statement in the Sinhalese Commentary (Sīhaḷa-aṭṭhakathā) of the Vibhaṅga that 'mind-produced matter ceases at the moment of arising of the seventeenth mind' contradicts this Yamaka Pāḷi. Since the Pāḷi is more authoritative than the Commentary, only what is stated in the Pāḷi is the standard.

In the question, 'For whom the bodily formation arises, for him the verbal formation ceases?', because the bodily formation arises at the moment of the mind's arising, and at that moment initial and sustained thought are not in the process of ceasing, the negative 'No' (no) is given. This is merely the method. By this method, the meaning should be determined in all questions and answers. The Chapter on Full Understanding (Pariññā-vāra) is as it is originally.

Now, after explaining the Saṅkhāra Yamaka, I shall present the explanation of the Anusaya Yamaka (Book of Latent Tendencies), which is taught immediately after the Saṅkhāra Yamaka, by taking a portion related to the phenomena such as the wholesome (kusala) taught in the Mūla Yamaka that are obtainable as latent tendencies. In that Anusaya Yamaka, first, the divisions of the Pāḷi text should be understood. This is because in this Anusaya Yamaka, the teaching of the Pāḷi is not conducted as in the Khandha Yamaka and others, but by another method. How? First, the Chapter on the Delimitation (Pariccheda-vāra) and others are taught to define the latent tendencies in order and to grasp them in three ways. Thereafter, the teaching of the Yamaka is conducted by associating the latent tendencies by way of the seven Great Chapters (Mahā-vāra). Among those chapters such as the Chapter on the Enumeration of Terms (Uddesa-vāra), this chapter 'Seven Latent Tendencies' (sattānusayā)...
317:
In that moment, initial thought (vitakka) and sustained thought (vicāra) cease; therefore, the negation "no" is made. In this manner, the determination of meaning should be understood in all instances. The Section on Full Understanding (Pariññāvāra) is just as usual.

## Explanation of the Section on Occurrence (Pavattivāravaṇṇanā).
## The Explanation of the Analysis of Formations (Saṅkhārayamaka) is finished.
## 7. Analysis of Latent Tendencies (Anusayayamaka)
## Explanation of the Section on the Enumeration of Defined Terms (Paricchedaparicchinnuddesavāravaṇṇanā)

Now follows the explanation of the meaning of the Analysis of Latent Tendencies (Anusayayamaka), which was taught immediately after the Analysis of Formations (Saṅkhārayamaka), by taking a portion of those dhammas such as the wholesome (kusala) and so forth, which were taught in the Root Analysis (Mūlayamaka), according to what is obtainable as latent tendencies. In that explanation, first, the classification of the Pali text should be understood. For in this Anusayayamaka, the teaching is not presented as in the Analysis of Aggregates (Khandhayamaka) and so forth, but the Pali teaching is presented in another way. How? First, in order to grasp the latent tendencies through three modes—by way of definition (pariccheda), by way of enumeration (uddesa), and by way of the place of arising (uppattiṭṭhāna)—three sections were taught: the Section of Definition (Paricchedavāra), the Section of the Enumeration of Defined Terms (Paricchinnuddesavāra), and the Section on the Place of Arising (Uppattiṭṭhānavāra). After that, the teaching of the Pairs (Yamaka) was presented by applying the latent tendencies by way of the seven Great Sections (Mahāvāra).

Among those sections, this section "Sattānusayā" (Seven Latent Tendencies) is called the Section of Definition (Paricchedavāra) because the latent tendencies are taught by defining them through number, as "only seven, neither more nor less than that." This section "Kāmarāgānusaya... Avijjānusaya" is called the Section of the Enumeration of Defined Terms (Paricchinnuddesavāra) because it briefly points out the mere names of the latent tendencies already defined by the Section of Definition, teaching "these are their names." This section "Where does the latent tendency to sensual lust lie... here the latent tendency to ignorance lies" is called the Section on the Place of Arising (Uppattiṭṭhānavāra) because it teaches the place of arising of those latent tendencies in this way: "In these such-and-such places, these latent tendencies lie."

Those seven Great Sections (Mahāvāra) by way of which the latent tendencies are applied and the teaching of the Pairs is presented, their names are: the Section on Latent Tendencies (Anusayavāra), the Section on Those Possessing Latent Tendencies (Sānusayavāra), the Section on Abandoning (Pajahanavāra), the Section on Full Understanding (Pariññāvāra), the Section on What Has Been Abandoned (Pahīnavāra), the Section on Arising (Uppajjanavāra), and the Section on Elements (Dhātuvāra). Among them, the first, the Section on Latent Tendencies (Anusayavāra), is of two kinds by way of the forward (anuloma) and reverse (paṭiloma) methods.
318: In that forward method (anuloma-naya), there are three intermediate sections (antaravāra) by way of person (puggala), location (okāsa), and both (puggallokāsa): "To whom does it lie? Where does it lie? To whom and where does it lie?" Among those three, in the first, the Section on Persons (Puggalavāra), there are six pairs (yamaka) having the latent tendency to sensual lust (kāmarāgānusaya) as the root, starting with: "To whom the latent tendency to sensual lust lies, does the latent tendency to aversion (paṭighānusaya) lie to him?" Furthermore, by way of not taking what has already been taken (agahitaggahaṇa), there are five pairs with the latent tendency to aversion as the root, four with the latent tendency to conceit (mānānusaya) as the root, three with the latent tendency to wrong view (diṭṭhānusaya) as the root, two with the latent tendency to doubt (vicikicchānusaya) as the root, and one with the latent tendency to lust for existence (bhavarāgānusaya) as the root. Thus, all the single-root (ekamūlaka) pairs are twenty-one. Again, there are fifteen other pairs such as those with two roots (dukamūlaka) appearing as "To whom the latent tendency to sensual lust and the latent tendency to aversion lie," four with three roots (tikamūlaka), three with four roots (catukkamūlaka), two with five roots (pañcakamūlaka), and one with six roots (chakkamūlaka). These fifteen pairs together with the previous twenty-one make thirty-six; thus, there are thirty-six pairs in the Section on Persons (Puggalavāra). Likewise in the Section on Locations (Okāsavāra), and likewise in the Section on Persons and Locations (Puggallokāsavāra), [each having thirty-six], so all the pairs in the forward method are one hundred and eight. Likewise in the reverse method (paṭiloma-naya), [there are one hundred and eight], so in the Section on Latent Tendencies (Anusayavāra), there are two hundred and sixteen pairs. One should understand that there are twice as many questions (pucchā) as those pairs, and twice as many meanings (attha) as those questions. Just as in this Section on Latent Tendencies, in these five sections as well—the Section on Those Possessing Latent Tendencies (Sānusayavāra), the Section on Abandoning (Pajahanavāra), the Section on Full Understanding (Pariññāvāra), the Section on What Has Been Abandoned (Pahīnavāra), and the Section on Arising (Uppajjanavāra)—the number of pairs in each section, the questions which are double the pairs, and the meanings which are double the questions should be understood. However, among these, there is this distinction in the first three sections (Sānusayavāra, Pajahanavāra, Pariññāvāra). In the Section on Locations (Okāsavāra), the teaching is presented using the ablative case (pañcamī-vibhatti) as "yato tato" instead of saying "yattha tattha". The rest of the arrangement is the same. There is that Section on Elements (Dhātuvāra) which is the very last of all; that section is established in two parts: the Section of Questions (Pucchāvāra) and the Section of Answers (Vissajjanāvāra). In the Section of Questions of that Dhātuvāra, it is taught as "to one who, having passed away from the sense sphere, is being reborn in the sense sphere," but it is not taught as "to one who, being reborn in the sense sphere, has passed away from the sense sphere." For what reason? Because there is no difference in meaning. For both these questions have the same meaning; therefore, asking only one question from each pair, at the end of all questions, according to the order of the questions...
319:
The answer has been given in the following manner: "For one who passes away from the sensual element (kāmadhātu) and is reborn in the sensual element, seven latent tendencies (anusaya) lie latent." In this Section on Elements (Dhātuvāra), there are six pure questions (suddhika-pucchā): "one who passes away from the sensual element and is reborn in the sensual element, in the fine-material element (rūpadhātu), in the immaterial element (arūpadhātu), in a non-sensual element, in a non-fine-material element, or in a non-immaterial element." There are three mixed questions (missaka-pucchā): "one who is reborn in an element that is neither sensual nor immaterial, neither fine-material nor immaterial, or neither sensual nor fine-material." Thus, there are nine forward questions (anuloma-pucchā) based on the sensual element (kāmadhātu-mūlaka). Similarly, there are nine based on the fine-material element and nine based on the immaterial element, making twenty-seven forward questions. Likewise, there are twenty-seven reverse questions (paṭiloma-pucchā) based on the non-sensual, non-fine-material, and non-immaterial elements. Furthermore, there are twenty-seven questions based on dyads (duka-mūlaka), such as "non-sensual and non-immaterial, non-fine-material and non-immaterial, and non-sensual and non-fine-material," totaling eighty-one questions. The answers in this Section on Elements are given by way of these questions; this is the established structure of the Pali text in the Section on Elements. In this way, the established structure of the Pali text in the entire Anusaya Yamaka should be understood.

Starting from the beginning, regarding the terms that are not clear, this is the explanatory discussion: For what reason are they called "latent tendencies" (anusaya)? They are so called in the sense of lying latent (anusayana). What is this sense of lying latent? It is the sense of being unabandoned (appahīnaṭṭha). Indeed, these defilements are called "latent tendencies" because they lie latent in the continuity of various beings in the sense of being unabandoned. "They lie latent" (anusenti) means they arise upon obtaining suitable causes. However, it might be argued: "The sense of lying latent is merely the mode of being unabandoned (appahīnākāra). It is not appropriate to say that the mode of being unabandoned arises; therefore, latent tendencies do not arise." The reply to that objection is: The mode of being unabandoned is not the latent tendency; rather, "latent tendency" refers to the defilement that has gained strength (thāmagata-kilesa) due to its unabandoned state. That defilement is associated with consciousness (cittasampayutta), has an object (sārammaṇa), is rooted in causes (sahetuka) by way of being conditioned, is exclusively unwholesome (akusala), and can belong to the past, future, or present; therefore, it is appropriate to say "it arises."

The evidence for this is as follows: In the Kathāvatthu of the Abhidhamma, all views such as "latent tendencies are indeterminate (abyākata)," "latent tendencies are rootless (ahetuka)," and "latent tendencies are dissociated from consciousness" were refuted. In the Paṭisambhidāmagga, after asking the question "Does one abandon defilements that are present?", it is stated, "One abandons the latent tendency that has gained strength..."
320:
..."abandons." In the Word-by-word Commentary (Padabhājanī) on Delusion (moha) in the Dhammasaṅgaṇī, it is stated: "The latent tendency of ignorance (avijjānusaya), the obsession of ignorance (avijjā-pariyuṭṭhāna), the shackle of ignorance (avijjā-laṅgī), delusion, the unwholesome root—this is the delusion at that time," thus describing the arising of the latent tendency of ignorance together with unwholesome consciousness. In this very Anusaya Yamaka, in the Section on Arising (Uppajjanavāra), which is one of the seven great sections (mahāvāra), it is stated: "For whom the latent tendency of sensual lust (kāmarāgānusaya) arises, for him the latent tendency of aversion (paṭighānusaya) arises," and so on. Therefore, the statement "lying latent (anusenti) means arising upon obtaining suitable causes" should be understood as well-spoken according to these scriptural evidences. The previously mentioned statement "associated with consciousness, having an object," etc., is also well-spoken. It should be concluded here that what is called a latent tendency (anusaya) is an unwholesome state that is produced (parinipphanna) and associated with consciousness. In terms such as "latent tendency of sensual lust" (kāmarāgānusaya), it is called "kāmarāgānusaya" because it is both sensual lust (kāmarāga) and a latent tendency (anusaya) in the sense of being unabandoned. The same method applies to the remaining terms.

## Commentary on the Section on the Summary of Divisions (Paricchedaparicchinnuddesavāra-vaṇṇanā).

## Commentary on the Section on the Place of Arising (Uppattiṭṭhānavāra-vaṇṇanā)

Now, to show the place of arising of those latent tendencies, the text says: "Where does the latent tendency of sensual lust lie latent?" and so on. Therein, "in the two feelings in the sensual element (kāmadhātu)" means in the two feelings—pleasant (sukha) and neutral (upekkhā)—in the sensual-sphere plane (kāmāvacara-bhūmi). Here, "the latent tendency of sensual lust lies latent" means it arises in these two feelings. That latent tendency of sensual lust lies latent in unwholesome feelings in two ways: by way of conascence (sahajāta) and by way of object (ārammaṇa). It arises being conascent with unwholesome pleasant feeling and neutral feeling. It also arises by making those feelings its object. However, it arises only by making the remaining sensual-sphere wholesome, resultant, and functional feelings its object. This latent tendency, which lies latent in the two feelings in the sensual element, also lies latent in the perception (saññā), mental formations (saṅkhāra), and consciousness (viññāṇa) associated with those feelings. This is because it is impossible for the latent tendency lying latent in feelings not to be conascent with the perception, etc., associated with those feelings, or to arise without making those associated perception, etc., its object. Thus...
321:
Even though this is the case, because only these two feelings (pleasant and neutral) are pleasant and peaceful, they are more prominent than the remaining associated states for the arising of the latent tendency of sensual lust (kāmarāgānusaya) in the sense of being enjoyed. Therefore, it is stated: "The latent tendency of sensual lust underlies these two feelings." This is for the sake of easily making those who are capable of being enlightened understand the Four Noble Truths by means of prominent feelings.

Does this latent tendency of sensual lust, when underlying by way of object, not underlie not only these two feelings and their associated states, but also agreeable objects such as visible forms? Indeed, it was stated in the Vibhaṅga: "Whatever in the world has an agreeable nature (piyarūpa) and a pleasurable nature (sātarūpa), therein the latent tendency of sensual lust underlies for beings." Also, in the reverse method (paṭiloma-naya) of the Anusaya-vāra in this Yamaka treatise, it is stated: "Where the latent tendency of sensual lust does not underlie, does the latent tendency of views (diṭṭhānusaya) not underlie there?" To which it is answered: "In painful feeling, the fine-material sphere (rūpadhātu), and the immaterial sphere (arūpadhātu), the latent tendency of sensual lust does not underlie; however, it is not that the latent tendency of views does not underlie there, for it does underlie. In the unincluded (supramundane) states, both the latent tendency of sensual lust and the latent tendency of views do not underlie."

In this Pāḷi text, because it is stated that the latent tendency of sensual lust does not underlie painful feeling, the fine-material sphere, and so on, it implies that—excluding painful feeling along with its associated states, the fine-material and immaterial sphere states along with their respective planes, and the nine supramundane states—the latent tendency of sensual lust underlies the remaining objects of visible forms, sounds, smells, tastes, and tangibles. Why are these objects such as visible forms not mentioned here? It is because they are not prominent. As mentioned above, only feelings are mentioned because they are prominent; and because objects like visible forms are not prominent, it is not directly stated that it underlies them, though it is obtained by way of meaning. Therefore, it should be understood that the latent tendency of sensual lust certainly underlies those objects like visible forms. The Teacher does not teach everything in every place. According to the capacity of beings who are to be enlightened, in some places He teaches everything that is applicable, and in some places He does not.

This is true. In some places, the Buddha asked, "Where does the latent tendency of views underlie?" and taught everything applicable by saying, "The latent tendency of views underlies all mundane states included in self-identity (sakkāya)." In another place, when answering, He said: "In the fine-material sphere and the immaterial sphere, the latent tendency of doubt (vicikicchānusaya), the latent tendency of pride (mānānusaya), and the latent tendency of views underlie. In the two feelings of the sense sphere, the latent tendency of doubt, the latent tendency of sensual lust, the latent tendency of pride, and the latent tendency of views underlie. In painful feeling, the latent tendency of doubt, the latent tendency of aversion (paṭighānusaya), and the latent tendency of views..."
322:
"...and the latent tendency of ignorance (avijjānusaya) also underlie." Without teaching all those applicable states, He taught only the three feelings along with the fine-material sphere and the immaterial sphere. Specifically, the mental states associated with feeling and all material phenomena were not mentioned. Even though they were not mentioned, the latent tendency of views certainly underlies these states. In the same way, although desirable objects (iṭṭhārammaṇa) such as visible forms are not mentioned here in showing the location of the latent tendency of sensual lust, the latent tendency of sensual lust certainly underlies these objects. Thus, the location where the latent tendency of sensual lust underlies should first be understood.

Regarding the location where the latent tendency of aversion (paṭighānusaya) underlies, according to the statement "in painful feeling," the three feelings—namely, the two types of unpleasant mental feeling (domanassa-vedanā) and the painful feeling associated with body-consciousness—are the locations where it underlies. That latent tendency of aversion underlies the unpleasant mental feelings in two ways: by way of conascence (sahajāta) and by way of object (ārammaṇa). However, in the remaining painful feeling (physical pain), it underlies only by way of object. When this latent tendency of aversion underlies those feelings, it also certainly underlies the aggregate of perception (saññākkhandha) and other states associated with those feelings. This is because the latent tendency of aversion is conascent with the feeling it arises with, and it is also conascent with perception and other states associated with that feeling. Furthermore, whatever feelings it takes as an object, it also takes the perception and other states associated with those feelings as an object. Even so, because painful feeling alone is an unpleasant painful experience and is superior to the remaining associated states for the arising of the latent tendency of aversion in the sense of having no enjoyment, it was stated: "The latent tendency of aversion underlies painful feeling." Indeed, this was stated for the sake of easily making those who are to be enlightened understand by means of what is prominent.

When this latent tendency of aversion underlies by way of object, does it not underlie not only painful feeling and its associated states, but also disagreeable objects (aniṭṭhārammaṇa) such as visible forms? Indeed, it was stated in the Vibhaṅga: "Whatever in the world has an unloved nature (appiyarūpa) and an unpleasant nature (asātarūpa), therein the latent tendency of aversion underlies for beings." In this Yamaka treatise also, in the reverse method of the Anusaya-vāra, it is stated: "In the two feelings of the sense sphere, this latent tendency of aversion does not underlie; it is not that the latent tendency of sensual lust does not underlie there. In the fine-material sphere, the immaterial sphere, and the unincluded (supramundane) states, both this latent tendency of aversion and the latent tendency of sensual lust do not underlie."

In fact, because it is stated in this Pāḷi text that it does not underlie the two sense-sphere feelings and the fine-material sphere etc., it implies that—excluding the two feelings along with their associated states, the fine-material and immaterial sphere states along with their planes, and the nine supramundane states—it underlies the remaining objects such as visible forms.
323:
It occurs. If it is asked why this (unpleasant visual object, etc.) is not mentioned here (in the section on the occurrence of the latent tendency of aversion)—it is because it is not gross (not prominent). Indeed, according to the method mentioned below, only painful feeling is gross; but because these (unpleasant visual objects, etc.) are not gross, it is not said that [the latent tendency] underlies these visual objects and so forth. However, since it is obtainable in terms of meaning, it should be understood that the latent tendency of aversion (paṭighānusaya) indeed underlies these (unpleasant visual objects, etc.) as well.

If it is asked: 'Do the other two feelings (pleasant and neutral) or pleasant objects (iṭṭhārammaṇa) not become objects of aversion (paṭigha)?' It is not that they do not; they indeed do. Indeed, for a person who has fallen away from jhāna, displeasure (domanassa) arises by way of remorse (vippaṭisāra) regarding those feelings (associated with jhāna) along with their associated states. Also, for one who reflects on the change of a pleasant object already obtained or the non-attainment of a pleasant object not yet obtained, displeasure arises.

However, that is merely displeasure; it is not the latent tendency of aversion. Indeed, the latent tendency of aversion is a defilement that has reached strength, arising by way of being struck by an unpleasant object (aniṭṭhārammaṇa). Therefore, although aversion (paṭigha) arises here along with displeasure (in the two feelings and pleasant objects), because it cannot perform its own function of aversion, it is not called the latent tendency of aversion and reaches the state of being negligible (not worthy of being called so).

Just as ill-will (byāpāda) arising together with the volition of taking life (pāṇātipāta-cetanā) is not called a mental kamma (mano-kamma) and reaches the state of being negligible, so too, it is not called the latent tendency of aversion and reaches the state of being negligible. With reference to this point, regarding certain pleasant objects or displeasure based on renunciation (nekkhamma), it was said: 'That kind of displeasure which is aversion, one abandons it with that (Path); the latent tendency of aversion does not underlie it' (M. Ni. 1.465). Thus, the place of occurrence for the latent tendency of aversion should be understood.

As for the place of occurrence for the latent tendency of conceit (mānānusaya), according to the words 'in the two feelings in the sense sphere,' etc., there are three types of places: the two sense-sphere feelings, the fine-material sphere, and the immaterial sphere. Regarding its underlying in unwholesome feelings, it should be understood as being conascent (sahajāta), like the latent tendency of sensual lust (kāmarāgānusaya). In all sense-sphere pleasant feelings and neutral feelings, as well as in the fine-material and immaterial spheres, together with their associated states, it underlies only by way of being an object (ārammaṇa).

In the reverse order (paṭiloma-naya) of the Section on Latent Tendencies, it is stated: 'In painful feeling and in the unincluded (supramundane) states, here the latent tendency of sensual lust does not underlie, and the latent tendency of conceit does not underlie.' Therefore, excluding painful feeling and the nine supramundane states, this latent tendency of conceit indeed underlies the remaining material and mental states. Thus, the place of occurrence for the latent tendency of conceit should be understood.

## Mahāvāra
## 1. Anusayavāra-vaṇṇanā
In the first section, the Anusayavāra (Section on Latent Tendencies) of the seven Mahāvāras, regarding the question: "Does the latent tendency of aversion (paṭighānusaya) underlie for one for whom the latent tendency of sensual lust (kāmarāgānusaya) underlies?", the answer given as "Āmantā" (Yes) seems as if it were given incorrectly. Why? Because sensual lust and aversion do not arise in the same single moment (ekakkhaṇe).

For example, when it is asked, "Does the mental-object-base (dhammāyatana) arise for one for whom the mind-base (manāyatana) arises?", the answer is given as "Āmantā." Also, in the teaching that "at the moment of inhalation and exhalation, the body-formation (kāyasaṅkhāra) arises and the verbal-formation (vacīsaṅkhāra) arises for them," etc., the mind-base and mental-object-base, as well as the body-formation and verbal-formation, arise in the same single moment. However, sensual lust and aversion are not like that. In fact, sensual lust arises in the eight types of consciousness accompanied by greed (lobhasahagata cittuppāda). Aversion arises in the two types of consciousness accompanied by displeasure (domanassasahagata cittuppāda). Therefore, they do not arise in the same single moment. Thus, in this context, a negation such as "No" (not so) should have been made. However, since the answer "Āmantā" was given without doing so, the usage of the present tense (vattamāna) here should not be taken by way of the present moment (khaṇapaccuppanna), as in the lower Yamakas, but should be understood in another way.

How should it be understood? It should be understood by way of being unabandoned (appahīna) by the Path. This present tense usage "underlies" (anuseti) is taught with reference to being unabandoned, not with reference to the actual present moment. Because it is taught with reference to being unabandoned, in the question, "Does the latent tendency of aversion underlie for one for whom the latent tendency of sensual lust underlies?", the meaning should be understood thus: "For one for whom the latent tendency of sensual lust has not been abandoned, and has not yet been brought to the state of non-arising, for that person, the latent tendency of aversion is also not abandoned."

Since among those latent tendencies, if one is not abandoned, the other is also certainly not abandoned, it was taught as "Āmantā."

If this is so, how should the meaning be understood in the answer "Āmantā" given to the question in the upper Uppajjanavāra (Section on Arising): "Does the latent tendency of aversion arise for one for whom the latent tendency of sensual lust arises?" In that answer too, the meaning should be understood either by way of being unabandoned, or by way of the arising not being prevented when the conditions for arising are present.

For example, painters and such who have started painting and have unfinished work, even at the moment when they are not doing that work, if they are asked by friends and associates wherever they are seen, "What are you doing these days?", they say, "I am doing painting work, I am doing wood carving work." Although they are not actually working at that moment of speaking, because they have unfinished work, they are called "working" by taking into account the moments already completed and the moments yet to be completed.

In the same way, in a continuity (santāna) where the latent tendencies are not abandoned, or in a continuity where their arising is not prevented when the conditions for arising are present, even if it is not the moment they are actually arising, by taking into account what has arisen before and what will arise in the future, the meaning should be understood as: "For one for whom the latent tendency of sensual lust arises, the latent tendency of aversion is also said to arise." Because of this explanation, other such answers should also be understood in this same manner. The word "nānuseti" (does not underlie) is taught because the Non-returner (anāgāmī) has completely abandoned sensual lust and ill-will (byāpāda). The phrase "tiṇṇam puggalānam" (of the three persons) refers to the three persons: the worldling (puthujjana), the Stream-enterer (sotāpanna), and the Once-returner (sakadāgāmī)...
326:
Even at the moment when it is not arising, by taking into account what has arisen before and what will arise in the future, the meaning should be understood as: "For that person for whom the latent tendency of sensual lust arises, the latent tendency of aversion is also said to arise." In other such answers from here on, the method is the same. The phrase "No ca tassa" (But not for him) is taught because the Non-returner (anāgāmī) has completely abandoned sensual lust and ill-will (byāpāda). "Tiṇṇam puggalānam" means the three persons: the worldling (puthujjana), the Stream-enterer (sotāpanna), and the Once-returner (sakadāgāmī). "Dvinnam puggalānam" means the two persons: the Stream-enterer and the Once-returner. In subsequent such places, the method should be understood in this same way.

In the first and second questions of the Okāsavāra (Section on Locations), because the latent tendency of sensual lust underlies two feelings in the sense-sphere (kāmadhātu), and the latent tendency of aversion underlies painful feeling (dukkhavedanā), the negation "No" was made. In the third question, because both the latent tendency of sensual lust and the latent tendency of conceit (mānānusaya) underlie two feelings in the sense-sphere, the answer "Āmantā" was given. In the fine-material sphere (rūpadhātu) and the immaterial sphere (arūpadhātu), however, the location where the latent tendency of conceit arises is a location that does not involve the latent tendency of sensual lust. Therefore, it was stated that the latent tendency of sensual lust does not exist there. In this way, by observing the section on the location of arising (uppattiṭṭhānavāra) for all latent tendencies, the common (sādhāraṇa) and uncommon (asādhāraṇa) locations of arising should be understood.

In the dyad-rooted (dukamūlaka) question, because the latent tendencies of sensual lust and aversion neither arise in a single location nor take a single phenomenon as an object, the rejection was made as "Natthi" (There is none). The intention here is this: there is no location at all where both these latent tendencies would underlie. Therefore, this question, "Where does the latent tendency of conceit underlie?", is not a proper question at all. In other such places, the method is the same.

In the Puggalokāsavāra (Section on Persons and Locations), "catunnam" (of the four) refers to the four persons: the worldling, the Stream-enterer, the Once-returner, and the Non-returner.

In the reverse order (paṭilomanaya), the question "For whom does the latent tendency of sensual lust not underlie?" is a question asked with reference to the Non-returner.
327:
Regarding the statement that for two types of persons—the Non-returner and the Arahant—the latent tendency of sensual lust does not underlie all things, it refers to the Non-returner and the Arahant. By taking 'the three feelings in the sensual realm,' it should be understood that by taking 'feeling,' the states associated with those feelings and their bases and objects are also taken, thus encompassing all sensual-sphere phenomena (kāmāvacara-dhamma). This is the concluding discussion on the Section on Latent Tendencies (Anusaya-vāra).

## Explanation of the Section on Latent Tendencies (Anusaya-vāra-vaṇṇanā)

## 2. Explanation of the Section on Those with Latent Tendencies (Sānusaya-vāra-vaṇṇanā)

66-131. In the Section on Those with Latent Tendencies (Sānusaya-vāra), when it is asked, 'Is a person who has the latent tendency of sensual lust one with latent tendencies (sānusaya)?', it is like the example of a person with a disease such as an intermittent fever; as long as they are not yet free from that disease, they are still called 'diseased' even at the moment when the disease is not manifesting. Similarly, as long as a being wandering in the round of rebirth (vaṭṭa) who possesses defilements has not yet completely eradicated the latent tendencies by the Noble Path (ariya-magga), they are still called 'one with latent tendencies' (sānusaya) even at the moment when those latent tendencies have not yet arisen. With reference to such a state of having latent tendencies, it is said, 'Yes' (āmantā). The remaining words in this section are just like those in the Anusaya-vāra.

In the Section on Occasions (Okāsa-vāra), if it were stated, 'In the fine-material realm and the immaterial realm, is one with latent tendencies here (ettha) by the latent tendency of conceit?', only the person's state of having latent tendencies in those realms would be clear, but the place of origin of the latent tendency would not be clear. This section is undertaken for the purpose of showing the place of origin of the latent tendency; therefore, it is stated, 'Is one with latent tendencies by the latent tendency of conceit from that (tato)?' When stated thus, the place of origin of the latent tendency is shown by saying that one is with latent tendencies by the latent tendency of conceit arising from those two realms. If the meaning of this fourth question were not explained, the meaning of the first question would not be clear; therefore, the first question was not explained first. Thus, that first question should be understood as follows: When it is asked, 'Is one with latent tendencies by the latent tendency of sensual lust arising from that (the two feelings of the sensual realm)? Is that person also one with latent tendencies by the latent tendency of repulsion arising from that (place)?', the prohibition 'No' (no) is made because these two latent tendencies cannot arise from the same single place. Regarding the statement 'The Arahant in all things,' it means that the Arahant is one without latent tendencies (nirānusaya) regarding any latent tendency that might arise in all phenomena. By virtue of this meaning, only the locative case (bhūmma-vacana) is used for places that are without division (all-inclusive). In this way, the determination of the meaning in all places should be understood.

## 3. Explanation of the Section on Abandoning (Pajahana-vāra-vaṇṇanā)

132-197. In the Section on Abandoning (Pajahana-vāra), 'abandons' (pajahati) means abandoning by the power of the full understanding of abandoning (pahāna-pariññā) through the respective paths, bringing about the state of non-arising in the future. The word 'Yes' (āmantā) is a response referring to the one standing on the path of Non-returning (anāgāmi-maggattha). 'Abandons that which is established in one' (tadekaṭṭhaṃ pajahati) is said with reference to being established in a single person as something to be abandoned. The prohibition 'No' (no) is made with reference to the one standing on the path of Arahantship (arahatta-maggattha).

'From which he abandons the latent tendency of sensual lust' (yato kāmarāgānusayaṃ pajahati) means he is in the process of abandoning the latent tendency of sensual lust that would arise from that (the feelings of the sensual realm). 'The eighth' (aṭṭhamako) means that when counting downwards starting from the one standing in the fruit of Arahantship, the one standing on the path of Stream-entry is called the eighth. Indeed, in the counting of those worthy of offerings (dakkhiṇeyya), the Arahant is first as the supreme worthy one, the one on the path of Arahantship is second, the Non-returner is third... and so on, and the one on the path of Stream-entry is the eighth. That person is called 'the eighth' (aṭṭhamako) here. Or, it is merely a designated name for that person. 'The others, excluding the one possessed of the path of Non-returning and the eighth person' refers to the trainees (sekha), non-trainees (asekha), together with worldlings (puthujjana). Among them, the worldling does not abandon because of the absence of the full understanding of abandoning. The others [do not abandon] because those latent tendencies have already been abandoned. 'Excluding the two possessed of the path' means excluding the two persons who are endowed with the path of Arahantship and the path of Non-returning. In this way, the determination [of meaning] should be understood everywhere.

## Explanation of the Section on Abandoning (Pajahana-vāra-vaṇṇanā)

198-263. In the Section on Full Understanding (Pariññā-vāra), 'fully understands' (parijānāti) means fully understanding through the three types of full understanding (pariññā). ## 5. Explanation of the Section on What Has Been Abandoned (Pahīna-vāra-vaṇṇanā)

264-274. In the Section on What Has Been Abandoned (Pahīna-vāra), the teaching is undertaken only by the power of those standing in the fruits (phalattha). For the Non-returner, both of these latent tendencies have been abandoned; therefore, it is said, 'Yes' (āmantā).
329:
275-296. In the Okāsavāra (Chapter on Locations), to the question: "In the place where the latent tendency of sensual lust (kāmarāgānusaya) is abandoned, is the latent tendency of aversion (paṭighānusaya) also abandoned there?", it is stated: "It should not be said that it is abandoned or not abandoned." Why is this stated? It is because their arising locations (uppattitthāna) are not common (distinct). Indeed, the arising location of the latent tendency of sensual lust is of one kind, and the arising location of the latent tendency of aversion is of another kind. For an individual who has not yet developed the Path in their own continuum, the latent tendency arises in a certain location; when the Path is developed, it is said to be abandoned in that very location. Among those locations, the latent tendency of aversion does not arise in the location where the latent tendency of sensual lust lies (the two feelings of the sense sphere), nor does the latent tendency of sensual lust arise in the location where the latent tendency of aversion lies (painful feeling). Therefore, in that location, it should not be said that the tendency is abandoned or not abandoned. Indeed, because that latent tendency of aversion is not abandoned in that location where the latent tendency of sensual lust is abandoned—which is not its own arising location—it should not be said to be abandoned there. Because the latent tendency of aversion does not exist in the arising location of the latent tendency of sensual lust, it should not be said to be not abandoned there either.

However, in the question: "In the place where the latent tendency of sensual lust is abandoned, is the latent tendency of conceit (mānānusaya) abandoned there?", the answer is given as "Āmantā" (Yes), referring to the common (shared) location. Indeed, the latent tendency of sensual lust lies in two feelings within the sense sphere (kāmadhātu): pleasant feeling and neutral feeling. The latent tendency of conceit lies in those two feelings as well as in the fine-material sphere (rūpadhātu) and the immaterial sphere (arūpadhātu). Excluding the uncommon locations (fine-material and immaterial spheres), that latent tendency of conceit is said to be abandoned along with the latent tendency of sensual lust in the common location. Therefore, it is stated as "Āmantā". In this manner, the state of being abandoned (pahīnatā) and the state of being unspeakable (navattabbatā) should be understood in the entire Okāsavāra. In places where "Natthi" (No/None) appears, the judgment is the same as what was stated below. The Puggalokāsavāra (Chapter on Persons and Locations) also follows the same course as the Okāsavāra.

297-307. In the inverse method (paṭilomanaya), the question: "To whom is the latent tendency of sensual lust not abandoned?" is asked with respect to the worldling (puthujjana), the Stream-enterer (sotāpanna), and the Once-returner (sakadāgāmī). Indeed, although it is true that these two latent tendencies are not abandoned for the six types of persons starting from the worldling up to those standing on the Path of Non-returning (anāgāmi-maggatṭha), in this Pahīnavāra, because it is later taught as "to three persons," "to two persons," etc., those standing on the Path (maggatṭha) are not intended. Therefore, "Āmantā" is stated referring only to the worldling, the Stream-enterer, and the Once-returner. "To two persons" refers to the Stream-enterer and the Once-returner. In this manner, the judgment in the Puggalavāra (Chapter on Persons) should be understood.

308-329. The Okāsavāra and the Puggalokāsavāra should be understood only by the method already stated below.

## 7. Dhātupucchāvāra-vaṇṇanā
332-340. In the Pucchāvāra (Chapter on Inquiries) of the Dhātuvāra, first, "How many latent tendencies lie (anusenti)?" means how many latent tendencies lie by following the continuum (santāna). "How many latent tendencies do not lie?" means how many latent tendencies do not lie by not following the continuum. ## 7. Dhātuvissajjanavāra-vaṇṇanā
341-349. In the Niddesavāra (Chapter on Expositions) of this Dhātuvāra, however, the statement "Seven latent tendencies lie in someone" is said with respect to the worldling (puthujjana). "Five lie in someone" is said with respect to the Stream-enterer (sotāpanna) and the Once-returner (sakadāgāmī). For those Stream-enterers and Once-returners, since the latent tendency of views (diṭṭhānusaya) and the latent tendency of doubt (vicikicchānusaya) have been abandoned, only five latent tendencies lie.

In that passage (such as "Seven latent tendencies lie in someone"), the term 'anusenti' (they lie) should not be taken with the meaning of 'uppajjanti' (they arise), as it was taken in the Anusayavāra. Why? Because they do not arise at that moment (of rebirth). For one who is reborn in the sense sphere, only the resultant consciousness (vipākacitta) and kamma-produced matter (kammasamuṭṭhāna-rūpa) arise; there is no unwholesome consciousness (akusalacitta). Latent tendencies arise only at the moment of unwholesome consciousness, not at the moment of resultant consciousness. Therefore, because they do not arise at that moment, the meaning should not be taken in that way (as arising).

If so, how should the meaning be taken? It should be taken only according to the possible manner. In what manner is it possible? It is possible by way of the sense of being not yet abandoned (appahīnaṭṭha). For example, just as a person who is possessed of wholesome or indeterminate consciousness is still called "one with lust, one with hatred, one with delusion" because lust, hatred, and delusion have not been abandoned; similarly, because they have not been abandoned by the Path, those respective latent tendencies are said to lie in those respective persons even at the moment of rebirth. Not only are they said to be so, but because they are not yet abandoned, they are truly known as "lying."

"Anusayā bhaṅgā natthi" means that for whichever person a certain latent tendency lies, it simply lies; whichever does not lie, it simply does not lie. There is no such thing as a latent tendency that can be analyzed as "this tendency both lies and does not lie," or "this tendency sometimes lies and sometimes does not lie." For someone reborn into the fine-material sphere (the statement that three latent tendencies lie is said with respect to the Non-returner)...
331:
Take it up to the point of 'massaging' (kneading); therefore, the Ṭīkā explains that 'bhaṅga means the sense to be analyzed, the sense to be performed in this context.' In this Commentary, 'to be analyzed' refers to the intended meaning (adhippāyattha).

7. Commentary on the Section of the Explanation of Elements (Dhātu-vissajjanā-vāra). Whichever latent tendency underlies, that latent tendency only underlies. Whichever latent tendency does not underlie, that latent tendency only does not underlie. There is no such latent tendency that should be analyzed as: 'This latent tendency both underlies and does not underlie, or sometimes underlies and sometimes does not underlie.'

Regarding the statement, 'To one who has attained the fine-material element (rūpadhātu), some three [latent tendencies]...', this is spoken with reference to the Non-returner (anāgāmī). Indeed, for that Non-returner, the four latent tendencies—namely, the latent tendency to sensual lust (kāmarāgānusaya), the latent tendency to aversion (paṭighānusaya), the latent tendency to wrong view (diṭṭhānusaya), and the latent tendency to doubt (vicikicchānusaya)—have been abandoned without remainder. Only the other three (the latent tendency to conceit, the latent tendency to lust for existence, and the latent tendency to ignorance) have not yet been abandoned. Therefore, it is said, 'To a certain person, three latent tendencies underlie.'

By the phrase 'not in the sensual element (kāmadhātu),' since the sensual element is excluded, it means the sense of one who has attained the remaining two elements (the fine-material element and the immaterial element). Why is it said 'only seven persons'? Because for a noble disciple (ariyasāvaka) who has passed away from the fine-material element, there is no such thing as rebirth in the sensual element; it occurs only for a worldling (puthujjana). Therefore, it is stated specifically as 'only seven persons.' The same method applies to the phrase 'only seven persons who have passed away from the immaterial element and attained the sensual element.' When it is said that there is no rebirth in the fine-material element, why is there none? It is because of the absence of the fine-material sphere jhāna (rūpāvacarajjhāna) which brings about rebirth. For one born in that immaterial realm has attained that immaterial element by completely transcending all perceptions of form (rūpasaññā), and thus he does not possess fine-material sphere jhāna there. It should be understood that because of the absence of that jhāna, there is no rebirth in the fine-material element. In the phrase 'for one who has passed away from the immaterial element, not in the sensual element,' only the immaterial element is intended. In this manner, the meaning should be understood in all answers.

Among those two sections, in the section on setting forth the matrix, there are from the beginning three pure major sections (suddhika-mahāvāra): the section on persons (puggala-vāra), the section on phenomena (dhamma-vāra), and the section on persons and phenomena (puggala-dhamma-vāra).

Among them, the section that proceeds by showing the distinctions such as the arising and cessation of consciousness by way of persons, thus: 'For whom consciousness arises, it does not cease,' is called the Puggala-vāra. The section that proceeds by showing the distinctions such as the arising and cessation of consciousness only by way of phenomena, thus: 'Which consciousness arises, it does not cease,' is called the Dhamma-vāra. After that, by way of the 16 terms such as 'For whom the consciousness is with lust (sarāgaṃ cittaṃ),' there are 48 mixed sections (missaka-vāra), which are distinct from the pure major sections and are qualified by terms such as 'with lust'—namely, 16 Puggala-vāras, 16 Dhamma-vāras, and 16 Puggala-dhamma-vāras. These mixed sections are abbreviated by showing only the terms such as 'with lust.' Following those mixed sections, by way of the 266 Abhidhamma matrix terms (mātikā-pada) such as 'For whom the consciousness is wholesome (kusalaṃ cittaṃ),' there are 798 mixed sections qualified by other terms such as 'wholesome'—namely, 266 Puggala-vāras, 266 Dhamma-vāras, and 266 Puggala-dhamma-vāras. These mixed sections are also abbreviated by showing only the terms such as 'wholesome.' Among these terms like 'wholesome,' those terms such as 'with-proffering' (sanidassana) which do not associate with consciousness are set forth as void questions (mogha-pucchā).

Among those three sections—the pure major section, the mixed section of terms like 'with lust,' and the mixed section of terms like 'wholesome'—in the very first pure major section on persons (suddhika-puggala-mahāvāra), there are 14 internal sections (antara-vāra): the section on the combination of the time of arising and cessation, the section on arising and arisen, the section on cessation and arisen, the section on arising, the section on cessation, the section on arising and cessation, the section on what is arising and cessation, the section on what is arising and arisen, the section on what is ceasing and arisen, the section on arisen and arising, the section on the past and future, the section on arisen and what is arising, the section on what has ceased and what is ceasing, and the section on the past time. Among these 14 internal sections, in these three sections—the section on arising, the section on cessation, and the section on arising and cessation—there are 18 pairs (yamaka) by making 6 each by way of the direct (anuloma) and inverse (paṭiloma) methods. In the section on arisen and arising, there are 4 pairs—2 by way of the direct and 2 by way of the inverse—through the power of the past and future times. In the remaining 10 sections—the 3 sections mentioned at the beginning, the 3 sections mentioned immediately after, and the 4 sections mentioned at the end—there are 20 pairs by making 2 each, 1 by way of the direct and 1 by way of the inverse. Just as it is in the single pure major section on persons, so also in the pure major section on phenomena and the pure major section on persons and phenomena; in these 3 major sections, 126 pairs, twice as many questions, and twice as many meanings should be understood. When this group of three sections is multiplied by 16 by way of terms like 'with lust,' and multiplied by 266 by way of terms like 'wholesome,' there are many thousands of pairs in this Citta-yamaka, with twice as many questions and twice as many meanings. However, the Pāḷi text is abbreviated. In this way, first, the classification of the Pāḷi in this Citta-yamaka should be understood.

## Exposition
## 1. Commentary on the Section on Persons
Now, in order to explain the matrix (mātikā) according to the established order, the text begins with: "For whomsoever consciousness is arising but is not ceasing..." and so forth. In that statement, "is arising (uppajjati)" means it is arising because it is endowed with the arising moment (uppādakkhaṇa). "Is not ceasing (na nirujjhati)" means it is not ceasing because it has not yet reached the dissolution moment (bhangakkhaṇa). By the phrase "that person's consciousness (tassa cittaṃ)," it is asked whether that person's consciousness, starting from that arising moment, will cease or will not arise. "Their consciousness (tesaṃ cittaṃ)" refers to the final death consciousness (parinibbānacuti-citta) of the Arahants who have delimited the suffering of the round of rebirths, whose arising moment is occurring. That very death consciousness of those Arahants is said to be "arising" because it has reached the arising stage, but it "is not ceasing" because it has not yet reached the dissolution stage. Now, however, having reached dissolution, that consciousness of those Arahants will cease; thereafter, because there is no further rebirth-linking, another consciousness will not arise. "Of the others (itaraesaṃ)" means, excluding the Arahant endowed with the final consciousness, for the remaining trainees (sekha), non-trainees (asekha), and worldlings (puthujjana), their consciousness will both cease and arise. In this context, that consciousness which has reached the arising moment will certainly cease. Furthermore, another consciousness will both arise and cease, whether in that same existence or in another existence. In the answer to the second question as well, "Yes (āmantā)" is said with reference to the consciousness of an Arahant of such nature. "Is not arising, is ceasing (nuppajjati nirujjhati)" refers to the final consciousness of an Arahant at the dissolution moment, as well as the consciousness of others that is currently breaking up. From the dissolution moment of that final consciousness onwards, it can be said that the Arahant's consciousness will not cease, but it cannot be said that it will arise. For the others, it can be said that consciousness will arise, but it cannot be said that it will not cease. Therefore, the rejection "No (no)" is made. In the second problem, the person for whom it is said that consciousness will not cease but will arise does not even exist; therefore, the rejection "There is none (natthi)" is made.

65-82. "Arisen (uppannaṃ)" is the name for consciousness endowed with the arising moment and for that which, having reached the arising stage, has not yet ceased. Therein, "Yes (āmantā)" is said with reference to being endowed with the arising moment, and "their consciousness has arisen (tesaṃ cittaṃ uppannaṃ)" is said with reference to having reached the arising stage but not yet ceased. "Not arisen (anuppannaṃ)" refers to consciousness that has not yet reached the arising stage. In the phrase "their consciousness has arisen in the past (tesaṃ cittaṃ uppajjittha)," the consciousness of all beings is said to have arisen in the past because it was a momentary present and the arising moment has passed. For those who have entered the attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti), it is said to have arisen in the past because it arose before the attainment of cessation; for the non-percipient beings (asaññasatta), it is said to have arisen in the past because it arose in a percipient existence. "It has both arisen in the past and is currently arising (uppajjittha ceva uppajjati ca)" means it has arisen in the past because it reached the arising stage, and it is currently arising because that arising moment has not yet passed.

"In the arising moment and the future consciousness (uppādakkhaṇe anāgatañca)" means the consciousness in the arising moment and the future consciousness.

In the Section on Transcended Time (Atikkantakālavāra), "the moment of arising (uppajjamānaṃ khaṇaṃ)" refers to the arising moment (uppādakkhaṇa). Therein, although the arising moment is not strictly "currently arising," it is spoken of in this way because it is the moment of that which is arising.
334:
It is spoken of in this way. "Having transcended the moment, it is called transcended time (atikkantakāla)" does not mean it passed a long time ago, but rather it is designated as transcended time because that very arising moment (the moment of arising) has passed. "The moment of ceasing (nirujjhamānaṃ khaṇaṃ)" refers to the moment of cessation (nirodhakkhaṇa). Therein, although the moment of cessation is not strictly "currently ceasing," it is spoken of in this way because it is the moment of that which is ceasing. When it is said "having transcended the moment, it is called transcended time," it is a question of whether that person's consciousness has also transcended the moment of cessation and is thus called transcended time. In that question, because the consciousness at the dissolution moment (bhangakkhaṇa) has transcended the arising moment, it is called transcended time; however, it has not transcended the moment of cessation (the dissolution moment), so it is not called transcended time. Past consciousness, however, has transcended both moments and is thus called transcended time. Therefore, the answer is given: "At the dissolution moment, consciousness has transcended the arising moment but has not transcended the dissolution moment; past consciousness has transcended both the arising moment and the dissolution moment."

In the answer to the second question, "past consciousness" is mentioned because past consciousness has transcended both moments and is thus called transcended time. In the answer to the inverse question, the consciousness at the arising moment and the future consciousness are not called transcended time because they have not transcended both moments, as those moments have not yet been transcended. Therefore, it is said: "consciousness at the arising moment and future consciousness." The second answer is quite clear.

84-113. In the Section on States (Dhammavāra) as well, the meaning of all answers should be understood by this same method. The Section on Persons and States (Puggaladhammavāra) follows the same course as the Section on States.

114-116. All the Mixed Sections (Missakavāra) are also summarized by showing only the opening, such as "For whomsoever consciousness with lust (sarāgaṃ cittaṃ)..." and so forth. Their detailed explanation should be understood according to the method mentioned below. In those sections, the question is similar because it should be expanded as: "For whomsoever consciousness with lust is arising but is not ceasing, will consciousness cease for that person but not arise?" However, because a consciousness with lust is never the final consciousness (paccimacitta), the answer is different, as it must be answered: "No (no)" to the question "For whomsoever consciousness with lust is arising but is not ceasing, will consciousness cease for that person but not arise?" This difference should be understood according to the suitability of each respective question.
