## 10. Indriyayamaka

Now, following the explanation of the Dhamma Yamaka, there is the commentary on the Indriya Yamaka, which is taught after the Dhamma Yamaka by encompassing a portion of those states such as the wholesome (kusala) and so forth, as taught in the Mūla Yamaka, according to what is obtainable. In this Indriya Yamaka, the determination of the Pali text should be understood in the same manner as stated in the Khandha Yamaka and others. Indeed, in this Indriya Yamaka, the three Great Sections (Mahāvāra) such as the Section on Designation (Paṇṇattivāra), as well as the remaining Intermediate Sections (Antaravāra) along with the divisions of time and so forth, are just similar to those appearing in the Khandha Yamaka and others. The distinction, however, is that due to the plurality of the faculties (indriya), there are even more pairs (yamaka) than in the Dhātu Yamaka.

Just as in the Section on Persons (Puggalavāra) and others mentioned below, in the methods based on the eye-base (cakkhāyatana-mūla) and the eye-element (cakkhudhātu-mūla), the tongue-base (jivhāyatana) and body-base (kāyāyatana) were not paired with the eye-base and eye-element, and the pairs based on the tongue-base and body-base were not taken at all; likewise, in this Indriya Yamaka, in the method based on the eye-faculty (cakkhundriya-mūla), the tongue-faculty (jivhindriya) and body-faculty (kāyindriya) are not paired, and the pairs based on the tongue-faculty and body-faculty are not taken. The reason for not taking these pairs should be understood in the same way as stated in that Āyatana Yamaka. As for the mind-faculty (manindriya), just as it is paired with those based on the eye-faculty and so forth, it also reaches a pairing with those based on the female-faculty (itthindriya) and so forth; therefore, it should be understood that it is not paired according to the order set in the matrix (mātikā), but is paired at the end with all faculties starting from the eye-faculty. The female-faculty, male-faculty (purisindriya), and life-faculty (jīvitindriya) are paired with the eye-faculty. The pleasure-faculty (sukhindriya), pain-faculty (dukkhindriya), and displeasure-faculty (domanassindriya) are not taken because they do not exist at the moment of rebirth (paṭisandhi). The joy-faculty (somanassindriya) and equanimity-faculty (upekkhindriya) are taken because of their evident existence at the moment of rebirth. Likewise, the five faculties starting with the faith-faculty (saddhindriya) are taken. The three supramundane (lokuttara) faculties are not taken precisely because of their absence at the moment of rebirth. Thus, the counting of pairs in the method based on the eye-faculty in this Indriya Yamaka should be understood by way of those faculties that are taken. As it is in this eye-faculty method, so it is everywhere. However, the pairs should not be counted by way of those faculties that are not taken. Or, if one wishes to count them, they should be counted by way of void questions (mogha-puccha). Thus, first of all, the determination of the Pali text in all sections should be understood.

## Commentary on the Section on Occurrence (Pavattivāra-vaṇṇanā)

1-86. In the determination of the meaning here, this following statement is the opening of the method: The words "For those with eyes who are not women" are spoken by way of the Brahmas of the Retinue of Brahma (Brahmapārisajja) and so forth who possess form, as well as by way of males and neuter beings. Indeed, for those fine-material Brahmas and neuter beings, the female-faculty does not arise. The words "For those with eyes who are not men" are spoken by way of the Brahmas who possess form, as well as by way of females and neuter beings. Indeed, for those fine-material Brahmas, females, and neuter beings, the male-faculty does not arise. The words "For those being reborn without eyes, the life-faculty arises for them" are spoken with reference to beings in the one-constituent (ekavokāra) realm, the four-constituent (catuvokāra) realm, and those in the sense-sphere (kāmadhātu) who lack eyes. The words "For those with eyes without joy (somanassa)" are spoken by way of the four Great Resultant rebirths accompanied by equanimity...
338:
are spoken by way of the four Great Resultant rebirths accompanied by equanimity. "For those with eyes without equanimity" is spoken by way of beings whose rebirth is accompanied by joy. "For those with equanimity without eyes" is spoken by way of rootless (ahetuka) rebirth. "For rootless individuals" is spoken because of the absence of the faith-faculty (saddhindriya) and so forth along with the rootless rebirth-consciousness. For in that rootless rebirth-consciousness, faith (saddhā), mindfulness (sati), and wisdom (paññā) are definitely absent. Concentration (samādhi) and energy (vīriya), however, do not reach the status of faculties (indriya). "For those with roots (sahetuka) without eyes" is spoken in connection with womb-born (gabbhaseyyaka) individuals and immaterial (arūpī) Brahmas. This is because there are no other rooted individuals without eyes besides the womb-born and immaterial Brahmas. "For those with eyes who are rootless" is spoken in connection with individuals who have spontaneous rebirth (opapātika) in the woeful states (apāya). "For those with eyes dissociated from knowledge" is spoken by way of individuals with double-rooted (duhetuka) rebirth in the sense-sphere. "For those with eyes associated with knowledge" is spoken with reference to Brahmas with form and sense-sphere devas and humans. "For those associated with knowledge without eyes" is spoken with reference to immaterial Brahmas and triple-rooted (tihetuka) womb-born individuals.

In the pairs based on the life-faculty (jīvitindriya-mūlaka), "For those being reborn without joy" is spoken with reference to both types of life-faculties (physical and mental). "At the arising moment of consciousness dissociated from joy during the course of existence (pavatti)" is spoken with reference to the mental life-faculty. By this method, the connection of the life-faculty should be understood in all places by way of rebirth and the course of existence. In the pairs based on the joy-faculty and so forth, the meaning should also be taken only by way of rebirth and the course of existence. In the reverse method (paṭiloma-naya) and in the section on cessation (nirodhavāra), the non-arising and cessation of these and other states should be understood in all three times: death (cuti), rebirth (paṭisandhi), and the course of existence (pavatti), according to what is obtainable.

In the Section on the Future (Anāgatavāra), "by this state only" means by this male state only, without becoming female in the interval, and only by taking rebirth as a male. "Having shown some existences, they will attain Parinibbāna" means that after taking some rebirths and without reaching the female state, they will attain Parinibbāna. In the second question also, this is the same method.

In the Section on the Present and Past (Paccuppannātītavāra), regarding the dissolution moment (bhaṅgakkhaṇa) of the rebirth-consciousness of the Suddhāvāsa Brahmas, the phrase "the mind-faculty (manindriya) has also not arisen before" should be understood not by way of passing the arising moment as in the Citta Yamaka, but by way of it never having arisen before in that existence. By this opening of the method, the determination of the meaning in the entire Section on Occurrence (Pavattivāra) should be understood.

## Commentary on the Section on Full Understanding

435-482. In the Section on Full Understanding (Pariññāvāra), among the pairs (yamaka) having the eye faculty as the root, only one pair—the eye as the root and the ear as the object—is shown. Although only this one pair is shown, the remaining mundane indeterminate (lokiya-abyākata) faculties and those mixed with mundane indeterminates are also to be fully understood (pariññeyya). Therefore, even if they are not directly shown, they are indeed shown by means of this eye-ear pair. Because the unwholesome (akusala) must certainly be abandoned, the wholesome (kusala) must certainly be developed within oneself, and the supramundane indeterminate (lokuttara-abyākata) must be realized, it is said: 'He abandons the faculty of grief (domanassindriya),' 'He develops the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (anaññātaññassāmītindriya),' and 'He realizes the faculty of one who has known (aññātāvindriya).'

Regarding the faculty of final knowledge (aññindriya), there is an aspect to be developed and an aspect to be realized; it is taken here only by way of the aspect of development.

In the passage (starting with 'develops the faculty of final knowledge'), 'two persons' refers to the person possessed of the path of Once-returning (sakadāgāmimaggasamaṅgī) and the person possessed of the path of Arahantship (arahattamaggasamaṅgī). Among these two, one (the Once-returner) is said not to be abandoning the faculty of grief because he is unable to cut it off completely. The other (the Arahant) is said not to be abandoning it because he has already abandoned hatred. In the passage 'He does not fully understand the eye faculty,' it means he is not currently fully understanding it because he is unable to bring about its non-arising. In this way, the meaning should be understood in all answers.

Standing in the instruction of that Blessed One, who has completed his task of the sixteen-fold path, even a group of young women, having well-established discipline, can transcend the authority of Yama.
In the midst of the assembly of devas in the city of devas, by that Supreme Deva of all devas, whose body hairs are pure and grow singly (not in pairs), the text named Yamaka was made known.
To show the method of defining the Pali text and the system of meaning in the questions and answers of that Yamaka, I have undertaken this Yamaka Commentary.
